ai_summary: CAISO is transitioning from Schedule Point (SP-Tie) to Generation Aggregation Point (GAP-Tie) modeling for intertie schedules. Under GAP-Tie, intertie schedules are modeled as sourcing from the aggregate generation in the adjacent balancing area rather than from a fictional generator at the intertie; this is expected to improve accuracy of day-ahead market results, congestion management, and price formation by better aligning day-ahead with real-time flows. The document also addresses Resource Adequacy import processes under the new design and introduces a second topic: phasing out intertie scheduling at EDAM internal interties between CAISO and other EDAM balancing areas, permitted only for RA and RPS contracts sourced outside the EDAM area or unknown. Informal stakeholder comments on today's workshop are requested by September 8, and a comparative LMP analysis under both modeling designs will be posted within two weeks; the next workshop will focus on EDAM internal interties.

ai_summary: CAISO is implementing three NERC reliability standards for Inverter-Based Resources with a compliance deadline of October 1, 2026. PRC-028-1 establishes disturbance monitoring and reporting requirements (event triggers, data sampling rates of 64 samples per cycle minimum, GPS time synchronization, and 15-day data response with 20-day retention). PRC-029-1 revises ride-through requirements for frequency and voltage excursions during grid disturbances (requires units to remain online for faults lasting up to 150 milliseconds under CAISO's Large Generator Interconnection Agreement). PRC-030-1 addresses mitigation of unexpected IBR power output changes and does not apply during the New Resource Integration (NRI) approval phase. CAISO's NRI process reconciles conflicting requirements between PRC standards and its existing interconnection agreements (LGIA/SGIA), applying the more stringent requirement when conflicts arise (e.g., requiring 1 millisecond UTC synchronization per LGIA rather than the 100 millisecond PRC-028-1 allows, and requiring prescriptive 10 millisecond inverter data logging per LGIA). A New Resource Implementation Forum is scheduled for October 7, 2026, to review current processes and highlight upcoming changes.

ai_summary: CAISO's Large Loads Straw Proposal (August 12, 2026) responds to FERC's June 18, 2026 Order to Show Cause by proposing tariff enhancements for transmission service and interconnection of large loads (defined as ≥50 MW at a single site). Key proposals include: (1) clarified application and study procedures with 60–90 day study timelines for large load interconnection studies; (2) new flexible interconnection service offerings—Flexible Interim Load Interconnection (FILI) for temporary flexibility during network upgrades and Flexible Load Interconnection–Permanent (FLIP) to avoid permanent upgrade costs; (3) rules for co-located large loads and behind-the-meter generation that align load and generator interconnection studies; (4) operational requirements including control technologies and protection systems for flexible loads; (5) data transparency and coordination with Participating Transmission Owners (PTOs) on cost allocation. CAISO declines to create separate transmission-service classes but proposes customized flexible interconnection configurations. The CAISO Board is scheduled to vote on October 28, 2026, with a draft final proposal expected September 21, 2026, and stakeholder comments due October 12, 2026.
hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydro or pumped storage. However, the framework directly affects storage operators' strategic options: flexible interconnection services (FILI and FLIP) and co-location rules now extending to generating facilities serving large loads create precedent for how storage (including PSH) may participate in serving behind-the-meter or co-located loads with operational flexibility constraints. The proposed 60–90 day study timeline and customized protection-scheme requirements for flexible resources set operational and study-process benchmarks that would apply to any resource offering ramping or temporal flexibility, including storage. Large load growth forecasts (1.8 GW by 2030, 4.7 GW by 2035) drive scarcity and congestion where hydro's energy-and-flexibility value would compound.

ai_summary: CAISO and SPP held the second workshop in a series on Western market seams (WECC, Salt Lake City, August 18, 2026), focusing on transmission constraint management and congestion resolution across market boundaries. Transmission operators and market staff from PGE, PacifiCorp, PNM, SPP, and CAISO presented frameworks for identifying and mitigating transmission constraints through seasonal studies, outage coordination, and day-ahead and real-time market tools. PNM described how WEIM market-based tools enable economic, real-time congestion management superior to manual curtailment, and advocated for advancing congestion coordination beyond tag-based curtailment toward automated dispatch signals. Seams coordination challenges identified include outage-conflict ownership, visibility of dynamic rating limits, and contingency activation alignment across market boundaries. The joint CAISO–SPP report on Western seams coordination is due to FERC on September 30, 2026, and the third workshop is scheduled for September 16, 2026, in Denver, Colorado; written comments on the August 18 workshop are due by end of day September 1, 2026.

However, transmission constraints and congestion management directly shape how variable and dispatchable resources—including conventional hydro and pumped-storage plants—are dispatched and curtailed across market seams. Hydro owners exporting across CAISO–SPP boundaries depend on real-time market coordination for economically efficient dispatch and reserve utilization; the workshop establishes that WEIM-style market tools are more cost-effective than manual curtailment or tag-based procedures, but full coordination across seams remains incomplete. The seams report due September 30 will likely influence how markets coordinate dispatch of all resources, including hydro, at intermarket interfaces in the West. Hydro operators in exporting balancing authorities like the Pacific Northwest should monitor whether automated dispatch signals and coordinated pricing frameworks extend to their resources at seams boundaries.

initiatives: Extended day-ahead market - congestion revenue allocation [Active]
ai_summary: CAISO presented Concept #3, a congestion-revenue allocation design for the Extended Day-Ahead Market (EDAM) that would allocate Day-Ahead congestion revenues to holders of Congestion Revenue Rights (CRRs) and eligible long-term firm OATT transmission rights based on their effectiveness on constraints, evaluated through a common Simultaneous Feasibility Test (SFT) across the EDAM footprint. Nominated CRRs and OATT rights (point-to-point and Network Integration Transmission Service) would be evaluated in annual and monthly SFT processes using tiered allocation at 50%, 66.7%, and 100% load metrics, with curtailments applied via Weighted Least Squares methodology when nominations exceed transmission capacity. Real-time congestion revenues would remain allocated to the balancing area where the constraint is located. CAISO is conducting a simulated SFT in August/September 2026 to evaluate feasibility. Stakeholder comments are due by August 27, 2026, and the next working group meeting is scheduled for early September.
hydro_read_through: Hydro operators exporting power or holding long-term transmission rights in the West benefit directly from how congestion hedges are allocated in EDAM. The proposed SFT-based allocation ties congestion-revenue entitlements to the physical effectiveness of transmission sources and sinks across the interconnected footprint, which could improve the hedging value of those rights compared to less-integrated allocation schemes. However, the tiered-feasibility approach and pro-rata "haircutting" under WLS mean that in constrained months, allocations may be reduced below nomination levels; hydro owners relying on congestion-revenue streams to underpin project economics should monitor how the simulated SFT results affect the feasibility of rights they currently hold or plan to acquire.

ai_summary: CAISO's Resource Interconnection Standards (RIS) Fair presentation explains the Cluster 16 interconnection process for projects under Appendix KK, beginning with application window 10/1/2026–10/15/2026, with completeness review within 5 business days and opportunity for correction until 1700 PPT 10/15/2026. Applicants must submit deposits and fees at submission: Application Fee $5,000; Study Deposit (< 80 MW: $35,000 + $1,000/MW; 80–200 MW: $150,000; ≥200 MW: $250,000); Commercial Readiness Deposit (2× Study Deposit, due by end of customer engagement window); and for merchant projects, Merchant Option Deposit ($10,000/MW of deliverable capacity, minimum $500,000, maximum $5,000,000). Site control must cover 90% of acreage, with minimum acreage requirements by technology (Hydro: 10 acres/MW) and must extend through commercial operation date. Regulatory Limitation Site Control Deposit option ($10,000/MW, minimum $500,000, maximum $2,000,000) is available for projects on public or trust lands awaiting regulatory approval. Projects tied after cluster intake criteria review will proceed to auction ($/MW sealed bid via GRIP); auction winners must post auction deposit by end of customer engagement window. Cluster Study begins January 2027. The presentation also covers NDA requirements for transmission planning participation, POI-constraint mapping, and restricted POIs.
hydro_read_through: Hydropower and PSH owners in CAISO's queue must navigate substantially higher and more complex deposit requirements under RIS, with a $5,000 application fee, size-scaled study deposits up to $250,000, a Commercial Readiness Deposit equal to 2× the study deposit, and conditional Merchant Option or Regulatory Limitation deposits—all due at submission or by defined milestones—raising the cost of entry and liquidity required to compete in Cluster 16. The 10 acres/MW minimum site-control requirement for hydro is more stringent than most competing technologies (solar 6 acres/MW, wind 30 acres/MW, BESS 0.06 acres/MW), creating a specific land-siting challenge for conventional run-of-river plants and requiring clear documentation of long-term lease or ownership through COD. The auction mechanism for tied projects and the auction-deposit structure add execution risk: if a project ties on intake criteria, it must submit a competitive bid by a fixed deadline or withdraw, with the winning bid amount then determining the deposit owed to the PTO—a feature that could amplify capital requirements for speculative or flexible projects.

ai_summary: CAISO held a training session on July 7, 2026, introducing Scheduling Coordinators (SCs) participating in the Western Energy Imbalance Market (WEIM) and Extended Day-Ahead Market (EDAM) to inter-SC trade functionality for energy. Inter-SC trades are optional settlement services that allow two SCs to reconcile bilateral-procurement arrangements and "flip the money" to reverse double-settlement exposures, without affecting dispatch or scheduling of resources. The training covers three types of energy trades: Physical trades (PHY) backed by a generating unit, allowing submission seven days prior through 11:00 hours the day before; Aggregated Pricing Node trades (APN) at trading hubs or default load-aggregation points; and Converted Physical trades (CPT), where a PHY that exceeds the day-ahead schedule of its resource becomes a hub-based trade. Day-ahead trades are settled hourly at the resource pnode/apnode locational margin prices (Charge Code 6301); real-time trades are settled at the average of four fifteen-minute-market interval LMPs (Charge Code 6371). SCs must submit matching trades in the SIBR (Scheduling Infrastructure & Business Rules) application and continue to submit energy bids in the day-ahead and real-time markets per standard rules. A market simulation with structured scenarios is scheduled for July 20–August 1, 2026, with connectivity testing July 6–19, 2026.
hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower, pumped storage, or run-of-river resources directly. However, inter-SC trades are a core settlement mechanism for dispatchable resources—including large conventional hydro and pumped-storage plants—that sell into bilateral contracts while also participating in WEIM/EDAM market-clearing. Hydro operators typically hold SC certification and use trades to manage the divergence between their contracted supply price and the nodal LMP at their resource location, a critical lever for revenue alignment across multi-zone markets. The expansion of this functionality from California ISO to WEIM and EDAM participants directly affects how hydro SCs in new member zones (PacifiCorp, Idaho Power, Puget Sound Energy, etc.) will reconcile bilateral sales with market settlement; getting the operational procedures right in simulation before the August activation date is essential to avoid settlement disputes and cash-flow mismatches on existing contracts.

ai_summary: CPUC Energy Division staff submitted comments on CAISO's Monthly Extended Day-Ahead Market (EDAM) June Performance Report presented at the Market Performance and Planning Forum Q3 on July 30, 2026 (submission deadline August 13, 2026). The comments raise eight specific questions: (1) consistency in supply-stack reporting for dedicated out-of-state resources like Palo Verde and Hoover alongside wind imports; (2) justification for RUC (Reliability Capacity Up) load adjustments of 592.50 MW on June 11 for alleged IRU (Imbalance Reserve Up) deficiencies when ED staff's analysis shows CAISO had 142.60 MW excess IRU; (3) similar RUC adjustments on August 4 of approximately 3,590 MW when the 90 percent uncertainty requirement appears fully resourced; (4) location of the 97.5 percent uncertainty level data in OASIS and how to use it; (5) request for counterfactual market results comparing CAISO day-ahead outcomes with EDAM day-ahead outcomes; (6) transparency on hourly virtual supply/demand and net virtual supply determination from OASIS; (7) explanation of why real-time IRU availability is only 80 percent; (8) cost-attribution methodology for RCU procurement and whether it can be distinguished by cause (underbid load vs. net virtual supply) in monthly reports; and (9) request for consistent color coding across presentation slides for BAA comparison.
hydro_read_through: This document does not name hydro or storage resources. However, CPUC staff's concerns about RUC load adjustments, IRU procurement transparency, and the relationship between load forecasting and reserve requirements directly touch the mechanisms that set real-time scarcity conditions and the prices hydro receives for flexibility and reserve provision. If CAISO's load-adjustment procedures (OP 1210) are being applied inconsistently or without clear justification — as ED staff questions on June 11 and August 4 — the resulting reserve procurements and locational scarcity signals would be distorted, altering both the reserve and energy revenues available to flexible resources. The request for virtual-supply and net-virtual transparency is similarly relevant: virtual bidding and net virtual position drive scarcity signals and co-optimize with generation dispatch, so opaque virtual reporting masks the true demand-elasticity signals that hydro and other dispatchable resources respond to. CAISO's IRU availability shortfall (80 percent in real-time) and the methodological questions around whether RCU is procurement-driven by load-forecast misses or by unscheduled virtual demand directly affect how much reserve headroom CAISO must maintain and thus the scarcity rents available to reserve suppliers.

ai_summary: The California Public Utilities Commission Energy Division presented findings from the SB 1174 (2025 Transmission System Assessment) requirement to report on changes to in-service dates of transmission and interconnection facilities needed to serve eligible renewable energy and energy storage resources. Analysis identified approximately 40.5 GW of new generation and storage resources with signed interconnection agreements in PG&E and SCE service territories; approximately 8.9 GW (~22%) are expected to be delayed due to transmission delays, with an additional 4.4 GW (~11%) at risk. PG&E's key delays stem from bundling dependencies (2.5 GW) and financing/design delays; SCE's from materials procurement (4.5 GW delayed, 2 GW at risk), bundling dependencies (4.4 GW), and unknown customer-initiated causes (3.7 GW). The CPUC recommended that transmission owners allocate more planning time for realistic in-service-date estimates, engage in proactive long-lead-material procurement, improve permitting-timeline data collection, and work with CAISO and state agencies to develop consistent metrics for high-impact project identification. Next steps include highlighting key issues through the 2026 Transmission Development Forum and state agency workshops on accelerating interconnection.

ai_summary: CAISO management is filing tariff revisions in early 2026 to clarify EDAM (Extended Day-Ahead Market) and DAME (Day-Ahead Market Enhancements) implementation details ahead of the May 1, 2026 launch. Key changes include: (1) transitional intertie modeling at ISO balancing-area scheduling points will continue modeling injections at the scheduling point itself rather than aggregate generation locations, preserving existing commercial arrangements while CAISO works with stakeholders on future transitions; (2) resource adequacy imports at EDAM transfer locations will be subject to new reassignment rules allowing unspecified system resources sourced from EDAM areas to bid capacity; (3) congestion-revenue-rights (CRR) funding from EDAM constraints will be clarified to zero dollars at EDAM start, with revenue instead allocated to EDAM balancing authorities; and (4) technical clarifications on imbalance-reserve charging, firm transmission service availability, and day-ahead contingency analysis tools for EDAM operators. The revisions received mixed stakeholder feedback during November–December 2025 workshops, with some stakeholders opposing intertie modeling and resource adequacy scheduling requirements; management's proposed revisions represent a compromise to preserve current ISO intertie practices on a transitional basis.
hydro_read_through: This document does not mention hydro or pumped-storage resources. However, EDAM's intertie modeling and resource-adequacy-import rules are directly material to how dispatchable external resources—including hydro-based system resources from neighboring balancing areas—can participate in CAISO's day-ahead market and reserve their transmission capacity to support day-ahead dispatch and RA import obligations. The transitional preservation of current ISO intertie modeling (rather than aggregation) protects existing commercial pathways for out-of-state system resources to compete in CAISO's market; any future shift to aggregation modeling could alter the locational granularity and congestion signals that external generation (hydro included) faces when bidding into California. Additionally, the CRR revenue treatment (allocating parallel-flow congestion to EDAM balancing authorities rather than the ISO) affects the overall congestion-cost landscape and uplift allocation that load-serving entities pass through or absorb, influencing the competitiveness of external versus internal resources.

The initiative modifies the reference-level change request process to allow more frequent use and adjusts cost thresholds for market participants whose gas hubs are more volatile than ISO calculated estimates. CAISO proposes providing additional flexibility during periods of significant forecast uncertainty (D+2→D+1 or D+1→real-time) to reflect costs of unexpected unit commitments, and creating after-the-fact cost recovery eligibility when physical supply disruptions occur after the adjustment deadline. The proposal also seeks expanded authority to use gas constraints as a reliability tool across the full ISO market footprint (currently limited to the southern part), and enhancement of the D+2 advisory market to better inform fuel procurement decisions. A 2018-approved commitment cost and default energy bid policy that was never implemented is being revisited for potential activation.
hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydro or PSH directly. However, the changes to default energy bid and reference-level adjustment processes are the same mechanisms used to govern offer behavior and cost recovery for all use-limited resources in the ISO and EDAM. Hydro and PSH operators use these same reference-level and default energy bid tools to reflect operational costs and scarcity conditions; any liberalization of cost thresholds, frequency of adjustment requests, or after-the-fact recovery eligibility would apply to them as well. Additionally, the expansion of these tools to full EDAM participation and the relaxation of cost-recovery eligibility rules during supply disruptions could improve revenue flexibility for hydro and PSH in stressed conditions, though the proposal's primary focus on gas procurement volatility means the specific mechanics may not be optimized for hydro seasonal or hydrologic variability.

ai_summary: CAISO staff briefing on the Spotlight Initiative—Price Formation Enhancements, presented to the WEM Governing Body on October 28, 2025. The briefing explains two foundational mechanisms: (1) BAA-level Market Power Mitigation (MPM), which detects and mitigates uncompetitive pricing when a balancing authority area becomes import-constrained and depends on a small number of suppliers; and (2) Scarcity Pricing, which allows prices to reflect the reliability value of reserves when available capacity is tight. The straw proposal discussed includes three BAA-level MPM changes: shift to a grouping approach testing connected BAAs together, include CAISO BAA in the test, and mitigate only pivotal suppliers to avoid unnecessary mitigation of fringe participants. For scarcity pricing, proposed changes include preserving scarcity signals to reflect opportunity cost of capacity from contingency reserves in the 5-minute market, triggering scarcity pricing for load-shedding events, and developing a comprehensive scarcity pricing design through stakeholder working groups. The briefing notes that CAISO will bring formal policy proposals to the WEM Governing Body and ISO Board of Governors for consideration in 2026.
hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage. However, the price-formation mechanisms described directly shape how hydro's energy sales are valued in scarcity conditions and how its bids are treated under market power rules. Scarcity pricing's focus on opportunity cost of capacity and use of contingency reserves is particularly material for run-of-river and storage-constrained hydro, which face chronically imperfect pricing of their flexibility value; changes to how CAISO reflects reserve scarcity could significantly alter the energy prices hydro receives during tight conditions. BAA-level MPM changes that shift from individual-supplier tests to grouping approaches and pivot-supplier logic may reduce unnecessary mitigation of hydro bids in constrained zones, but the document does not specify how the revised framework treats use-limited resources or whether it alters the opportunity-cost reference-price methodology that has historically undervalued hydro's strategic value.

ai_summary: Vitol presented to CAISO's Price Formation Enhancements initiative on October 28, 2025, advocating for implementation of an enhanced operating reserve demand curve (ORDC) in both real-time and day-ahead markets. The proposal calls for scarcity pricing to reflect the reliability value of reserves using a Loss of Load Probability multiplied by Value of Lost Load (LOLP×VOLL) framework before reserve shortages occur, rather than only during load-shed events. Key design elements outlined include scarcity detection methodology (one-hour-ahead LOLP measurement), VOLL valuation based on customer data segmented by load class and outage duration, minimum contingency reserve thresholds, and reserve types to be included in the requirement. Vitol supports CAISO's initial proposal to ensure energy prices reflect shortage costs during involuntary load-shed events but argues that an enhanced ORDC would improve price signals ahead of shortages, enabling supply and demand response before constraints tighten.
hydro_read_through: The document does not name hydro or PSH, but it directly affects how dispatchable resources including conventional hydro are compensated for energy and reserve provision during tight system conditions. Enhanced scarcity pricing through LOLP×VOLL would raise energy prices more gradually and predictably as reserves tighten, creating higher and earlier price signals that reward hydro's ability to ramp quickly and sustain output. This contrasts with CAISO's current design where prices spike sharply only during declared emergencies; a continuous ORDC would increase hydro's revenue in the 10–100 hour window before physical shortages occur—precisely where hydro's marginal value is highest. The outcome depends on CAISO's adoption of this proposal and the VOLL magnitude it chooses; understating VOLL would limit the benefit.

ai_summary: CAISO's Demand and Distributed Energy Market Integration (DDEMI) initiative proposes to allow behind-the-meter exports from authorized end-use customers within a demand response aggregation to count toward measured load curtailment, provided the aggregation does not net export. Currently, individual customers net exporting (e.g., solar + battery) have their load "zeroed out" in performance calculations; the proposal would instead apply a floor at the aggregation level, capping credited demand response energy at the baseline value. The initiative also commits to convene a working group to explore real-time bidding constructs for flexible load and pumped-storage resources. Track 1 stakeholder engagement included meetings on March 13, June 18, and July 9, 2026, with 101–111 attendees and 15–23 comments per session.
hydro_read_through: Although the document does not name hydropower or PSH, the real-time bidding working group for "pumped-storage resources" (explicitly mentioned on page 2) is directly relevant to PSH owners' participation options in CAISO markets. The aggregation rule change for demand response with behind-the-meter storage may alter how quickly and how much distributed storage can displace or complement utility-scale flexibility, affecting price signals and dispatch patterns that hydro and PSH operators face. The framework for net-export treatment at the aggregation level also establishes a template that could influence how future distributed-storage or hybrid rules treat exports—setting precedent for how energy exports from any co-located generation or storage facility are modeled and compensated.

evidence.quote: Lastly, there are several unaddressed issues that the ISO has stated will need to be revisited in the context of default values and modeling process. These include the seasonality of default values, unforced capacity, and the interaction of interdependent policies such as outage substitution, the resource adequacy availability incentive mechanism, and capacity procurement mechanism.

stakeholders: Eric Hildebrandt (California Independent System Operator (CAISO), Department of Market Monitoring)
ai_summary: The California ISO Department of Market Monitoring (DMM) submitted comments supporting two proposals (Track 1 and Track 3A) from ISO Management on resource adequacy modeling and program design. Track 1 proposes updating default methodologies for planning reserve margin and qualifying capacity to meet a 0.1 LOLE (one loss-of-load event every 10 years) standard; DMM supports this and the inclusion of a resource-specific unforced capacity framework for some resource types, including a methodology for storage resources that includes a measure of energy sufficiency. DMM notes that the Track 1 proposal defers net-qualifying-capacity finalization to the California Public Utilities Commission and cautions that capacity accounting differences across local regulatory authorities could incentivize additional capacity sales. Track 3A proposes informational enhancements to improve ISO visibility into available capacity for procurement through the capacity procurement mechanism; DMM supports this as a reliability tool to facilitate bilateral procurement when competitive solicitation is unavailable. DMM recommends the ISO address seasonality of default values, unforced capacity, and interactions with outage substitution, resource-adequacy availability incentive mechanism, and capacity procurement mechanism as parallel policy processes conclude.
hydro_read_through: The document does not name hydropower or pumped storage directly. However, the DMM comments address resource-adequacy accreditation methodology and qualifying-capacity rules that apply to all dispatchable resources, including conventional and pumped-storage hydro. The energy-sufficiency measure for storage resources is particularly significant: it recognizes that storage value depends on both power capacity and energy availability, a distinction central to hydro operations and central to how correctly accounting for PSH—which faces binding state-of-charge constraints—differs from energy-unlimited resources. The unforced-capacity framework and default qualifying-capacity rules also govern how hydro's seasonal and intermittent contributions are accredited for system reliability, directly affecting seasonal and annual capacity revenue. DMM's caution about cross-jurisdictional capacity-accounting arbitrage (note 3) suggests default values may create incentives to source capacity from areas with favorable qualifying-capacity treatment, a concern hydro operators should monitor as the default framework is finalized.

ai_summary: CAISO approved expansion of its authority to model loop flow (unscheduled flow) in the annual CRR process to improve alignment between CRR and day-ahead market modeling, reduce CRR revenue inadequacy, and strengthen CRRs as hedging instruments. The ISO's February 2025 root-cause analysis identified loop flows as a significant structural driver of revenue inadequacy; the proposal adds loop-flow adjustments to the annual CRR capacity calculation, mirroring authority already present in the monthly CRR process. Implementation will use existing modeling capabilities and configurable transmission constraints; targeted manual adjustments will begin in the 2027 annual CRR process (starting July 2027). The ISO received 74 sets of written comments between January and June 2026 and will proceed to Phase 2 evaluation of auction efficiency and product definition in Q3 2026.
hydro_read_through: The document does not name hydropower or pumped storage directly, but CRRs are the primary transmission-hedging product available to hydro owners in CAISO, and improving their revenue adequacy and modeling accuracy directly affects locational revenues and the reliability of congestion-price signals that guide dispatch and long-term resource decisions for transmission-constrained plants. Better modeling of loop flows should reduce the frequency and magnitude of CRR funding shortfalls that currently leave hedges underfunded relative to their notional value.

ai_summary: CAISO management proposes to expand the ISO's authority to model loop flows in the annual congestion revenue rights (CRR) process, effective for the 2027 annual CRR process. The proposal addresses revenue inadequacy in the CRR market by improving the accuracy of the CRR model to better align with power flows observed in the day-ahead market. A root-cause analysis identified three sources of CRR revenue inadequacy: missing power flow contributions from injections below the 2% shift factor threshold, loop flows consuming transmission capacity without contributing to congestion rent collection, and divergence between the CRR network model and the day-ahead market. Stakeholders expressed support for the proposed expansion of ISO authority, though they requested additional detail on the loop flow modeling approach to be provided through the annual CRR process. Phase 2 will continue discussions on auction efficiency, product definition, and additional revenue adequacy measures in Q3 2026.
hydro_read_through: The document never mentions hydro specifically. However, CRRs are a primary financial hedge for generators—including hydro—that are exposed to transmission congestion costs, particularly in the California grid's constrained zones. Improving the accuracy of CRR modeling by capturing loop flows and correcting for missing power-flow contributions would reduce "revenue inadequacy" (the shortfall between modeled and actual congestion rents), directly increasing the value of CRR auctions to holders. Hydro generators with exposure to constrained interfaces would see improved hedging effectiveness and more accurate price signals if the model more closely tracks real power flows.

ai_summary: CAISO proposes a tariff amendment to establish a cost-recovery mechanism for Regional Organization for Western Energy (ROWE) start-up debt financing. The ROWE is a new independent entity that will assume governance responsibilities over regional energy markets operated by CAISO, with the goal of promoting broader participation in WEIM and EDAM and reducing electricity costs. Start-up costs are projected at $7–8 million, to be incurred from early 2026 through early 2028. The ISO would guarantee a commercial loan or line of credit not to exceed $8.5 million, with repayment scheduled to begin and end during 2028. The cost-recovery mechanism establishes two new settlement charges—a market services charge and a real-time dispatch charge—modeled on existing Grid Management Charge components, allocating 68% to market services and 32% to real-time dispatch. Based on 2026 forecasted volumes, combined charges would be less than 2 cents per MWh. The charges will be collected like other settlement charges and adjusted monthly beginning February 1, 2028. California utilities (PG&E, SDG&E, SCE, and Six Cities) and the CPUC Energy Division expressed concern that the day-ahead/real-time combined allocation could disproportionately affect California ratepayers and create inequitable outcomes for WEIM-only participants; Management rejected this position. The Western Energy Markets Governing Body is asked to approve the tariff amendment, and the ISO Board of Governors will consider it on its consent agenda at the April 30, 2026 meeting.
hydro_read_through: Although the document does not name hydropower or pumped-storage facilities, conventional hydro operators in the Western Interconnection—particularly those in CAISO, WEIM, and EDAM—will face direct settlement impacts from this mechanism. The new ROWE charges will be allocated to all market participants based on their day-ahead and real-time market volumes, meaning every MWh of hydro generation and ancillary-service supply in the Western markets will carry a proportional portion of ROWE start-up debt service. For hydro owners, this is structurally a fixed cost per unit energy output (less than 2 cents per MWh) over the 2028 repayment window, reducing effective energy revenue and raising their all-in operational costs in those markets. The allocation methodology—blending day-ahead and real-time volumes—means hydro's contribution is weighted by its participation in both timeframes, a departure from pure real-time-only cost allocation that some participants opposed on equity grounds.

ai_summary: The CAISO Department of Market Monitoring (DMM) supports Management's proposed enhancements to gas-resource cost recovery and bidding flexibility in CAISO, WEIM, and the upcoming extended day-ahead market (EDAM). The package includes: (1) more flexible options for determining gas cost inputs in energy bid mitigation and commitment-cost bids; (2) expanded after-the-fact cost recovery for physical supply disruptions occurring after the 8 a.m. day-ahead bidding deadline; (3) changes to two-day-ahead advisory market runs to improve fuel-procurement forecasts; and (4) gas nomograms to manage system limitations. DMM supports these changes but notes their effectiveness will depend on implementation details and recommends the ISO perform additional analysis as it implements them. DMM also supports proactive increases to reasonableness thresholds when forecasted gas demand rises significantly and recommends extending the 8 a.m. deadline for real-time reference-level change requests. The memo notes the Market Surveillance Committee's concern that EDAM scheduling may expose gas resources to unanticipated exports and higher gas-price volatility, and encourages implementation of dynamic market-power mitigation for commitment-cost bids, a feature under development since 2009.
hydro_read_through: This document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage directly. However, it addresses market-power mitigation design and cost-recovery mechanisms for use-limited resources facing supply constraints and uncertain scheduling—the exact problem domain in which conventional hydro and PSH operate. The reference-level-change-request process, default multipliers (125% for commitment costs, 110% for energy), and reasonableness thresholds that DMM discusses are the same mitigation frameworks applied to hydro. The EDAM expansion flagged here as creating scheduling and cost-recovery challenges for gas resources—where resources may be scheduled to support export without prior gas procurement—establishes a precedent for how multi-day-ahead market expansion affects dispatch uncertainty and cost management for all use-limited resources. If the ISO implements customizable multipliers and expanded after-the-fact cost recovery for gas, similar provisions would become available to hydro; conversely, if gas carve-outs are created in EDAM pricing or mitigation that do not extend to hydro, hydro owners would face a competitive disadvantage in the same market.

ai_summary: The Market Surveillance Committee of CAISO issued a final opinion in December 2025 on the Gas Resource Management (GRM) proposal, examining how CAISO's mitigation of commitment-cost and energy-offer caps affects gas-fired resource participation in EDAM (Extended Day-Ahead Market), which launches in 2026. The opinion identifies four core challenges: enabling EDAM participants to reflect current gas costs in offer prices given morning-market gas purchasing deadlines, providing after-the-fact cost recovery when afternoon gas markets force higher purchases, improving day-ahead schedule forecasts (D+2) to inform morning gas procurements, and preventing locational market power abuse. The MSC finds that existing Reference Level Change Request (RLCR) processes are underused by Western EIM entities due to tight 8 a.m. submission deadlines, complex SIBR interface requirements, and poor approval rates (only 8 of 72 manual requests approved since 2021); supports proposed improvements to RLCR and after-the-fact recovery mechanisms as long as implementation costs remain low; but expresses deep concern that absent a market-power test for commitment-cost caps, all gas units continue receiving blanket mitigation regardless of market position, creating both inefficient suppression of competitive offers and potential over-generous bounds for units with genuine market power. On D+2 forecasts, the MSC concludes that historical data show considerable day-to-day error in CAISO's forecasts, and questions whether the CAISO will achieve sufficient accuracy at the individual balancing-area level before EDAM go-live to support morning-market gas purchasing decisions, particularly on days with volatile gas prices or when supporting EDAM exports. The opinion recommends treating D+2 forecasts as unreliable at launch and ensuring EDAM participants retain offer-price flexibility to manage gas-market risk; highlights that cost-recovery allocations would shift unrecovered afternoon-market gas losses onto balancing-area load rather than the exporting resource; and calls for developing a workable market-power test for commitment costs as a high priority.
hydro_read_through: This document does not address hydropower or pumped-storage hydro directly. However, it examines the foundational market-power mitigation and cost-recovery frameworks that govern how use-limited resources are constrained in offer formation and whether their actual costs can be recovered when system schedules exceed prior expectations—the same category of rules that shape pumped-storage participation and accreditation in CAISO and EDAM. The MSC's core finding—that blanket commitment-cost caps applied without a market-power test simultaneously suppress competitive offers from resources lacking market power while potentially tolerating inflated offers from those with power—has immediate relevance to how storage resources accreditation, dispatch incentives, and cost recovery would be designed under parallel EDAM frameworks. The opinion also surfaces the tension between requiring resources to forecast operating costs far in advance (8 a.m. for day-ahead market) and the market's inability to reliably forecast dispatch schedules and prices days ahead—a problem that applies equally to any dispatchable resource, including storage, attempting to manage its state-of-charge and charging cost in a co-optimized day-ahead-plus-real-time market design.

ai_summary: CAISO's Board approved interconnection process enhancements (IPE 5.0) effective April 22, 2026, reforming the interconnection request intake process, deliverability allocation, and queue management. ai_summary: CAISO's Board of Governors voted in October 2025 to update the ISO's default resource adequacy rules (last revised in 2006) to modernize qualifying-capacity criteria and planning-reserve-margin methodology. The proposal replaces one-size-fits-all accreditation with differentiated approaches: dispatchable hydro and run-of-river hydro will now be accredited using Average Effective Load Carrying Capability (ELCC) based on forced outage rates and generation during critical periods respectively; pumped-storage hydroelectric resources will use Unforced Capacity (UCAP) calculated from three years of historic outage data (Winter: November–April; Summer: May–October). The ISO will conduct an annual transparent process to establish values, with stakeholders (including local regulatory authorities such as CPUC, Northern California Power Agency, and Six Cities) able to adopt these defaults or set their own methodologies. The Board authorized Management to file tariff amendments with FERC. Concurrent Track 2 and Track 3 efforts will address resource adequacy availability incentives and other related provisions.
hydro_read_through: Conventional hydro owners face a material shift in capacity accreditation. The shift from historic net-dependable-capacity (NERC GADS) to average ELCC for dispatchable hydro and to ELCC based on critical-period generation for run-of-river hydro changes how much capacity a plant can offer into the market; the values will now reflect dynamic system conditions and the resource's actual contribution to meeting peak needs during scarcity events, rather than nameplate or historical-average metrics. Pumped-storage operators benefit from direct UCAP accreditation (a more straightforward outage-rate adjustment) rather than being bundled with thermal or nuclear. Annual recalculation introduces some uncertainty for multi-year revenue planning, but the transparent modeling process and CPUC coordination create opportunity to influence methodology design. The new framework is designed to align with CPUC's pending UCAP framework for 2028 implementation.

ai_summary: GridLab consultant Ed Smeloff submits comments supporting CAISO's Draft 2025-2026 Transmission Plan and proposes a Granular Scenario Planning approach for future cycles to address concentrated load growth in specific grid locations. The proposal uses historical locational marginal price (LMP) data from CAISO's OASIS platform as a vulnerability filter, applies three load-growth scenarios to production-cost models to generate predictive shadow prices, and recommends a "least-regrets" decision matrix to prioritize non-wires alternatives, hybrid battery, or reconductoring investments based on whether congestion appears across all scenarios or only extreme cases. Smeloff recommends the Board support a Special Study of the Los Angeles Basin in the upcoming planning cycle to operationalize this framework through collaboration with the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power.

Hydro's high capital cost and low marginal cost make it chronically dependent on scarcity pricing at binding transmission interfaces; the extent to which CAISO's planning explicitly models future LMP risk at specific nodes, and whether it commits transmission solutions to alleviate high-shadow-price nodes, will reshape the set of locations where hydro generators can expect sustained margin in the decade ahead.

ai_summary: CAISO presented a spotlight briefing on the Extended Day-Ahead Market (EDAM) congestion revenue allocation Phase 2 initiative to the WEM Governing Body in June 2026. Phase 1 design, approved June 2025, allocated congestion revenues to the EDAM balancing area where congestion occurs and provided congestion hedges tied to firm transmission rights. Phase 2, launched December 2025, evaluates enhancements and long-term design to address potential self-scheduling incentives and asymmetry between CAISO and EDAM allocations. Three design concepts are under evaluation: (1) enhanced allocation based on cleared schedules, expanding eligibility beyond balanced self-schedules to economically bid and cleared schedules with reciprocal treatment for ISO balancing area; (2) historical baseline rights framework establishing historical transmission rights eligible for expanded congestion hedges; and (3) ongoing simultaneous feasibility framework using annual and monthly feasibility tests to assign financial entitlements to congestion revenues. Four stakeholder working groups met from December 2025 onward with an average of 117 attendees, producing 49 comments. Targeted milestones are Q4 2026–Q1 2027 for proposal development and Q2 2027 for WEM Governing Body decision presentation.
hydro_read_through: This document does not mention hydropower directly. The Phase 2 redesign—shifting from balanced self-schedule eligibility to economically bid schedules, and potentially using simultaneous feasibility or historical baseline frameworks—would change which hydro resources qualify for hedging and how much value they recover per MW of transmission right. Hydro operators participating in EDAM as either balancing-area resources or external participants depend on clarity around congestion-hedge rules to model inter-temporal dispatch value and transmission-dependent export strategies.

ai_summary: CAISO's Market Surveillance Committee reports on the CRR Enhancements initiative, which proposes to address revenue adequacy problems in CAISO's congestion-rights auction. The initiative published a straw proposal on June 1, 2026, and a narrowed draft final proposal on June 23, 2026. Phase 1 now focuses solely on expanding CAISO's authority to model loop flows (unscheduled power flows from neighboring systems) in the annual CRR process, deferring the minimum-price floor to Phase 2. The MSC supports loop-flow modeling as a modest step to improve revenue adequacy, which has averaged roughly 79% since 2019 and accumulated a shortfall of approximately $856 million. The MSC opposes the minimum-price approach at this stage, finding that low-priced CRRs account for only 23% of total realized payout despite representing 38% of auction volume, and noting concerns about implementation risk and effects on LSE resale liquidity. The memo also flags broader CRR reform discussions, including a Department of Market Monitoring proposal for a willing-seller willing-buyer framework, and recommends further scrutiny of the allocation process as auction scope narrows.

ai_summary: CAISO's Director of Market Performance presented analysis of congestion cost patterns in the prospective Extended Day-Ahead Market (EDAM) footprint spanning nine balancing authorities (BANC, CAISO, IPCO, LADWP, PACE, PACW, PNM, PGE, TID). The analysis found that on average 137 congestion constraints are active in the CAISO area—about 86 percent of all constraints—with approximately 34 percent impacted by parallel flows from EDAM-area transactions. Key constraints like Path 26 experience up to 40 percent flow impacts from transactions between PacifiCorp east and west. Congestion is concentrated during solar hours and increases during evening peak hours in summer months. CAISO constraints drive most congestion pricing across EDAM areas, while constraints in non-CAISO EDAM areas have negligible frequency of congestion and minimal price impact on other EDAM regions. The analysis used historical 2024 WEIM congestion data and shift factors as a proxy for projected EDAM congestion patterns.
hydro_read_through: Hydropower plants exporting power across the EDAM footprint—particularly from the Pacific Northwest into California—will face transmission congestion charges shaped by the parallel-flow patterns and locational price spreads this analysis documents. The finding that CAISO constraints generate the largest price separations (e.g., negative prices in Southwest desert areas, positive in PNW) directly affects the value of hydro at different locations and the revenue from selling energy into different nodes. Hydro operators need to track which transmission paths are most frequently congested and how parallel flows from other EDAM regions will influence the congestion rent distribution that determines their payment or charge per MWh.

ai_summary: CAISO's Congestion Revenue Allocation Phase 2 working group (meeting July 28, 2026) evaluates three design concepts for allocating Day-Ahead congestion revenues across the broadened EDAM footprint. Concept #1 would allocate revenues to EDAM entities based on cleared balanced schedules associated with firm OATT transmission rights (long-term firm PTP and NITS), with reciprocal treatment for CAISO's CRRs; stakeholder feedback showed qualified support for this incremental improvement but concern about implementation feasibility and persistent self-schedule incentives. Concept #3, with broader stakeholder support, proposes a common Simultaneous Feasibility Test (SFT) to evaluate CRRs and eligible firm OATT rights' effectiveness on constraints across the entire EDAM footprint, with annual and monthly nomination cycles mirroring current CRR processes; Concept #2 faced broad opposition for relying on historical baselines. Stakeholder comments are due August 10, 2026, and the next working-group meeting will be scheduled in August following comment review.
hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower, pumped storage, or run-of-river resources. However, congestion revenue allocation mechanisms set the financial hedges that use-limited resources (hydro's canonical category) receive on transmission paths. Concept #1's broadening of allocation from self-schedule-only to cleared balanced schedules could affect how a generator with firm OATT rights monetizes simultaneous market bids; Concept #3's common SFT across the EDAM footprint would establish congestion entitlements jointly with other transmission rights, potentially changing the baseline against which a hydro owner with legacy OATT capacity competes for congestion revenue funding. The shift from internal-balancing-area allocation (Phase 1) toward footprint-wide constraint effectiveness testing could either improve or degrade congestion hedges depending on how parallel flows and network topology changes interact with a given plant's transmission path.

ai_summary: SCE presents a framework for allocating EDAM congestion revenue that treats CAISO-BAA and non-CAISO (OATT-based) BAAs differently. SCE proposes Option 3 ('Simultaneous Feasibility'), which would guarantee congestion-revenue backing only for transmission sales that are simultaneously feasible with all other EDAM transactions. Additional transmission sales would be allowed but without expectation of full EDAM congestion-revenue funding. SCE frames the change as preventing cost-shifts among EDAM transmission providers and creating a path for willing EDAM BAAs to migrate from OATT transmission contract rights to CAISO-style CRRs (Congestion Revenue Rights).
hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower directly. However, EDAM congestion-revenue allocation affects all market participants' transmission-use costs and revenue recovery from transmission rights. Hydropower plants, particularly those in non-CAISO footprints joining EDAM, would face changes in how their transmission costs are calculated and how any transmission rights they hold are backed by congestion revenue. The shift toward physics-based transmission pricing rather than contract-right-based allocation could alter the locational signals and cost-recovery mechanisms that hydro operations depend on, especially for plants relying on existing transmission contract positions.

ai_summary: Six Cities and allied California load-serving entities submitted comments to CAISO's Price Formation Enhancements initiative (presented March 3, 2026) opposing immediate comprehensive scarcity-pricing reform. ai_summary: On September 19, 2025, California signed Assembly Bill 825 into law, authorizing CAISO and California electrical corporations to participate in voluntary energy markets governed by an independent Regional Organization (RO) if specified requirements are met. AB 825 requires CAISO to maintain technical capability to operate energy markets, continue its functions as a balancing authority, develop an annual report on ISO and independent RO activities with annual legislative presentation, and by December 31, 2026, conduct a study of the independent RO's impacts on job retention and creation in California. The Western Energy Markets Governing Body celebrated the passage and CAISO is working with the Pathways Initiative Formation Committee to implement AB 825 requirements. PacifiCorp and Portland General Electric received FERC approval in August 2025 to join EDAM in 2026, with PacifiCorp on track for May 2026 activation following successful EDAM Market Simulation launch in early September; Nevada Energy plans to file its EDAM application on October 22, 2025.
hydro_read_through: AB 825 and concurrent EDAM expansion reshape California's energy-market governance by creating an independent Regional Organization parallel to CAISO, which directly affects where California and Western hydro resources can participate and how their products are priced and accredited. Hydro owners must track whether the independent RO will adopt different capacity accreditation, ancillary-service pricing, or ramping-product designs than CAISO, and whether EDAM's May 2026 launch in PacifiCorp's territory (which includes significant hydro) alters incentives for participating resources or creates new obligations for existing plants. The West-Wide Governance Pathways Initiative framework and job-impact study deadline of December 31, 2026, will determine whether the RO operates a unified market or carve-outs that fragment hydro's revenue opportunities.

SP-Tie versus GAP-Tie modeling affects whether existing forward-market conventions can accommodate large scheduled transfers (typical for hydro-rich footprints moving output to load centers), and congestion-reversal and NETC timing rules reshape the margin available on otherwise economic trades. A hydro operator wheeling power daily across multiple BAAs, as TEA's description suggests its clients do, would face material changes to transaction efficiency and economic exposure depending on which scheduling framework CAISO adopts.

ai_summary: TEA, providing Scheduling Coordinator services to Load Serving Entities in CAISO and PacifiCorp EDAM BAAs, supports CAISO's planned adjustments to DAME Configurable Parameters for EDAM Go-Live as outlined at the March 24, 2026 stakeholder meeting. TEA specifically endorses the reduction of Imbalance Reserve Up and Down (IRU/D) procurement confidence intervals from 97.5/2.5 to 90/10, which affects day-ahead market clearing and hourly Resource Sufficiency Evaluation (RSE) requirements. TEA additionally requests that CAISO tune the confidence intervals for the load-based component of RSE targets to the same 90/10 level to address compliance burden on third-party LSEs in non-CAISO EDAM BAAs facing volatile hourly requirements and limited access to bilateral supplemental supply and intertie markets, proposing reassessment once EDAM achieves scale and market liquidity improves.
hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage directly. However, hydro and storage resources participate in EDAM's day-ahead and real-time markets and are subject to RSE requirements and reserve adequacy rules affecting their ability to clear bids and manage scheduling obligations. Changes to IRU/D confidence intervals and RSE load-based determinants alter the reserve obligations load-serving entities must procure, which indirectly shifts the day-ahead demand curves and scarcity pricing signals that hydro and storage resources face—tighter confidence intervals generally reduce procurement quantity and lower opportunity costs, while looser intervals increase them. The request to align load-based RSE confidence intervals with the IRU/D adjustment would further ease the reserve-procurement burden across EDAM's footprint, potentially flattening price risk and improving the value proposition for flexible supply resources including hydro and storage.

ai_summary: The WEM Governing Body Market Expert briefs on Comprehensive Scarcity Pricing (CSP) design for the Western Electricity Market, discussing how scarcity pricing increases electricity prices when supply is insufficient to meet load and reserve targets, thereby eliciting incremental supply and demand reductions. The document examines two competing approaches—an Operating Reserve Demand Curve (ORDC) linked to reserve deficiency, and a latent supply margin design that creates a price adder as available supply tightens—and notes that the CAISO had planned CSP discussion concurrently with incremental enhancements proposed in August 2025, but stated on July 2, 2026 it would "resume discussion of [comprehensive scarcity pricing] ... after the governance decision on current [scarcity pricing] changes." The briefing addresses stakeholder concerns about CSP's impact on reliability, conceptual design challenges (particularly accommodating multiple BAAs rather than a single balancing authority), and financial impacts on ratepayers, and recommends two focused projects: evaluation of the latent supply approach for simplicity and unintended consequences, and assessment of scarcity pricing with co-optimization of a 30-minute reserve product.
hydro_read_through: This document does not mention hydropower or pumped-storage facilities. However, CSP design is directly relevant to hydro revenue: scarcity pricing mechanisms determine how much additional energy and reserve prices rise during physically constrained periods—the conditions when hydro's flexibility and stored energy command the highest marginal value. Hydro's participation in ancillary-services and reserve products under either ORDC or latent-supply-margin designs would depend on the co-optimization assumptions, reserve product definitions (10-minute vs. 30-minute), and whether scarcity prices flow through those products. The briefing's emphasis on triggering scarcity pricing prospectively to signal developing shortages—rather than only when load is shed—directly affects how much notice and price signal hydro and other flexible resources receive to increase output or adjust dispatch timing. ai_summary: WPTF submits comments on CAISO's Price Formation Enhancements (PFE) initiative, criticizing the current proposal as insufficient to meet reliability objectives established in 2021 following the August 2020 blackout events. WPTF argues that the proposal delays meaningful price signals until scarcity is already occurring, rather than allowing prices to rise gradually as supply tightens, and contends that relying solely on future Flexible Ramping Product (FRP) and Ancillary Services (AS) enhancements risks another five-to-ten-year delay in developing robust scarcity pricing. WPTF also objects to CAISO's plan to apply BAA-level market power mitigation to the CAISO footprint absent forward-looking competitiveness analysis, arguing that such mitigation without counterbalancing robust scarcity pricing would artificially suppress prices during tight conditions when accurate pricing is essential to attract additional supply and maintain reliability. WPTF requests that the WEM Governing Body direct CAISO to fully develop a scarcity-pricing design with gradual price-rise mechanisms in the current PFE phase and to conduct a robust competitiveness study before implementing BAA-level mitigation.

ai_summary: The Western Energy Imbalance Market (WEIM) delivered $411.98 million in economic benefits during Q3 2025, bringing cumulative benefits to $7.82 billion through Q3 2025. The market's 23-member footprint continues to generate large volumes of economic transfers via real-time price convergence, with moderate prices in WEIM remaining below bilateral prices in Q3. Prices trended upward following higher summer loads, with congestion on transmission constraints (notably in TID, BANC, and LAWDP areas) driving locational price variation. This market-performance update was presented to the WEM Governing Body in December 2025.
hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage directly. However, the WEIM is a foundational strategic option for Western hydro owners: it enables real-time energy balancing across a 23-balancing-area footprint, unlocking arbitrage revenue through price convergence and allowing Northwest and other hydro-rich regions to export flexibility into higher-value areas. Congestion patterns (TID, BANC, LAWDP) signal where transmission-constrained areas value flexible ramping resources like hydro; demonstrating sustained high transfer volumes and economic benefits validates WEIM participation as an ongoing revenue stream that justifies hydro plants' operational commitments to the market.

title: Presentation - Resource Adequacy Modeling and Program Design - Track 2 - Jul 22, 2026
relevance_reason: CAISO's revised RAAIM (Resource Availability and Accuracy Incentive Mechanism) directly reshapes penalty exposure and revenue-recovery allocation for hydropower and storage resources during stress events, moving from a monthly netted assessment to per-event tiered triggers that substantially increase payoff volatility and compliance burden for use-limited resources.
initiatives: Resource adequacy modeling and program design  [Active]
ai_summary: CAISO proposes overhauling its RAAIM availability-penalty mechanism, replacing a $4.40/kW-month fixed charge assessed over monthly AAH windows with event-based tiered pricing: Tier 1 (Elevated Reliability Risk) at day-ahead LMP, and Tier 2 (Critical Capacity Insufficiency, keyed to EDAM RSE failures) at $2,000/MWh. Hydro, storage, VERs, thermal, and DR would receive technology-specific treatment: hydro and thermal face shown-RA-based availability assessment against bids and outage status; storage's obligation is tied to SDM-modeled feasibility limits and SOC nonlinearity (not automatic outage exposure); VERs are exempted from low-wind/solar/ambient variability but remain exposed for forced equipment outages. Co-located and hybrid resources receive configuration-specific rules. The proposal eliminates the <1 MW exemption and tightens exemptions overall. Stakeholder feedback flagged that storage and hydro need duration, state-of-charge, and hydrologic limits recognized; that Tier 2 exposure should reflect cost causation not any EDAM failure; and that penalty exposure must not exceed shown RA. No vote or comment deadline is stated in this presentation; next steps are listed as pending.

title: Presentation - Storage Design and Modeling - Jul 22, 2026
relevance_reason: CAISO is redesigning default energy bids for storage and hybrids, which directly affects the opportunity-cost offer framework for pumped storage and creates a precedent being leveraged across EDAM/WEIM; storage DEB is the primary mitigation-compliant bidding pathway for PSH and energy-limited resources.
initiatives: Storage design and modeling [Active]
ai_summary: CAISO is evaluating two methodologies to reform storage default energy bids (DEBs): a time-of-day approach that incorporates hydro DEB elements with hourly multipliers (1.4 pre-opportunity-cost hour, 1.0 after) and a static hydro-based approach. The time-of-day approach, currently preferred by CAISO, applies upward-only scaling of price proxies and addresses a core PSH challenge—that current static DEBs using day-ahead LMPs become 'stale' in real-time and prevent WEIM-only storage from accessing the DEB option at all. The time-of-day approach enables WEIM-only resources to use real-time DGAP and LMP scaling, and extends this framework consistently across EDAM and WEIM. A revised straw proposal is due September 2, 2026, with comments due September 30, 2026; final proposal is targeted for October 28, 2026. Pumped storage operators reliant on negotiated DEBs or using stale price proxies gain material upside if the time-of-day approach adopts the 1.4 multiplier on opportunity cost; conversely, stakeholders opposing time-of-day multipliers below 1.0 or favoring simpler hydro-based static methods will shape whether the structure is simplified or retained.

initiatives: Resource adequacy modeling and program design  [Active]
ai_summary: CAISO's Resource Adequacy Modeling and Program Design (RAMPD) Track 2 Revised Straw Proposal (July 17, 2026) proposes replacing the current static, monthly RAAIM structure with an event-based availability framework that assesses availability during periods of elevated reliability risk rather than averaging across all availability assessment hours in a month. The proposal introduces three outage classifications — planned (maintenance/construction with advance notice), urgent (increased risk but still operable), and forced (little/no notice) — and eliminates short-notice opportunity outages. It proposes a "shopping cart" workflow for substitute-capacity trading among scheduling coordinators (displayed in CIRA with seller confirmation) rather than ISO-centralized matching, and revises must-offer and RAAIM settlement rules so resources are penalized only on shown RA capacity, not on capacity above their shown RA. Comments on the proposal are due August 5, 2026.
hydro_read_through: Conventional hydropower, being inherently use-limited and weather-dependent, is highly sensitive to changes in when availability is assessed and how forced outages are treated in RA revenue. The shift from monthly averaging to event-based assessment during stressed-system conditions could concentrate RAAIM penalties on the hours hydro actually needs to be on-line (typically summer peaks), rather than diluting them across the whole month; this could either increase or decrease a hydro owner's exposure depending on how the final "elevated reliability risk" periods are defined. The new urgent-outage category and elimination of short-notice opportunity outages may reduce hydro's flexibility to take unplanned maintenance on short notice without RA penalty, making forced-outage rates and substitute-capacity costs more material to revenue; conversely, the revised RAAIM rule limiting penalties to shown RA (not MOO) could reduce exposure if a plant shows less than its full nameplate. The substitute-capacity shopping-cart mechanism replaces bilateral searching with a platform tool, but the document does not specify whether hydro, as a fast-ramping resource, would face different availability-assessment hours or outage-substitution priorities than thermal or battery resources.

initiatives: Storage design and modeling [Active]
ai_summary: CAISO proposes enhancements to storage resource participation in energy and ancillary-services markets through three pathways: (1) replacement of the current static storage default energy bid with a time-of-day approach that incorporates temporal cost differentiation while remaining administratively implementable; (2) extension of default energy bid rules to hybrid resources using a "greater-of" method based on the highest-cost component with minimum-share guardrails; and (3) a reframing of non-generator resource bidding to allow storage to submit a single terminal state-of-charge bid reflecting willingness to pay/accept for ending an optimization period with higher or lower energy stored, relative to a reference state, rather than interval-by-interval bid curves. The ISO sequences default energy bid and bidding-structure improvements as near-term work, with a comprehensive uplift (bid cost recovery) redesign to follow by end of 2026. Comments are due August 5, 2026, following stakeholder discussion on July 22, 2026.
hydro_read_through: The document does not name hydropower or pumped storage directly; however, it addresses storage resource market participation rules that apply categorically to all use-limited storage, which includes conventional hydropower and pumped-storage facilities. The three proposed changes would affect how storage operators recover costs and value state-of-charge opportunity costs: default energy bid improvements would permit more frequent cost reassessment reflecting daily price variation (directly important for run-of-river and seasonal hydro), the hybrid framework would govern hydro paired with solar or wind, and the terminal state-of-charge bidding concept would replace the current hourly bidding structure with a single value-of-energy offer that propagates backward through dispatch optimization. The sequencing of default energy bid reform ahead of uplift redesign signals that CAISO is treating marginal-cost recovery as foundational to any future changes to bid cost recovery policy—a framework within which conventional hydro has historically received mitigation treatment as a canonical use-limited resource. The reframing concept would also change how day-ahead and real-time dispatch treat state-of-charge deviation, potentially affecting the price-following incentives that hydro operators currently use to manage storage-like flexibility.

title: WPTF Presentation - UCAP Implementation and RAAIM - Jul 22, 2026
relevance_reason: MECHANISM: UCAP implementation and RAAIM redesign directly affect how CAISO accredits and pays hydro/PSH capacity in resource-adequacy showings, and how availability is measured and penalized — touching both the accreditation revenue stream (through changes to counting rules, must-offer obligations, and deliverability ceilings) and compliance obligations (RAAIM performance metrics and penalty exposure).
initiatives: Resource adequacy modeling and program design  [Active]
ai_summary: WPTF presents CAISO's path to implement CPUC-adopted UCAP (Unforced Capacity) methodology for 2028 RA year, arguing that CAISO must define separate capacity values post-UCAP — Pmax, PmaxRA (deliverable accredited capacity), LRA-specific QC, maximum NQC, and shown RA — because one value cannot serve every CAISO function (forward counting, deliverability studies, must-offer formulas, RAAIM exposure, exports, and backstop procurement) without double-counting or losing capability. On RAAIM, WPTF argues the current design does not need redesign: forced-outage data show no correlation with load or prices, UCAP itself does not justify price increases, and a 94.5% monthly availability floor is conceptually consistent with UCAP's removal of expected outages from the forward MW value. The presentation urges CAISO to establish demonstrated failure (via resource availability trends, substitution-request analysis, and event-level causation) before changing RAAIM penalties or exposures. This touches hydro and PSH by redefining which capacity value applies to RA accreditation, must-offer, and RAAIM calculations — especially for partially deliverable resources and storage with variable seasonal contribution — and by proposing to keep RAAIM pricing unchanged while clarifying what 'shown RA' means, which will determine both the compliance exposure and the RA revenue hydro owners receive in forward showings.

ai_summary: CAISO's June 23, 2026 BPM Change Management meeting presented 18 Proposed Revision Requests (PRRs 1669–1686) spanning storage and market design. Key hydro/storage items: PRR 1678 (now at Recommendation stage, next: ISO Final Decision) clarifies how state-of-charge constraints in Day Ahead ensure adequate SOC to cover energy, ancillary services, and capacity products, and in Real Time cover energy, ancillary services, and flexible ramping — directly governing storage's ability to stack AS revenue without depletion penalties. PRR 1679 (Initial stage, next: ISO Recommendation) updates battery/storage telemetry points (Instantaneous SOC, Maximum/Minimum Continuous Energy Limit) to add clarity on state-of-charge monitoring. PRR 1677 (Initial stage, next: ISO Recommendation) clarifies outage-reporting requirements for non-generator resources and adds storage-specific cause codes to the Outage Management BPM. PRR 1671 (Recommendation stage, next: ISO Final Decision) incorporates new default resource-adequacy rules affecting how hydro and storage are accredited. EDAM transition PRRs 1670 and 1672 (both Recommendation stage, effective May 1, 2026) govern HE1 self-schedule initial conditions and transition-period pricing for EDAM entities. title: Presentation - Price Formation Enhancements - Scarcity Pricing - Jul 14, 2026
relevance_reason: CAISO's scarcity pricing proposal directly affects energy price formation during system stress, which is a primary revenue mechanism for hydro and pumped-storage resources that supply emergency flexibility and reserves.
ai_summary: CAISO's Revised Straw Proposal on scarcity pricing (Day 2 of Phase 2 Price Formation Enhancements, July 14, 2026) modifies two mechanisms: (1) load-shed pricing extends the scarcity signal into both real-time dispatch (RTD) and 15-minute forecasting markets (FMM) when a BAA enters EEA Level 3 emergency and operators shed firm load, treating curtailed load as unserved demand to prevent market prices from collapsing; and (2) armed-reserve pricing adds an opportunity-cost adder in RTD to reflect when reserve capacity is released into energy markets, capturing the scarcity value that the 15-minute ancillary-service procurement (RTPD) process already recognizes. Both mechanisms include operational safeguards: operators can pause either mechanism, and the load-shed signal turns off after four cumulative hours of load shedding in a 24-hour window. The proposal defers comprehensive scarcity redesign to a future phase. Feedback on grouping, CAISO BAA treatment, load-shedding implementation options (verified MW vs. forecast approach), and whether the mechanisms adequately preserve scarcity signals without over-mitigation is requested before the draft final proposal.

title: Presentation - Price Formation Enhancements - BAA-Level Market Power Mitigation - Jul 13, 2026
relevance_reason: BAA-level market power mitigation (MPM) redesign directly affects how hydro's market-power-limited capacity is tested and mitigated during scarcity — grouping, load-serving obligation subtraction, and pivotal-supplier filtering all reshape the offer floor and mitigation surface for dispatchable resources with geographically-dispersed generation or storage.
initiatives: Price formation enhancements [Active]
ai_summary: CAISO's Revised Straw Proposal reforms BAA-level MPM by grouping BAAs via Marginal Export Capacity and export-transfer connectivity (instead of testing each in isolation), subtracting interval-specific load-serving obligations from withholdable capacity, and mitigating only pivotal suppliers after a grouped BAA fails the 3PS test. CAISO BAA retains default-competitive status and will not be subject to the BAA-level test as a group — a deferent to concerns that economic intertie imports are undervalued by the current framework. The proposal advances grouping and LSO changes near-term but defers comprehensive scarcity pricing and CAISO BAA mitigation to a broader future phase, with Day 2 stakeholder feedback to focus on scarcity-pricing mechanics, implementation choices, and safeguards. For hydro operators, especially those with multi-BAA footprints or export capability (e.g., Northwest PSH and reservoir operators), the grouping and LSO logic could narrow the suppliers subject to mitigation during tight intervals, raising energy prices and ancillary-service value when genuinely pivotal capacity is constrained — but the deferral of scarcity pricing means no new scarcity-pricing adders are being adopted yet. Most exposed: large dispatchable generators and PSH with withholdable capacity in grouped BAAs; comment deadline not stated in document.

title: Presentation - Monthly Extended Day-Ahead Market (EDAM) May Performance Report - Jun 25, 2026
relevance_reason: EDAM/DAME implementation affects hydro revenue through new flexibility products (imbalance reserves), ancillary-service pricing, GHG allocation/pricing, and regional price separation; May performance data shows how hydro (especially in PACW) is clearing in these markets and how transfer economics are reshaping dispatch.
ai_summary: CAISO's May 2026 EDAM performance report documents the first month of operations across the expanded day-ahead footprint (CAISO, PacifiCorp East, PacifiCorp West), including two new products: imbalance reserves (IRU/IRD) and reliability capacity (RCU/RCD). Hydro operators see direct implications: (1) imbalance reserve procurement in PACW was supplied primarily by transfers and hydro, while reliability capacity pricing trends lower than energy and varies sharply by area, reshaping the value of flexible capacity; (2) GHG allocation reached 256 MW peak and is now BAA-specific rather than system-wide, affecting export economics from non-California balancing areas; (3) ancillary-services cascading frequency changed (regulation-up cascading fell from 28.8% to 4.7%), with spin cascading rising to 85.6%, altering the stacking and pricing of traditional AS products hydro supplies. Energy prices showed regional separation (PACE lowest, PACW higher, CAISO highest), and transfer flows indicate active cross-BAA dispatch. This is preliminary first-month data; no member action deadlines are stated in the report itself.
