initiatives: Demand and distributed energy market integration [Active]
ai_summary: CAISO's Track 1 Draft Final Proposal for Demand and Distributed Energy Market Integration permits individual customers within demand-response aggregations to export behind-the-meter battery and storage output to the grid (subject to utility approval), while limiting the aggregation as a whole to remain non-exporting. The proposal maintains DR's load-curtailment categorization and preserves existing deliverability frameworks, but introduces revised baseline and settlement methodologies to credit performance when BTM resources discharge. This expands the wholesale DR market to capture full capability of distributed storage (especially batteries and potentially small pumped storage), competing directly with conventional hydro's flexibility value in the ISO BAA; the framework applies to both Proxy Demand Response (PDR) and Reliability Demand Response Resources (RDRR). No vote date or next-step deadline is stated in the excerpt; the document is dated July 8, 2026.

initiatives: Demand and distributed energy market integration [Active]
ai_summary: CAISO's DDEMI Track 1 proposal would allow demand response aggregations to include behind-the-meter exports from utility-authorized end-use customers (e.g., rooftop solar + battery, behind-the-meter pumped storage), while capping the aggregation's net export at the resource level rather than the individual-customer level. Currently, customers exporting more than they consume are 'zeroed out' individually, preventing aggregators from accessing the full export capability of behind-the-meter storage; the proposal shifts the floor from customer to aggregation level to reflect market topology. This affects how pumped-storage and battery-backed demand response resources are metered, settled, and compensated for their dual load-curtailment and export capability. Stakeholders have until July 16, 2026 to submit written comments; the proposal applies to both Proxy Demand Resource (PDR) and Reliability Demand Response Resource (RDRR) models across all BAAs.

Intermountain West and Pacific Northwest became dominant WEIM exporters during non-solar hours in Q1 2025, with PacEast and Idaho Power identified as main peak-hour exporters; transfer congestion into/out of those hydro-rich regions occurred in ~20% of 5-minute intervals, creating locational scarcity signals. The report is observational and carries no proposals or compliance deadlines, but provides a baseline on how hydro's FRP-market participation, export positioning, and regional pricing have shifted in the WEIM footprint — useful for understanding Q1 2025 hydro revenue dynamics and transmission-constrained export opportunity.

ai_summary: CAISO's Department of Market Monitoring reports Q2 2025 real-time market conditions: electricity prices in the West rose 12% versus Q2 2024, driven by south-to-north congestion and California greenhouse-gas costs; Northwest prices were higher during solar hours, California during non-solar hours—indicating hydro's value shifts with solar generation patterns. WEIM transfer congestion into or out of Pacific Northwest areas occurred over 20% of 5-minute intervals, and Mid-Columbia and Palo Verde bilateral prices converged with ISO market prices, suggesting arbitrage opportunities narrowed. Pacific Northwest coal output rose despite more outages, and transfers from the Intermountain West during non-solar hours declined Q-o-Q, signaling reduced availability or changed dispatch incentives. For hydro owners, these trends show tightening price signals in hydro-export corridors, persistent congestion reducing transmission access to California, and seasonal shifts in the regional generation stack that affect dispatch positioning and revenue timing.

title: Draft - On-Peak Deliverability Study Methodology - Jun 03, 2026
relevance_reason: CAISO refines its on-peak deliverability assessment methodology — the mechanism by which generators (including hydro and storage) qualify for full or partial capacity credit toward resource adequacy; changes to Pmax assumptions, scenario hours, and dispatch modeling directly affect how much RA capacity hydro and pumped storage can claim and at what cost.
ai_summary: CAISO has refined its generator on-peak deliverability study methodology, effective January 2024 and documented here as of June 2026, to address bottleneck risk as the generation fleet diversifies and solar penetration shifts peak net load. The methodology now assesses two distinct scenarios: (1) highest system need (hours 19–22 in summer, peak sale with low solar), where non-intermittent generators' Pmax is set to highest summer Qualifying Capacity in the prior three years, and intermittent generators at 20% exceedance level; and (2) secondary system need (hours 15–18, peak consumption with high solar output), where Pmax for intermittent resources is 50% exceedance level and energy storage Pmax is 50% of 4-hour discharge capacity. For hybrid and energy-storage projects, Pmax is limited by requested maximum output. Hydro and pumped-storage owners face a direct revenue impact: the Pmax values used in deliverability studies directly determine how much capacity credit they can claim in RA markets and interconnection queues; storage capacity credit in secondary scenarios is capped at half the 4-hour discharge rating, potentially disadvantaging long-duration or seasonal storage relative to short-duration batteries.

meeting_title: Comments due - On-Peak Deliverability Assessment Methodology Refinements

ai_summary: CAISO proposes three refinements to its on-peak deliverability assessment methodology: (1) modeling proposed resources identified in transmission planning as needed for local reliability in the base case dispatch (rather than only when they relieve constraints), conditional on reasonable certainty of completion before deliverability is needed; (2) including existing demand response in the base case to avoid over-allocating deliverability; and (3) reducing the dispatch value of generators in the base case from 80% to 70% of maximum study amount to reflect the increased planning reserve margin (from ~15% to 25%). The refinements affect how new hydro and PSH projects are studied during interconnection—projects that would need to compete with modeled proposed resources to secure a deliverable position in queue. Comments are due June 25, 2026. Most exposed are developers of new hydro or PSH seeking interconnection in California who will compete for deliverability allocation against projects CAISO assumes will be built to meet identified local needs.

ai_summary: CAISO's Commitment Cost Bidding Flexibility (CCBF) working group is developing a market power mitigation framework for commitment cost offers, replacing a static cap with a competitiveness-based test that identifies uncompetitive conditions using a three-pivotal-supplier test for commitment-specific constraints. The framework will mitigate commitment costs identified as exercising market power by assessing them against the resource's cost-based reference level, with phased caps of 300% in competitive conditions and 110% in uncompetitive conditions. Dispatchable hydro and pumped-storage operators face direct revenue exposure: inflated commitment-cost bids that currently clear under the static cap could be suppressed or capped when the test identifies the resource as pivotal to binding transmission constraints; conversely, owners with low reference levels could bid more competitively. Workshop 2 (this meeting, June 18, 2026) identifies policy choices on structural competitiveness testing and mitigation criteria; next steps and comment deadlines not stated in this presentation excerpt.

title: Final Market Surveillance Committee Opinion - Extended Day-Ahead Market Congestion Revenue Allocation - Jun 16, 2025
relevance_reason: EDAM congestion revenue allocation rules directly affect how hydro operators recover transmission-congestion hedges and how parallel-flow costs from hydro schedules are reallocated across balancing authorities — a core revenue-protection mechanism for dispatchable and use-limited resources in the Western interregional market.
stakeholders: Benjamin F. Hobbs (Market Surveillance Committee, CAISO (paid consultant))
James Bushnell (Market Surveillance Committee, CAISO (paid consultant))
Scott M. Harvey (Market Surveillance Committee, CAISO (paid consultant))
ai_summary: The CAISO Market Surveillance Committee issued a final opinion (June 16, 2025) on EDAM's proposed congestion revenue allocation scheme for parallel flows, evaluating a Year 1 interim design that would reallocate congestion revenues from BAAs where congestion occurs to BAAs that sold firm point-to-point and NITS transmission rights when those holders self-schedule. The MSC has significant reservations about the Year 1 design because it creates perverse incentives to self-schedule instead of participating in economically efficient co-optimized dispatch, potentially distorting bidding and causing unintended cost shifts — a concern particularly acute for hydro and other dispatchable resources whose flexibility value depends on competitive economic dispatch. The opinion does not block the proposal but calls for detailed pre-EDAM-launch empirical analysis of dispatch distortion and market-price effects from self-scheduling incentives, and notes that Year 2 alternatives linked to flexibly-bid resources would worsen below-cost-offer incentives; the framework recommended for future exploration is financial flowgate rights rather than transaction-linked reallocation.

title: Final Market Surveillance Committee Opinion on Gas Resource Management - Dec 15, 2025
relevance_reason: CAISO's Gas Resource Management proposal affects how gas-fired resources' commitment costs and default energy bids are calculated — reference levels that are the canonical mitigation tool for use-limited resources including hydropower, and directly impact EDAM participation by Western resources including hydro operators in the WEIM/EDAM footprint.
stakeholders: Benjamin F. Hobbs (Market Surveillance Committee, CAISO)
Scott M. Harvey (Market Surveillance Committee, CAISO)
ai_summary: The CAISO Market Surveillance Committee issued a final opinion (Dec. 12, 2025) supporting three of four enhancements in CAISO's Gas Resource Management proposal: improved reference-level change-request processes, expanded after-the-fact cost-recovery rules, and multi-day advisory dispatch forecasts to help gas resources anticipate EDAM schedules and procure fuel more efficiently ahead of morning gas nominations. The MSC supports these changes to address EDAM coordination challenges as EDAM expands westward. However, the MSC emphasizes a critical gap: the absence of any market-power test for commitment-cost mitigation means all gas units are indiscriminately mitigated in every dispatch interval, creating inefficient offer bounds that may favor units with actual market power while constraining flexible suppliers. The MSC calls development of a workable commitment-cost market-power test "long overdue and should be a high priority." This is material to hydro owners because reference-level design directly affects whether hydro (a canonical use-limited resource) can offer flexibility without artificial caps, and the expansion of EDAM brings Western hydro into closer coordination with gas-constrained EDAM pricing and scheduling — misaligned gas-cost accounting upstream could distort the scarcity signals and ancillary-service values hydro depends on.

title: MSC Final Opinion - Rules for Bidding Above the Soft Offer Cap - Price Formation Enhancements - May 2024
relevance_reason: CAISO proposes revisions to Order 831 soft-offer-cap rules for battery storage and hydropower, directly affecting how energy-limited resources price their opportunity costs and manage state of charge — a core revenue mechanism for hydro and especially pumped storage.
stakeholders: Benjamin F. Hobbs (Market Surveillance Committee of the California ISO)
James Bushnell (Market Surveillance Committee of the California ISO)
Scott M. Harvey (Market Surveillance Committee of the California ISO)
ai_summary: The CAISO Market Surveillance Committee (MSC) issued a final opinion (May 15, 2024) supporting CAISO's proposed changes to Order 831 bidding rules for summer 2024, specifically allowing battery storage and hydropower to bid above the $1000/MWh soft cap by reflecting future-hour opportunity costs rather than only same-hour alternatives. The MSC found that current rules force premature discharge and systematic underestimation of stored energy value, creating inefficiencies that risk curtailments under tight supply conditions; the root problem is that Order 831's Maximum Import Bid Price (MIBP) mechanism was designed for thermal resources and mischaracterizes the temporal opportunity cost of energy-limited resources. The changes apply to both CAISO and Western EIM resources; the MSC also flagged that deeper reforms to local market power mitigation as applied to energy-limited resources and the real-time market's 75-minute offer-update lag remain unresolved and require future work, but the summer 2024 proposal is a necessary interim step.

title: MSC Final Opinion on Extended Day-Ahead Market
relevance_reason: EDAM's day-ahead market coordination across western balancing areas directly affects hydro's revenue from inter-BAA energy and reserve arbitrage, co-optimization of dispatch across large footprints, and participation incentives for flexible resources like pumped storage; the MSC opinion on RSE, GHG accounting, and transmission design shapes whether hydro's scarcity-pricing and flexibility value is preserved or diluted in the expanded market.
stakeholders: Benjamin F. Hobbs (CAISO Market Surveillance Committee)
Scott M. Harvey (CAISO Market Surveillance Committee)
ai_summary: The CAISO Market Surveillance Committee issues a final opinion (January 27, 2023) endorsing the Extended Day-Ahead Market (EDAM) as a beneficial expansion of RTO-style coordination into a day-ahead voluntary market across western BAAs, while flagging unresolved design ambiguities in resource-sufficiency evaluation (RSE), greenhouse-gas accounting, and inter-BAA transmission pricing that require detailed simulation before implementation. The MSC emphasizes that EDAM will pool scarcity pricing and reserve requirements across participants—meaning a shortage in one BAA will raise prices and impose reserve penalties across the entire footprint—and notes that design choices allowing bilateral contracts and demand-reduction programs to count toward RSE requirements, combined with pooled WEIM RSE treatment, could create perverse incentives for resource-insufficient BAAs to lean on the pool. For hydro and PSH operators, EDAM's inter-BAA optimization and removal of 'pancaking' transmission charges will increase dispatch flexibility and inter-regional arbitrage opportunities, but the MSC warns that unresolved details on export constraints, shortfall allocation (especially when multiple BAAs cannot meet their EDAM schedules simultaneously), and GHG export formulation could materially affect scarcity-pricing signals and the value of flexible ramping; the committee recommends flexibility in software design to allow parameter adjustments as EDAM begins operations with an initial small set of BAAs and expands.

title: Market Surveillance Committee Addendum to Final Opinion on Day-Ahead Market Enhancements
relevance_reason: CAISO's Imbalance Reserves cost-allocation mechanism affects how hydro and storage operators are charged for uncertainty-procurement costs and how those costs flow through nodal pricing and congestion settlement — touching energy revenue and price-formation outcomes.
stakeholders: Benjamin F. Hobbs (Market Surveillance Committee of CAISO)
James Bushnell (Market Surveillance Committee of CAISO)
Scott M. Harvey (Market Surveillance Committee of CAISO)
ai_summary: The Market Surveillance Committee clarifies its May 2023 opinion on CAISO's Day-Ahead Market Enhancements (DAME), specifically correcting its description of how Imbalance Reserves (IR) costs will be allocated across Balancing Area Authorities. IR costs are now understood to be calculated per BAA based on nodal prices and cleared quantities of uncertainty, less payments for IR supplied at locations within the BAA — with net charges/payments aggregated across the EDAM and any resulting congestion rents allocated to transfer and transmission constraints in the same manner as energy-flow congestion. This nodal cost-allocation mirrors energy settlements, making the mechanism transparent and competitively neutral. For hydro and PSH operators, this clarification is material because it determines how uncertainty-procurement costs flow through the nodal price signal they face and how their own IR supplies (especially from PSH) are valued and credited at their location — affecting both the cost side of operations and the compensation for flexibility supply.

The MSC identifies EDAM timing (day-ahead schedules posted after morning gas nominations close) as exacerbating these challenges across the expanded Western footprint, and recommends development of a workable market-power test for commitment costs as a high priority going forward. title: Market Surveillance Committee Final Opinion - Storage Bid Cost Recovery - Nov 01, 2024
relevance_reason: CAISO proposes changes to real-time bid cost recovery (BCR) calculations for battery storage, directly affecting how storage resources recover losses and manage state-of-charge — a canonical storage-revenue mechanism that sets precedent for pumped-storage participation and cost allocation in real-time markets.
stakeholders: Benjamin F. Hobbs (Market Surveillance Committee, California Independent System Operator)
James Bushnell (Market Surveillance Committee, California Independent System Operator)
Scott M. Harvey (Market Surveillance Committee, California Independent System Operator)
ai_summary: CAISO's Market Surveillance Committee (MSC) evaluates CAISO's revised proposal to modify real-time bid cost recovery for storage resources, targeting elimination of 'phantom losses' — BCR payments on losses that don't reflect actual economic harm — and improving incentives for storage operators to manage state-of-charge efficiently across the day. The MSC conditionally supports implementation of CAISO's draft final proposal as a near-term check on inflated BCR but notes that empirical data on phantom-loss materiality is incomplete; the MSC recommends immediate follow-up in Phase II to achieve deeper reforms and eliminate BCR on phantom losses before expanding storage bidding flexibility. Pumped-storage owners relying on cost-recovery mechanisms for charging losses and state-of-charge management should monitor whether CAISO's approach—which changes how discharge offers and charging bids factor into BCR calculations—narrows or preserves their ability to recover legitimate operating losses, and should engage if Phase II designs begin to collapse BCR scope more broadly.

title: Market Surveillance Committee Final Opinion on Day-Ahead Market Enhancements
relevance_reason: CAISO's Day-Ahead Market Enhancements (DAME) proposal fundamentally restructures co-optimization of energy and flexibility products, creating new imbalance-reserve procurement rules and state-of-charge constraints on storage that directly affect how pumped-storage hydro earns revenue from flexibility supply and interact with residual unit commitment pricing.
stakeholders: Benjamin F. Hobbs (Market Surveillance Committee, CAISO)
Scott M. Harvey (Market Surveillance Committee, CAISO)
ai_summary: CAISO's Market Surveillance Committee (MSC) issued a final opinion on May 3, 2023, supporting the Day-Ahead Market Enhancements proposal, which introduces a new Imbalance Reserves (IR) co-optimized product to replace ad-hoc operator load-biasing, updates residual unit commitment into a Reliability Capacity (RC) process, and improves storage state-of-charge modeling in day-ahead and RUC runs. The proposal moves forward with stated intent to consult stakeholders during testing and implementation, but the MSC identifies substantial untested elements: nodal IR demand-curve calculation, locational uncertainty estimation, IR deliverability constraints, and storage state-of-charge equation parameters all lack operational precedent outside CAISO and may require rapid iterative adjustment. Pumped-storage operators face direct exposure through IR constraints limiting 30-minute rampable capacity supply, storage participation rules in IR procurement, and potential changes to RUC/RC pricing interaction; the design's success depends on whether operators' flexibility needs are genuinely met by IR pricing or whether hidden costs migrate to uplift.

The MSC emphasizes substantial testing before implementation and calls for a rapid-cycle monitoring and tuning process (not traditional multi-year stakeholder proceedings) to adapt IR quantity calculations, penalty values, and storage state-of-charge parameters — all of which will materially affect PSH flexibility revenue and constraints on charging energy treatment. Implementation timing and parameter lock-in deadlines are not specified in this excerpt, but the opinion signals that CAISO will move faster than historical pace, exposing PSH and long-duration hydro to mid-course design changes.

title: Market Surveillance Committee Update - May 2023
relevance_reason: CAISO's Day-Ahead Market Enhancements (DAME) proposal directly affects energy price formation, imbalance-reserve procurement (a ramping/flexibility product), storage state-of-charge modeling, and resource-adequacy interactions — all core revenue and operational mechanisms for hydro and pumped storage in CAISO's footprint and the emerging west-wide EDAM.
stakeholders: Benjamin F. Hobbs (CAISO Market Surveillance Committee)
Scott M. Harvey (CAISO Market Surveillance Committee)
ai_summary: The CAISO Market Surveillance Committee (MSC) issued a May 4, 2023 opinion supporting the Day-Ahead Market Enhancements (DAME) initiative, which proposes new co-optimized imbalance-reserve products, updates to residual unit commitment (RUC), and improved storage state-of-charge modeling to replace ad-hoc operator load-biasing and improve market transparency. The MSC endorses the proposal as a necessary step toward a west-wide day-ahead market (EDAM) but flags substantial uncertainties: nodal imbalance-reserve calculation methods, storage state-of-charge parameter-setting, and 30-minute ramp-constraint limits on reserve supply are untested design elements with no precedent in other RTOs. The MSC recommends conservative implementation with guardrails, pre-implementation software testing, and a rapid feedback cycle with stakeholders to adapt the design; the imbalance-reserve demand curve — which caps up-reserve prices at $55/MWh and sets penalty values influencing energy prices — will be critical to monitor. Hydro and pumped-storage operators should track parameter tuning during testing and go-live, as the storage state-of-charge equations and imbalance-reserve locational requirements will reshape the value of flexibility and multi-hour discharge capability; the MSC notes this framework has no ISO precedent and will evolve based on operational experience.

ai_summary: CAISO Market Surveillance Committee presentation analyzing the potential impact of the revised Congestion Revenue Allocation (CRA) methodology on historical WEIM congestion patterns ahead of Extended Day Ahead Market (EDAM) go-live. The analysis examines three scenarios: (1) exercise of transmission rights for PACE-to-PACW transfers, estimated to generate $2.34 to $6.96 million per month in congestion rents depending on transfer-capability assumptions (300 MW to 1200 MW); (2) incentives for self-scheduling internal generation in PacifiCorp areas, estimated at $2.2 million per month in 2024 and $1.1 million in 2025; and (3) resulting counter-flow payments of approximately $1 million per month at maximum transfer levels. The ISO committed to further analysis of revised CRA methodology impacts prior to EDAM go-live, with phase-one findings published in December 2025. Congestion rents are highly concentrated in a small number of transmission constraints, with 87–95 percent accruing to the top 20 constraints. The assessment uses historical WEIM real-time congestion and shift factors as proxies, with caveats that real-time congestion may exceed day-ahead levels and not all WEIM elements directly transfer to EDAM pricing.
hydro_read_through: The document does not name hydropower or pumped-storage facilities directly, but the CRA methodology analysis is material to hydro owners because PacifiCorp's generators in both PACE and PACW areas—which include conventional and run-of-river hydro resources—will be subject to these transmission-right and self-scheduling incentives in EDAM. The estimated monthly congestion rent flows ($1.6–$2.5 million and upward) represent revenue that will accrue to or be charged against PacifiCorp-area generators under the revised allocation rule, affecting the financial case for dispatch and transmission-constrained operation of existing hydro units. The concentration of rents in a handful of constraints means hydro output dispatch will be economically sensitive to specific transmission bottlenecks under the new regime.

title: Presentation - Extended Day-Ahead Market (EDAM) Configurable Parameters - Feb 06, 2026
relevance_reason: EDAM configurable parameters directly affect imbalance reserve (IR) pricing, procurement, and the opportunity-cost bidding environment for all dispatchable resources including hydro and pumped storage, plus storage-specific envelope constraints and state-of-charge treatment.
ai_summary: CAISO's configurable-parameters working group completed sensitivity analyses on five EDAM design parameters: envelope constraint multiplier, IR bid cap, IR/RC default availability bids, deployed imbalance reserve factor, and transmission constraint enforcement. Key findings: higher envelope multipliers reduce battery IR procurement and raise IR prices (storage-specific impact); DIR factor and constraint enforcement interact to affect congestion and local pricing; bid caps temper clearing prices. Parallel operations (extended through April 30, 2026) will test envelope multipliers (starting at 85%, assessing lower values), DIR factor (starting at 100%, assessing reductions), and transmission constraint enforcement hierarchies; IR bid cap and DAB cap remain fixed at $55 per tariff. For pumped-storage operators, the envelope multiplier and DIR factor tuning during parallel ops directly affects how much IR PSH can procure and at what price — these govern the opportunity-cost treatment of state-of-charge constraints. Results will be assessed using parallel-ops market cases; no go-live decision date is stated, but the extended parallel window and commitment to post-go-live monitoring suggests continued parameter adjustment risk through mid-2026.

The presentation compares settlement outcomes across three designs using historical congestion data from June 2024, January 2025, and July 2025, finding that go-live EDAM produces materially different charge allocations depending on prevailing vs. counterflow conditions and the magnitude of internal vs. interregional congestion. The analysis is part of the Market Surveillance Committee's evaluation of EDAM design impacts; no immediate vote or deadline is stated, but the document supports ongoing MSC deliberation on EDAM revenue allocation fairness across the Western footprint—directly relevant to how hydro and PSH resources sited on transmission bottlenecks (especially in the Pacific Northwest interconnecting to California) will be paid for energy and congestion services under EDAM go-live.

title: Presentation - Extended Day-Ahead Market (EDAM) Congestion Revenue Allocation - Mar 06, 2026
relevance_reason: EDAM congestion revenue allocation design directly affects how hydro and other dispatchable resources' energy sales are priced and settled across the Western balancing-area seam; Phase 2 evaluation of self-schedule incentives and parallel-flow revenue allocation will reshape revenue capture for hydro exports and intra-EDAM transactions.
ai_summary: CAISO is executing Phase 2 of EDAM congestion revenue allocation design, following FERC's August 2025 approval of a transitional Phase 1 design that launched EDAM in May 2026. The Phase 1 design allocates internal constraint congestion to the balancing area where the constraint sits, and allocates parallel-flow congestion from balanced self-schedules to the exercising balancing area. Phase 2 stakeholder working groups (two sessions completed as of this presentation) are now evaluating design concepts to address two key issues: (1) eliminating or reducing self-schedule incentives that discourage economic bidding, and (2) creating further symmetry in parallel-flow congestion allocation for the CAISO balancing area. The Market Surveillance Committee recommends exploring a negotiated-entitlement approach and has flagged questions about how negotiated entitlements would apply to Western market structures, existing inter-balancing-area operational agreements managing loop flow, and the basis for establishing entitlements (historical flows, dollar limits, etc.). The next phase of stakeholder working groups runs late March through May 2026. Hydro operators exporting across EDAM seams or managing run-of-river dispatch with balanced schedules face direct revenue exposure: parallel-flow congestion allocation affects the net LMP received, and the Phase 2 pivot away from self-schedule incentives toward economic bidding may reshape the value of storage and flexible hydro in managing loop-flow congestion. Owners of reservoir hydro with flexible dispatch and pumped-storage facilities in the Western Interconnection are most exposed.

title: Presentation - Extended Day-Ahead Market (EDAM) Imbalance Reserve Costs Market Surveillance Committee - Feb 06, 2026
relevance_reason: EDAM imbalance reserve market design and pricing directly affects storage and dispatchable hydro revenue from flexibility products and reserve provision; the analysis identifies design choices (15-minute start constraint, 30-minute ramp limits, 0.85 attenuation factor for storage energy usage, reserve procurement levels) that materially drive up reserve costs and reshape which resources are economical to deploy.
stakeholders: Scott Harvey (California ISO Market Surveillance Committee)
ai_summary: Scott Harvey (Market Surveillance Committee member) presents analysis of EDAM imbalance reserve pricing in simulations, finding average reserve-up costs of ~$20–$40/day appear materially higher than efficient-market levels. The high costs stem from five key market design choices: 15-minute dispatch requirement, 30-minute ramp limits, 0.85 attenuation factor on storage energy usage, tying storage state-of-charge to reserve schedules (disconnected from real-time RTD dispatch), and the reserve procurement level and demand-curve shape. These design features inflate thermal commitment costs and create high opportunity costs for storage, making both thermal and storage sources expensive providers of imbalance reserves. Harvey notes some costs may be simulation artifacts (low storage energy offer prices, high reserve offer prices, constraint modeling differences), but warns the high prices may accurately reflect actual EDAM design if storage energy usage must be tied to reserve schedules. The analysis does not recommend specific changes but flags the disconnect between high reserve prices and relatively low energy prices as requiring investigation before market launch.

stakeholders: Scott Harvey (California ISO Market Surveillance Committee)
ai_summary: Scott Harvey presents CAISO's analysis of loopflow congestion pricing and allocation in EDAM, arguing that the go-live design's requirement for self-scheduling to receive congestion-charge rebates creates inefficient use-it-or-lose-it incentives and may shift costs between market participants. Harvey notes that loopflows—inter-balancing-area power transfers that create congestion on parallel constraints—can significantly impact market efficiency and proposes moving toward a long-run financial-congestion-hedge design (akin to PJM/MISO firm-flow entitlements and joint congestion management) that decouples rent allocation from self-schedule requirements. An interim step would assign internal-constraint congestion rents to balancing areas based on flow entitlements rather than self-scheduling. This is relevant to hydro because reservoir and pumped-storage hydro participating in EDAM would face distorted dispatch incentives under the current self-schedule-based rebate structure, particularly in scenarios with large new loads (data centers) and remote renewable generation; loopflow-impact allocation also affects the transmission value and export economics of hydro-rich regions like the Northwest. The presentation does not identify a formal comment deadline or board vote date.

title: Presentation - Market Power Mitigation Issues - Market Surveillance Committee - Jan 16, 2026
relevance_reason: MECHANISM: Market power mitigation design directly affects how hydro and storage are tested for market power and when their offers are capped to default energy bids — the document critiques proposed changes to CAISO's three-pivotal-supplier test and discusses conduct-and-impact alternatives that would reshape which use-limited resources (battery, pondage hydro) face mitigation triggers and cost-cap enforcement.
stakeholders: Scott Harvey (California ISO, Market Surveillance Committee)
ai_summary: Scott Harvey (CAISO Market Surveillance Committee member) presents critical analysis of CAISO's August 22, 2025 straw proposal on market power mitigation, arguing that the ISO has not demonstrated non-competitive outcomes in recent years and that proposed system-level market-power tests applied to constrained regions lack evidence of actual withholding. Harvey contends that counterfactual simulations conflate volatile gas-cost methodology (understated gas input prices) with genuine market power and that applying mitigation to constrained-down regions is unwarranted. He separately explains conduct-and-impact test mechanics, noting that CAISO's competitive-LMP approach caps offers to default energy bids even when a resource's output would have zero price impact — a key distinction for batteries and pondage hydro. The presentation does not state a formal recommendation or next step, but signals Harvey's view that CAISO should require empirical proof of withholding days and accurate cost bases before expanding mitigation design. For PSH and battery owners, this is a critical opportunity to submit comments opposing overly broad mitigation triggers; the August 2025 straw proposal appears to be the active consultation document being critiqued.

title: Presentation - Price Formation Enhancements - Market Surveillance Committee - Jan 16, 2026
relevance_reason: CAISO is redesigning BAA-level market power mitigation (affecting mitigation of storage and use-limited hydro offers) and advancing scarcity pricing — two mechanisms that directly shape hydro revenue through default energy bids, opportunity-cost offer treatment, and energy price formation during tight supply.
stakeholders: Joint LSEs (SCE on behalf of IOUs, POUs, and Six Cities) (Southern California Edison and Joint CA Load-Serving Entities)
WPTF (Gridwell Consulting) (Western Power Trading Forum / Gridwell Consulting)
ai_summary: CAISO is pursuing two parallel tracks in its Price Formation Enhancements initiative. Track 1 advances BAA-level market power mitigation (BAAMPM) by incorporating load-serving obligations (LSO) into the competitiveness test, mitigating only net-pivotal suppliers rather than all suppliers in a failed BAA group, and formalizing a grouping algorithm that includes the CAISO BA itself. This refinement directly affects how CAISO identifies whether hydro and storage operators have market power and thus whether their offers face mitigation — the LSO adjustment should reduce false positives by exempting capacity genuinely needed to serve an affiliate's retail load. Track 2 defers comprehensive scarcity pricing redesign, with CAISO planning incremental improvements (ensuring scarcity prices when load is shed, enhancing pricing when load is 'armed') before undertaking more expansive work; the Joint LSEs (SCE on behalf of IOUs, POUs, and Six Cities) oppose Track 2, while the Western Power Trading Forum urges full development of an energy supply margin framework. The LSO proposal has outstanding design questions for WEIM-only BAAs on handling merchant affiliate allocation. Most exposed are pumped-storage operators and large reservoir hydro with significant market power footprints in multi-affiliate BAAs, and any hydro owner relying on opportunity-cost mitigation exemptions; the competitiveness test changes could tighten or relax mitigation exposure depending on how LSO allocation evolves in stakeholder discussion.

title: Presentation - Price Formation Issues - Market Surveillance Committee - Jan 16, 2026
relevance_reason: CAISO Market Surveillance Committee presentation on price-formation issues and reserve-product design directly affects hydropower revenue through scarcity-pricing mechanisms, reserve-procurement rules, and co-optimization of reserves with energy—all core inputs to hydro dispatch value and ancillary-service compensation.
stakeholders: Scott Harvey (California ISO / Western EIM Market Surveillance Committee)
ai_summary: Scott Harvey, CAISO Market Surveillance Committee member, presents two critical price-formation issues for the California ISO balancing area: (1) real-time price signals in stressed conditions (August 2020 case study shows low real-time prices failed to incent import supply despite high day-ahead prices, and current rules cap prices at $1,000 during non-spinning-reserve dispatch, understating shortage value to suppliers and consumers); and (2) absence of explicit 30- or 60-minute reserve products, forcing CAISO to procure thousands of MWs of buffer capacity via expensive load-conformance purchases (energy bought in FMM and settled at RTD imbalance prices, with costs varying wildly). Harvey recommends CAISO adopt a tiered reserve product with graduated demand-curve pricing (referencing NYISO's 10-step design: $0–$750 depending on shortage MW), co-optimized with energy, but cautions that existing flexiramp and imbalance-reserve implementation flaws (battery state-of-charge accounting, nodal-delivery tests, locational modeling) must be fixed first—work that will take years. Hydropower operators (especially pumped storage and flexible dispatchable units) are directly affected: better-designed reserve markets with co-optimization and scarcity-responsive pricing would raise the value of fast-response capacity and reduce reliance on out-of-market load conformance, increasing revenue certainty and reducing demand-side rationing risk.

title: Presentation - Scarcity Pricing - Market Surveillance Committee - Jan 16, 2026
relevance_reason: Scarcity pricing mechanisms directly affect hydro and storage revenue through energy price formation and penalty-value settings that influence investment signals and intra-day dispatch incentives.
ai_summary: James Bushnell (CAISO Market Surveillance Committee) presents an analysis of scarcity-pricing approaches in CAISO's pricing-enhancements initiative, arguing that penalty-value reassessment is more straightforward than adding new reserve products. The power-balance constraint (PBC) penalty currently stands at $1,000/MWh ($2,000 during 831-trigger conditions) and has remained unchanged for decades; at 2010 value it would equate to roughly $1,500 today. Bushnell argues that higher penalty values would strengthen incentives for storage resources to retain energy for scarce conditions, incentivize delivery of scheduled imports, and improve EDAM's ability to compete for scarce import MWh during tight western conditions. His recommendation is that penalty values be raised and coordinated across markets, potentially stepped up over time once a schedule is agreed, and that major new reserve products should await live EDAM experience. The implication: PSH and conventional hydro with storage capability would face stronger economic incentives to withhold energy for peak scarcity, increasing real-time dispatch revenue during tight periods but potentially affecting energy-market pricing dynamics in both day-ahead and real-time.

title: Presentation - Updated Analysis on Price Formation Enhancements - Market Surveillance Committee - Jan 16, 2026
relevance_reason: CAISO is updating its Bidding Adjudication Algorithm (BAA) under the Mitigation and Pass-Through (MPM) mechanism — a market-power mitigation rule that directly affects how hydro and storage operators' opportunity-cost offers are tested and potentially rejected or accepted; changes to the grouping logic, LSO treatment, and CAISO testing parameters alter the revenue risk and bid acceptance likelihood for use-limited resources.
ai_summary: CAISO's Market Performance and Advanced Analytics team presented updated analysis of eight algorithm variants for the BAA-MPM test, evaluated on Q3 2025 data (July–September). The variants combine three design factors: adjusted grouping logic, addition of a Load Serving Obligation (LSO) component to the Residual Supply Index calculation, and testing CAISO as a balancing-area entity. Adding the LSO component materially increased pass rates across most balancing areas, particularly in import-constrained midday hours in the Pacific Northwest and Central/Mountain regions (PSEI, SCL, TPWR saw +19–21% improvements), while testing CAISO reduced pass rates for several BAAs in peak evening hours (19–21). The presentation does not state a next step or decision date, but the analysis supports continued refinement of offer-acceptance criteria for resource-limited suppliers.

relevance_reason: MECHANISM: Establishes mandatory timelines and conditions for retaining interconnection service capacity and deliverability rights when hydroelectric or pumped-storage facilities cease operations, mothball, or repower — directly affecting whether a hydro owner can preserve its grid position and capacity value during outages or strategic transitions.
ai_summary: CAISO's Draft Final Proposal (May 11, 2026) codifies rules requiring non-operating generating facilities to either return to service, enter the generator interconnection queue, or begin repower construction within specified timeframes to retain deliverability allocations and interconnection service capacity rights; failure to act within these windows forfeits the rights, releasing capacity back to the system. MECHANISM: The proposal creates a hard-deadline retention regime that affects hydro owners planning extended maintenance, mothballing, or repowering. Facilities reaching physical derate (reduced maximum output) lose deliverability commensurate with the loss if the derate exceeds 3 years; those exiting wholesale markets to serve behind-the-meter load are treated as permanent retirements triggering reliability reviews and potential RMR (Reliability Must Run) obligations. SCOPE: All hydroelectric resources in CAISO territory, particularly those contemplating maintenance windows beyond 3 years, repower projects, or transitional mothball periods, are exposed. Generators choosing not to follow notification processes forfeit their rights, and the proposal strengthens ISO enforcement of 90-day advance notice and retirement affidavits. Next step: Draft Final Proposal status indicates Board action is pending (typical CAISO timeline ~Q3 2026); stakeholders should monitor for final tariff vote and implementation timeline.

title: Apparent Ride-Through Failure Presentation_FINAL
relevance_reason: ERCOT ride-through standards (Section 2.13 NOG) establish compliance obligations for synchronous and inverter-based resources to maintain grid stability under fault conditions — a precedent for how storage, batteries, and potentially hydro-like dispatchable resources must be governed in other RTOs, and the enforcement framework (APF reporting, ERM escalation, timelines) shows a model for resource-specific performance requirements.

evidence.quote: RE for Resource with APF, RE must: Develop plan to ensure Resource meets applicable ride-through requirements (maximized or Required Criteria) Submit plan to ERCOT for approval w/n 90 days If ERCOT approves plan, implement it w/n 180 days (unless ERCOT approves longer timeline)

ai_summary: ERCOT presented the Resource Integration Working Group with actions following apparent ride-through failures under Nodal Operating Guide Section 2.13. The framework requires resources with approved exemptions or extensions to submit their maximum ride-through capabilities to ERCOT as a compliance benchmark. When a resource fails to ride-through based on its maximized capabilities, the resource owner must investigate the apparent performance failure (APF), report its cause, perform model validation, and submit to ERCOT within 90 days a plan to meet applicable ride-through requirements, with implementation required within 180 days or per ERCOT-approved extension. Resources failing to ride-through between the required and maximized capability bands (but not below required criteria) are excluded from escalation to the Electric Reliability Monitor (ERM) if the owner fully satisfies the investigation and planning requirements, providing an incentive for resources to design to maximum equipment capability.
hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage. However, ERCOT's approach to ride-through compliance—establishing resource-specific maximized capabilities, linking enforcement to the APF investigation process, and using ERM escalation as a penalty mechanism—creates a precedent relevant to how hydro owners would be treated if they operated in ERCOT or if similar regimes were adopted elsewhere. The 90-day and 180-day timelines for remediation plans show how an RTO structures operational compliance obligations for dispatchable resources; this model could influence how other RTOs (including those with significant hydro fleets) impose similar winterization, outage, and ride-through requirements on synchronous generators and storage assets.

ai_summary: ERCOT reports results of its annual 2026 Under-Frequency Load Shedding (UFLS) survey, conducted May 6, 2026, measuring transmission operators' compliance with automatic load-shedding requirements at five frequency thresholds (59.3 Hz down to 58.5 Hz). All ERCOT TOs met minimum relief requirements, with actual load shed ranging from 6.92% at 59.3 Hz to 31.20% at 58.5 Hz against a total system load of 52,790 MW. Two pending nodal operating guide changes (NOGRR247 and NOGRR226, both effective no earlier than October 1, 2026) will modify the UFLS program by increasing standard stages from three to five, establishing uniform 5% incremental relief per stage, and adding a six-cycle (0.1 second) minimum delay, plus optional supplemental anti-stall stages at 59.5 Hz with 90/120/150-second delays. Six TOs have completed implementation of the new standard stages; four have completed the anti-stall stages. Results show year-over-year improvement from 2025 (e.g., 59.5 Hz anti-stall performance rose from 0.31% to 1.34% at the 90-second delay).

ai_summary: ERCOT's Netted Networks proposal (presented 21 August 2026) offers an alternative registration path to Private Use Networks (PUNs) for co-located load, generation, and battery energy-storage systems. The construct allows Energy Storage Resources (ESRs) to register as market resources (Generation Resources or ESRs), qualify for Wholesale Storage Load (WSL) treatment, offer gross capacity (rather than surplus MW) into the market, and have their co-located load counted as ERCOT load rather than non-ERCOT load. Energy settlement remains netted at the point-of-interconnection, but dispatch and commitment processes gain visibility into the full generation and storage capacity. The proposal compares Netted Networks to existing IGF and non-IGF PUN structures and identifies open policy decisions on load-ratio-share and transmission cost (TCOST) allocation treatment.

However, the Netted Networks construct sets a direct precedent for how ERCOT—which lacks a conventional hydro fleet—structures the registration, visibility, and market participation of dispatchable and energy-limited resources co-located with load. The WSL-eligibility mechanism and the shift from net-to-gross capacity offerings in settlement could inform PSH and run-of-river designs in hydro-rich RTOs, particularly where merchant hydropower or PSH operates behind-the-meter or co-located with large loads (LLWG context). ai_summary: ERCOT's Large Load Working Group is discussing a "Netted Networks" concept (presented August 21, 2026) that would create an alternative registration path for co-located load, generation, and energy storage systems. Under current rules, such sites must register as Planned Use Networks (PUNs) and net their generation and storage against load for settlement and dispatch, which limits ERCOT's visibility into generation/storage capacity and prevents batteries from receiving Wholesale Storage Load (WSL) treatment. The Netted Networks proposal would require all generation and storage at such sites to register as market resources (Generation Resources or Energy Storage Resources), offer their full gross capacity into markets (not just surplus after serving co-located load), treat the co-located load as part of ERCOT's overall load pool, make batteries eligible for WSL treatment, and maintain net settlement at the point of interconnection. Energy settlements would remain netted for the site, but several technical elements (4CP, Load Ratio Share allocation, meter pricing) are flagged as requiring policy decisions. The proposal is in early discussion phase with no stated vote or implementation timeline.
hydro_read_through: This document does not address hydropower directly. However, the Netted Networks construct is relevant to hydro as precedent for how dispatchable and storage-capable resources co-located with load are modeled in wholesale markets. The restructuring principles—separating visibility and dispatch rights (gross capacity into the market) from settlement treatment (netted)—and the treatment of storage as eligible for flexible monetization pathways (WSL) anticipate how similar hybrid participation models might eventually accommodate pumped-storage or conventional hydro facilities operating in coordination with co-located industrial or data-center loads. The framework also shows ERCOT's approach to reconciling high system-visibility requirements with resource-level operational flexibility, a design choice that could influence how other RTOs structure participation models for storage and dispatchable resources.

ai_summary: ERCOT is conducting four integrated stability studies on Large Load voltage ride-through (VRT): (1) a System Operating Limit study to identify frequency and voltage stability limits in areas with high electronic-load penetration, expected Q4 2025; (2) a Frequency Limit Study to assess how inertia and down-PRC (primary frequency response) conditions affect load-loss frequency stability, including the potential benefit of a down-frequency-response Ancillary Service, expected Q4 2025; (3) a Benefits of Transmission Improvements Study evaluating synchronous condensers and GFM STATCOMs, expected Q4 2025; and (4) a Large Load VRT Proposal Study to test whether proposed VRT parameter requirements would mitigate frequency stability issues without voltage problems, outcome date to be determined. The studies cover 3,055 MW of large loads in the West Texas study case and aim to establish SOLs and mitigation plans to keep the system within limits.
hydro_read_through: This document does not address hydropower or pumped storage directly. However, the frequency and voltage stability studies establish the operating environment and control-room constraints that synchronous and fast-response resources (including conventional hydro units if operated in ERCOT or similar grids) must accommodate. The studies identify how much load loss causes frequency excursions and whether down-frequency response ancillary services would improve stability margins—findings that would affect the range of frequency-response products and accreditation criteria offered to or required of dispatchable generation. The emphasis on synchronous condensers and grid-forming control in transmission improvements also signals ERCOT's preference for synchronous support, which could shade future requirements for other resources.

The Committee designated NPRR826 (Mitigated Offer Cap for RMR Resources) and NPRR1264 as high-priority, and designated NPRR1171 and NPRR1213 as high-priority items. ai_summary: The Planning Working Group reviewed PGRR 147 (Allowable Non-Consequential Load Loss Alignment), sponsored by Rayburn County Electric Cooperative, which proposes to expand ERCOT's allowance for non-consequential load loss in transmission planning. LCRA opposed the proposal, arguing that relaxed load-loss criteria could shift planning toward customer interruption as a reliability solution rather than transmission investment. ERCOT Operations agreed, noting that NERC requirements are minimum standards and ERCOT maintains stricter N-1-1 criteria to prevent non-consequential load loss during routine transmission outages. Rayburn and Oncor proposed a narrower approach limited to contractually interruptible customers on dedicated facilities, using predefined operational measures as an interim bridge pending long-term transmission upgrades. ERCOT Operations cautioned that widespread use of curtailment procedures for new large loads could be difficult to manage and blur the planning-operations boundary. Participants raised questions about contractual enforceability and quantification of costs under current criteria. The PGRR was tabled pending further language proposals from Rayburn, Oncor, and other stakeholders.
hydro_read_through: This document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage directly. However, the debate over non-consequential load loss and emergency curtailment as a planning solution sets precedent for how ERCOT (and by extension other RTOs) may treat dispatchable and storage resources' operational flexibility as a substitute for firm transmission capacity. If load-loss exceptions expand, hydro operators may face stronger dispatch obligations during peak conditions and less certainty about when they can schedule maintenance or reserve capacity. Conversely, if transmission planning remains stringent as ERCOT Operations advocates, scarcity signals from load growth will support higher energy and ancillary-service prices where hydro can participate. The outcome also signals how the RTO will treat operational measures and state-of-charge flexibility in large-load interconnection decisions going forward.

NPRR 1278 (Advanced Grid Support Service as an Ancillary Service) and NPRR 1333 (incentive program offering $1,500/MW capped at $25 million for AGS adoption) are tabled for additional discussion; ERCOT explained NPRR 1333 aims to accelerate near-term adoption while technical work continues on the market product. NPRR 1340 would allow Energy Storage Resources capable of sustaining maximum output for at least four hours to participate in the Dispatchable Reliability Reserve Service (DRRS), consistent with PUCT guidance; TCPA (represented by Vistra) supports ESR participation but recommends evaluating whether the four-hour duration should be based on reliability needs rather than the statutory minimum. For 2027 ancillary-services methodology, ERCOT identified a 3,700 MW average underestimation in the 2026 probabilistic model for ECRS and Non-Spin and proposes increasing daytime risk credits to 50% for online/offline resources and 64% for batteries while maintaining 60% nighttime credits.

ai_summary: ERCOT has set heat-rate-based offer caps for the 2026–2027 Fuel-Fired Supplemental Service (FFSS) obligation period under 16 TAC § 25.520. The determination establishes three separate caps—one per resource category—using category-specific heat rates combined with fuel prices and a 48-hour deployment window: Category 1 (on-site fuel oil) heat rate 13.52 MMBtu/MWh and offer cap $17,083/MW; Category 2 (resource-controlled natural gas) heat rate 11.36 MMBtu/MWh and offer cap $14,163/MW; Category 3 (contractual off-site natural gas) heat rate 12.62 MMBtu/MWh and offer cap $2,183/MW. Categories 1 and 2 heat rates are grounded in EPA historical operating data at the 90th percentile from 2022–2026; Category 3 uses ERCOT-approved Verifiable Cost data, with ERCOT selecting the higher Simple Cycle average (12.62 MMBtu/MWh) over Combined Cycle (8.04 MMBtu/MWh) to preserve competitive incentives. The presentation to the Wholesale Market Subcommittee on August 5, 2026, describes the methodology but does not indicate next steps or stakeholder comment deadlines.

ai_summary: NPRR 1337 proposes two changes to ERCOT's Emergency Response Service (ERS), a demand-side reliability tool that pays Qualified Scheduling Entities (QSEs) to curtail load or inject energy during emergencies. Change 1 tightens the Alternate Baseline test so that only loads that are genuinely unpredictable—not merely price-responsive—qualify to bypass the default baseline. Change 2 replaces a single QSE-portfolio-level availability factor per contract term with availability measured separately for each ERS Resource and each ERS Time Period, so high-availability periods no longer offset poor ones within the same term. ERCOT staff supports approval as enhancing reliability. The NPRR was posted May 26, 2026; WMS is voting today (August 5, 2026); PRS will be requested for urgent status and vote August 12, 2026; and TAC review is scheduled August 26, 2026, with ERCOT aiming for September Board review.
hydro_read_through: The document does not name hydropower or storage, but it addresses demand-response program design in ERCOT, which sets precedent for how other RTOs and FERC evaluate the competitive positioning of demand-response versus supply-side flexibility and reserves. Tightening ERS qualification and making availability scoring resource-specific and time-period-specific reflects a move toward more granular performance accountability in demand response; similar logic could be applied to how storage and conventional hydro—both capable of delivering fast response and high availability in critical periods—are tested and compensated for ancillary services and flexibility products. The shift away from portfolio-level averaging to period-level evaluation mirrors the market-design principle (increasingly common in other regions) that capacity and performance should be credited only when it is actually available to meet the highest-risk operating conditions, not hidden in aggregate numbers.

ai_summary: ERCOT's Alternate Baseline Test (ABT) Concept Paper describes a two-step process for assigning baselines to ERS Loads. Step 1 evaluates resources against five default baseline methods (M810, MDP, REG, MBMA, NEAR20); a method passes if P95 is 20% or less and absolute bias is 5% or less. Step 2 applies ABT only to resources failing all five defaults. ABT compares actual load against a reference load calculated from the 10 most recent qualifying same-day-type, non-price historical intervals at the same time of day; an interval is counted as reduced when actual load is at or below 50% of reference load. A resource fails ABT only when the high-price reduction rate exceeds 50% AND the non-price reduction rate is below 20%. The final baseline becomes the single approved baseline used for ERS offers and performance analysis.

ai_summary: ERCOT's BAL-001-TRE evaluation process establishes a rolling 12-month performance scorecard for all generating units' primary frequency response during Frequency Measurable Events (FMEs). Resources must maintain a rolling average PFR score of 0.75 or above; those failing to meet this threshold or scoring below 0.75 for three consecutive FMEs become subject to reduction in their Ramping Reserve Service (RRS) MW allocation based on past performance. Market participants have 30 days from MIS posting to request exclusions for legitimate operating conditions that impaired normal PFR performance; ERCOT makes final determinations, though the PDCWG may be asked to advise. This scheme links frequency-response performance directly to reserve-service capability — a dispatchable resource's ability to provide RRS is capped by its demonstrated PFR capability during disturbances, creating a performance-based ratchet on flexibility services.

initiatives: Capacity Auction Reforms [Active]
ai_summary: ISO-NE presented tariff revisions implementing the Capacity Auction Reforms–Seasonal/Accreditation (CAR-SA) program. The proposals replace Seasonal Claimed Capability and Passive Demand Response audits with Global Maximum Capability, Seasonal Maximum Capability, and Seasonal Dependable Capability values derived from observed performance (effective after August 31, 2027). Qualified Capacity would be replaced by seasonal Marginal Reliability Impact Capacity (MRIC) values; qualification processes would introduce seasonal accreditation, revise import and distributed-resource requirements, establish formulas for ambient-air offer quantities, and align demonstration deadlines with the Capacity Auction Calendar. The Committee debated ambient-air offer construction (formula using Summer MRIC versus expected output at 100°F), treatment of multi-year rate elections, balancing-ratio capping (retaining 1.0 cap proposed but stakeholder concerns on underfunding to continue discussion in August), and Capacity Zone formation using seasonal inputs. The transition from current rules would use QC-to-MCap ratios from FCA 18's third Annual Reconfiguration Auction; concerns were raised that this approach places disproportionate weight on a single final SCC audit value in August 2027. The next substantive update is scheduled for the August 11–13, 2026 Markets Committee meeting.
hydro_read_through: The CAR-SA framework establishes how seasonal capacity accreditation will work for non-energy-limited resources—the category into which most conventional hydro plants fall. The shift from annual to seasonal accreditation and the reliance on observed performance data (rather than engineering claims) will reshape how hydro's winter and summer dependability translate into capacity revenue. The ambient-air formula and seasonal MRIC calculations directly affect offer construction for resources whose output declines predictably at extreme temperatures or whose availability is duration-constrained—both central to hydro economics. The transition mechanism's reliance on a single SCC audit through August 2027 could disadvantage resources with variable seasonal performance if that one final audit does not capture typical conditions. Pumped storage's treatment under these rules—including how state-of-charge constraints interact with seasonal accreditation—is not addressed in this document but remains an open item in parallel CAR-SA work.

ai_summary: ISO-NE staff (Manasa Kotha) presented continued discussion of capacity zone formation under a seasonal construct. initiatives: Capacity Auction Reforms [Active]
ai_summary: ISO-NE proposes Capacity Auction Reforms–Seasonal Accreditation (CAR-SA) with three conceptual amendments affecting capacity qualification and pricing. Amendment 1 addresses Equivalent Forced Outage Rate on Demand (EFORd): ISO-NE proposes to accredit resources based on GADS-reported outage data over 10 like seasons using a continuous methodology, with fleet-average substitution for resources lacking 10 seasons of data; NEPGA proposes allowing resources to demonstrate that replaced or fully remediated equipment should exclude historical forced outages from EFORd calculation, either through demonstration process (limited to twice per ten-year period) or automatic exclusion of outages embedded in planned outages and forced-outage hours exceeding two weeks' duration. Amendment 2 proposes a Capacity Offer Price Threshold Floor (COPT) equal to the Common Value Component—the expected value of scarcity revenues calculated as Expected Scarcity Hours × Expected Balancing Ratio × Performance Payment Rate. Amendment 3 proposes excluding system-backed exports from capacity qualification; NEPGA opposes this, arguing it lacks resource-specific rigor. For outages before June 1, 2028, NEPGA's alternative would exclude forced-outage hours from planned outages and unplanned outages exceeding a defined duration; on or after June 1, 2028, only for resources not holding a Capacity Supply Obligation during that period.

initiatives: Capacity Auction Reforms [Active]
ai_summary: FirstLight Energy proposes an amendment to ISO-NE's Capacity Accreditation Rules-Seasonal Adjustment (CAR-SA) and pay-for-performance (PFP) framework addressing the Capacity Balancing Ratio (BR) cap. Under CAR-SA, resource accreditation is adjusted downward from seasonal maximum capability based on marginal contribution to reliability and forced-outage rates, making the fleet-wide Net Installed Capacity Requirement much lower than under the existing framework. FirstLight argues that a BR cap of 1.0 times Capacity Supply Obligation (CSO) is inconsistent with CAR-SA's lower accreditation basis and proposes adjusting the BR cap to 1.0 divided by the fleet-wide capacity-weighted average Relative MRI of all capacity resources. The proposal includes three implementation steps: (1) CSO-wide adjustment to the BR cap formula, (2) resource-specific caps ensuring no resource's PFP performance obligation exceeds its seasonal maximum capability, and (3) shortfall allocation reducing over-performance payments. Tariff redlines are presented implementing all three steps, with the ISO having expressed concerns about potential distributional inequities under Step 2. The amendment was presented to the NEPOOL Markets Committee on 2026-09-08.

Resources must qualify through a Seasonal Capacity Auction with submission deadlines in December/February (Summer) and June (Winter), qualification demonstration in March/April and September respectively, and auctions in April/May and October. The tariff specifies qualification rules (Section III.15.2-3), auction conduct (Section III.15.4), monthly reconfiguration and bilateral trading (Sections III.15.5-6), capacity performance and payment mechanisms (Section III.15.7-8), and publication of auction data (Section III.15.9). A transition rule applies to resources with prior Forward Capacity Market awards through April 30, 2030, using a blended "Transition Seasonal MRI Capacity" formula that gradually weights toward full seasonal accreditation. Energy storage resources receive special Relative MRI adjustments in winter qualification. Non-commercial resources under critical path schedule monitoring must report quarterly on project milestones and face termination if milestones slip more than two years (Section III.15.A).

However, conventional hydro and pumped-storage facilities are 'Capacity Resources' subject to this seasonal accreditation and auction structure, meaning their revenue model is shifting from a single annual capacity product to separate summer and winter capacity obligations and payments. The seasonal split requires hydro and storage operators to re-qualify twice annually and could alter the accreditation level (Seasonal MRI Capacity or its transition-period proxy) that governs seasonal capacity revenue; the mechanics here—qualification deadlines, demonstration requirements, zonal interface limits, clearing prices by season—set the frame for how seasonal scarcity in each season will be priced and compensated. initiatives: Capacity Auction Reforms [Active]
ai_summary: ISO-NE tariff redlines to Section III.A.21–III.A.23 establish rules for buyer-side market power review and Capacity Offer Floor Price determination for capacity not previously offered into an Annual or Seasonal Capacity Auction. Capacity exempt from review includes: resources ≤5 MW; Passive Demand Response Resources; import capacity not tied to transmission investment; and resources backed by a Load-Side Relationship Certification (demonstrating the Lead Market Participant is not a load-serving entity or receives no out-of-market revenues from one). Resources subject to review must submit detailed documentation including capital costs, operating costs, expected revenues, depreciation, taxes, and discount-rate assumptions to the Internal Market Monitor, which performs a conduct test calculating a break-even price using a 20-year discounted-cash-flow model (adjustable for contract life where documented). If the requested offer price falls below the break-even price and the Lead Market Participant fails to demonstrate lack of incentive to exercise buyer-side market power, the break-even price becomes the Capacity Offer Floor Price. Submission windows vary by auction type: Summer Capacity Auctions associate with Capacity Commitment Periods beginning May 1, 2030 and later allow submissions starting the first Business Day of January of the third calendar year prior; Winter Capacity Auctions beginning November 1, 2029 allow submissions starting June 1 of the third year prior. For Summer 2028 and Winter 2028 auctions and Summer 2029, the earliest submission date is the first Business Day of June 2026. Final submissions are due the first Business Day of the month prior to the relevant seasonal auction (June 1 for Summer, November for Winter). A Lead Market Participant whose offer is mitigated may file a Section 205 cost-recovery petition with FERC within 60 days of auction results if threshold conditions are met, requesting additional costs as the positive difference between the offered price and the Capacity Clearing Price, plus regulatory costs. The pivotal supplier test applies at system level and per import-constrained Capacity Zone, examining whether removal of a supplier's capacity leaves requirements unmet; certain capacity (single-resource offers with one price-quantity pair) is treated as non-pivotal. Results are made available to pivotal suppliers before auction results are published.
hydro_read_through: This document does not mention hydro or pumped storage by name. However, the redlines directly govern how conventional hydro and PSH developers must justify and defend their Capacity Offer Floor Prices—the cost-recovery baseline in ISO-NE's capacity market. Because hydro and PSH are quintessential use-limited resources, the 20-year DCF model, requirement to document out-of-market revenues and discount rates, and conduct test that compares requested price to computed break-even will set the accreditation methodology for their seasonal capacity revenue. The Load-Side Relationship Certification exemption is critical: if a PSH owner or affiliated merchant hydro developer has any financial relationship with a load-serving entity—common in corporate-owned or co-located arrangements—it loses the exemption and must submit full financial documentation. The Section 205 cost-recovery pathway opens for mitigated resources only if awarded capacity in the auction; hydro or PSH receiving a CSO below the break-even price would have standing to seek FERC relief for the MW-month shortfall, but only if the threshold conditions (at least one Proposed Capacity Offer price-quantity pair and Internal Market Monitor determination) are met—a new procedural right affecting revenue certainty.

ai_summary: ISO-NE presents tariff revisions to Appendix A (Market Rule 1) implementing Capacity Auction Reforms–Seasonal/Accreditation (CAR-SA), moving to seasonal capacity auctions with modified resource accreditation based on Maximum Realistic Intra-day (MRI) methodology. The revisions span buyer-side and supply-side market power review, pivotal supplier testing, capacity offer floors, and offer price thresholds—revised to reflect seasonal auction timing and MRI-based accreditation. The document summarizes changes to Tariff Sections III.A.21–III.A.23 with proposed effective date Q2 2027. Follow-up presentations on Definitions, Bilateral Transactions, Capacity Zones, Demand Curves, and Financial Assurance are forthcoming. Stakeholder feedback on redline tariffs is requested by September 21, 2026, with ISO returning in October with incremental changes.
hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or storage directly. However, conventional hydro and pumped storage are accredited as 'Non-Energy Limited Resources' in ISO-NE's capacity market and participate in seasonal auctions. The shift from annual to seasonal accreditation using MRI-based calculations would reset how a resource's seasonal capacity contribution (and thus its offer floor and cost-recovery targets) is determined. For hydro owners with seasonal availability variation, the seasonal auction structure and recalculation of break-even prices prior to each seasonal auction (per III.A.21.3(i)) may materially change their revenue recovery pathway and must-offer obligations, particularly if seasonal median availability differs from annual averages. The revised treatment of capacity offer price thresholds under the initial, transition, and steady-state formulas (III.A.22.2.1.A) affects what hydro and storage operators can offer and still pass mitigation review.

ai_summary: ISO-NE presented and the NEPOOL Reliability & Transmission Committee discussed the Capacity Auction Reforms - Seasonal/Accreditation (CAR-SA) framework at a July 7–9, 2026 meeting. The proposal moves from annual Qualified Capacity to seasonal Marginal Reliability Impact Capacity (MRIC) accreditation over a three-year glide path (2028-29 through 2030-31), with separate winter and summer seasons and auctions. A post-processing adjustment targets energy-limited resource accreditation by correcting the GE MARS model's limitation on charging during constrained hours. Storage and energy-limited resources would face updated accreditation calculations using forced outage rates, duration-based reliability modeling, and a non-firm gas demand curve for winter with a requirement that gas-only resources demonstrate 20-day firm gas contracts or accept lower payment under a non-firm constraint. The Committee raised concerns about whether the seasonal payment rate framework is internally consistent with an annual Net CONE reference, whether the gas constraint reflects a physical or pricing scarcity, whether storage accreditation underestimates real-world charging opportunity, and how class-average performance ratios would be applied during the transition. The ISO committed to return with transition mechanism details in August and to consider import sensitivities, modeling transparency on stochastic assumptions, and whether the BR cap and stop-loss protections on winter capacity sales should be modeled.

initiatives: Capacity Auction Reforms [Active]
ai_summary: NESCOE (New England States Committee on Electricity) proposes three conceptual amendments to ISO-NE's CAR-SA capacity-market redesign for implementation beginning 2028/29. Amendment 1 recommends aligning the CONE proxy resource performance assumption to a NERC class-average EFORd of 4.10% for combustion turbines, reducing the annual MRI-based Net CONE from $14.119/kW-mo to $11.432/kW-mo and seasonal payments from $8.501–$17.885/kW-mo to $7.372–$15.492/kW-mo. Amendment 2 proposes a four-period transition capacity price cap (stepping 1.0× to 1.6× annual Net CONE over the transition) to protect consumers from potential shortage pricing exceeding $3 billion in total seasonal market cost, versus ISO's three-period cap. Amendment 3 recommends phasing in the gas-only demand curve over three periods using proportional blending with today's zero-discount clearing, allowing more non-firm gas capacity (~3,000–3,500 MW) to clear in winter rather than the ISO's proposed hard limit of ~4,500 MW. The document indicates states' positions are still evolving and welcomes stakeholder feedback on these amendments.
hydro_read_through: The document does not directly mention hydropower or pumped storage. However, CAR-SA's core mechanism—seasonal accreditation, marginal-reliability-impact-based capacity payment, and revised demand curves—governs how all dispatchable resources, including conventional hydro and pumped-storage facilities, are credited and compensated for capacity supply. The CONE proxy resource (a combustion turbine) and its performance assumptions set the benchmark against which all non-energy-limited resources, including hydro, are measured for accreditation; NESCOE's lowering of that benchmark would reduce the capacity-payment floor for the entire fleet. The multi-year transition in the price cap and gas demand curve postpones the full revenue impact of seasonal accreditation, giving hydro owners longer visibility into how their seasonal availability and performance factors translate to capacity revenue under the new design. The $3 billion seasonal-cost volatility flagged in Amendment 2 matters to all capacity suppliers, not just gas resources.

initiatives: Capacity Auction Reforms [Active]
ai_summary: ISO-NE's Markets Committee reviewed the Capacity Auction Reforms—Seasonal/Accreditation (CAR-SA) design at its July 7–9, 2026 meeting in Meredith, New Hampshire. The proposal replaces the current annual Qualified Capacity construct with seasonal accreditation based on Marginal Reliability Impact (rMRI) values, separating summer and winter auctions and introducing a winter demand curve for non-firm gas capacity. Key design elements include: Seasonal Payment Rates (SPR) anchoring method, a three-year transition glide path (blending Estimated Qualified Capacity with Marginal Reliability Impact Capacity through 2030–31), resource-specific corrections for storage and energy-limited resources, and firm-gas contract requirements for gas-only resources (16 hours per day across 20 days). The Committee raised extensive technical questions on the firm-gas requirement's relationship to modeled stress events, the storage adjustment's magnitude for short-duration resources, the applicability of class-average ratios to heterogeneous resources, the durability of transition-based investment signals, and the commercial feasibility of the assumed firming costs. The ISO committed to returning in August with remaining transition details and indicated it would consider sensitivities on import availability, storage-charging treatment, and phased gas-contract stringency. The activity schedule establishes a Qualification Data Submission Deadline roughly ten months before the seasonal auction, with resources able to enter through seasonal auctions, monthly reconfiguration events, or monthly bilateral periods even if they miss the primary seasonal deadline.
