ai_summary: MISO's Technical Compendium establishes a reliability-based framework for emerging large loads—data centers, AI computing facilities, crypto mining, and similar computational loads—interconnecting to the MISO transmission system. Large Loads must provide real-time SCADA/ICCP telemetry and, if classified as Computational Loads, phasor measurement units (PMUs) at the point of withdrawal prior to the later of service commencement or September 1, 2027. Computational Loads must comply with ramp limits on real and reactive power changes, meet voltage and frequency ride-through performance criteria during disturbances, and be subject to transient stability, forced oscillation, system strength, and sub-synchronous oscillation assessments. The framework applies scalably based on demonstrated reliability risk and facility characteristics; it complements existing MISO planning (MTEP), interconnection (EPR), and operational processes rather than replacing them. Study results and compliance demonstrations are submitted through MTEP and EPR.
hydro_read_through: Although the compendium targets computational loads, not hydro, it establishes technical and operational precedent relevant to hydro owners. The mandatory telemetry, ride-through, ramp, and stability assessment requirements signal how MISO and Transmission Owners may eventually extend similar obligations to dispatchable resources and storage; the ride-through and frequency-disturbance performance expectations are particularly relevant because conventional hydro synchronous units already ride through disturbances and could face parallel requirements if MISO extends this framework. The forced-oscillation screening (10 MW per five-second window) and system-strength expectations also bear on how power-electronic interactions are evaluated, which matters if MISO later applies similar criteria to hydro plants with inverter-based controls or co-located storage. Load-growth visibility and forecasting requirements affect transmission planning and the value of hydro's flexibility to absorb or respond to large, rapidly changing demand.

ai_summary: MISO proposes the Large Load Addition Resource Study (LARS), a new process for studying 250+ MW loads and paired generation in parallel over 120 calendar days, versus the current sequential approach taking 180+ days. The process limits generation interconnection service to a maximum of 150% of identified load need, requires generation to reach commercial operation within 3 years, imposes a $250,000 nonrefundable application fee plus a ~15% increase in study deposit and $30,000/MW milestone payment, and mandates electromagnetic transient modeling at submission for inverter-based resources. Load and generation must be geographically aligned to the same Local Resource Zone (LRZ) and connected to the same point of interconnection (POI) and point of withdrawal (POW). The process is designed to harmonize with FERC's interconnection-speed directives and produces MTEP-approved transmission for load withdrawal and a Generator Interconnection Agreement (GIA). Stakeholder feedback, addressed on pages 7–10, raised questions on the 250 MW threshold, 150% service cap, fee treatment if projects fall through, LRZ boundary flexibility, dispatch requirements, and modeling assumptions. MISO requests feedback by Thursday, September 10, 2026, and plans to finalize tariff language and file tariffs in Q3 2026.

However, LARS creates a new queue pathway for generation serving large loads, which affects both conventional hydro and PSH owners considering participation in such pairings. The 120-day concurrent study process, the 150% interconnection-service cap, the requirement for geographically aligned generation, and the 3-year commercial operation window all establish new participation rules that differ from the standard interconnection queue (GIP) or expedited processes (ERAS). PSH and conventional hydro facilities would face a new set of submission costs, milestone payments, and modeling requirements if pursuing LARS qualification; the parallel study model and strict geometric and service-quantity constraints may advantage or disadvantage hydro depending on load-pairing feasibility and site characteristics. The 120-day timeline and earlier cost certainty could improve hydro's business case for large-load partnerships, but the modeling and readiness requirements add compliance complexity.

ai_summary: MISO proposes separating bidirectional regulation into two directional products—regulation up and regulation down—to more efficiently manage anticipated Large Load fast-ramping patterns and system contingencies. Simulation analysis on a three-bus, three-unit conceptual model compared four reserve-procurement architectures: existing bidirectional regulation, separated regulation up/down, a new down contingency reserve product, and a combination of separated regulation plus down contingency reserve. For moderate load contingencies (100 MW loss), separated regulation up/down showed cost savings versus bidirectional regulation and is recommended as the next step; for large contingencies (300 MW loss), a combined model (separated regulation plus down contingency reserve) was cheaper. MISO defers recommending a new down contingency reserve product and will evaluate load contingency size further. Stakeholder feedback is requested by September 17, 2026, and MISO will present an update in Q4 2026. PJM is implementing regulation up/down effective October 1, 2026; SPP, ERCOT, and CAISO have already adopted it.
hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydro or pumped storage directly. However, MISO's proposed separation of regulation into directional products fundamentally alters how fast-ramping dispatchable resources compete in the ancillary-services market and recover capacity and marginal costs. Conventional hydro and PSH, both of which routinely provide multi-directional regulation and ramping services, would face both new revenue opportunities (if they can offer lower-cost down regulation than the incumbent mix) and new compliance risks (if asymmetrical up/down requirements demand capability they cannot physically deliver at the required ramp rates or must-offer scale). The cost-modeling work shown here uses DIR (dispatchable intermittent resource) participation as a cost lever in down regulation, signaling that MISO expects non-traditional resources to compete for that product; the implication for conventional hydro's pricing power and role in reserve portfolios depends on how offer requirements and ramp-rate assumptions are finalized in the design phase.

ai_summary: MISO's Business Practices Manual (BPM-032) Section 11, effective December 4, 2026, establishes mandatory ride-through requirements for Computational Loads connected to the transmission system. The requirements specify voltage ride-through envelopes (0.15–2.0 seconds at various voltage magnitudes), frequency ride-through limits (continuous operation at 58.8–61.2 Hz; up to 299 seconds at 57.0–58.8 Hz and 61.2–61.8 Hz), and active power recovery of at least 90% within two seconds following voltage recovery above 0.90 pu. Loads must tolerate six disturbances within 90 seconds and maintain rate-of-change-of-frequency (RoCoF) below 5.0 Hz/s. Transmission customers must demonstrate compliance by the Service Commencement Date using planning studies, models, or operational event data; MISO may require EMT analysis where positive-sequence simulation is insufficient. Operational performance verification procedures are to be established in a future BPM revision.
hydro_read_through: The document does not address hydropower directly. However, these ride-through standards for large computational loads—which often employ fast power-electronic controls—establish the reliability baseline MISO expects during voltage and frequency disturbances. Synchronous generators including conventional hydro are already subject to similar ride-through obligations under NERC standards; this rule codifies comparable requirements for loads, potentially shifting the relative burden of frequency and voltage stabilization. The 5.0 Hz/s RoCoF threshold and the 90-second multi-disturbance tolerance are operational compliance metrics that may inform MISO's expectations for all dispatchable resources during transients, and hydro operators should monitor whether ride-through compliance becomes a prerequisite for interconnection or ancillary-service eligibility as large load penetration increases.

ai_summary: BPM-025-r14, effective December 4, 2026, implements Large Load Interconnection Reliability Requirements into MISO's Operational Forecasting procedures. The manual requires Transmission Customers serving Large Load (e.g., data centers) to submit hourly load forecasts spanning 168 hours ahead and 5-minute load forecasts spanning 6 hours ahead; forecasts must be updated whenever expected consumption materially changes and at least hourly by defined deadlines. Large Load forecast submissions are removed from MISO's statistical models and incorporated separately into the Short-Term and Medium-Term Load Forecasts at the CPNode level. Forecast obligations commence no later than September 1, 2027, or the Large Load's Service Commencement Date, whichever is later. MISO uses the submitted forecasts in reliability commitment (RAC), real-time 5-minute dispatch (SCED), look-ahead commitment (LAC), and in setting Economic Maximum Limits for dispatchable resources.
hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage directly. However, the new Large Load forecasting regime materially affects hydro revenue because it changes how load growth from data centers and large industrial facilities—the source of increased scarcity and higher energy prices—is represented in MISO's commitment and dispatch processes. By requiring separate, facility-specific forecasting of these loads instead of leaving them embedded in regional statistical models, MISO can now dispatch more efficiently to localized demand, reducing forecast error and the frequency of high-uplift scenarios from which hydro typically benefits. The directive that Large Load forecasts are incorporated at the CPNode level into both RAC (which commits generation to meet forecasted needs) and 5-minute SCED (which sets real-time dispatch targets) means that hydro's ability to capture scarcity rents and fast-response premiums depends on the accuracy of these separated forecasts; large misses in Large Load forecasts could either undersupply energy (raising prices and hydro revenue) or oversupply commitment (raising regulation and flexibility demand). The assessment found elevated loss-of-load expectancy (LOLE) ranging from 0.3–1.1 days per year in planning year 2025/26, with capacity shortfalls ranging from 289 to 914 MW across pockets, driven by geographic and topographic constraints limiting import capability. Planned generation investments (0–2,851–3,002 MW) and transmission enhancements (476–2,231 MW import increase) are expected to improve conditions by 2030, though some pockets may see tighter margins through that year. The findings are being incorporated into the LRTP South process, which began in 2026 and will evaluate long-term transmission and generation solutions addressing identified reliability needs. MISO requested stakeholder feedback by September 9, 2026, with a response to be provided by September 23, 2026.

ai_summary: Manual 012 (MISO Business Practices Manual—Transmission Settlements) redefines the treatment of Electric Storage Resources under transmission-charge settlement. ESRs that are MISO-dispatched to provide Regulating Service or Down Ramp Capability, or that have Economic Energy Dispatch Status, may qualify for an exemption from transmission charges; when the exemption applies, the original OASIS reservation capacity is reduced by the exempted amount and TSR Billable Capacity is used for charge calculations. The rule is based on FERC Order 841 and 841-A and Module B of the MISO Tariff. The document specifies that when an ESR charges for Regulating Service or Down Ramp Capability, it does not become network load unless the ESR fails to qualify for the exemption; in all other circumstances, the ESR is responsible for applicable transmission charges. ESR owners must coordinate with the local Transmission Owner to ensure accurate metering and billing determinants are reported to MISO so that exempted services are excluded from network-load calculations.

This rule, by exempting dispatched Regulating Service and Down Ramp Capability withdrawals from transmission charges, creates a pathway that PSH operators could follow if MISO applies the same logic to PSH when operated for grid services. ai_summary: BPM-020 revision 34 updates MISO's Transmission Planning Business Practices Manual Section 5.3.2.2 to establish network-analysis study procedures for transmission service requests (TSR) and Electric Storage Resource (ESR) energy-withdrawal capacity. For ESR energy-withdrawal studies, three modeling cases are used: a near-term case simulating forecasted light-load conditions within the next eighteen (18) months of the TSR request date; an out-year case simulating conditions in the out year using the Light Load MTEP model; and an optional third model examining other system conditions if MISO planning staff determine the analysis would provide sufficient value. Base cases are built using the Model on Demand (MOD) platform updated monthly; MISO modeling includes all previously queued Original and Renewal TSRs with Study, Accepted, or Confirmed status; MTEP Appendix A projects expected in service; generator-interconnection transmission upgrades with signed GIAs; and—for ESR studies specifically—ensures all ESRs in the area and Tier 1 ESRs are dispatched to charge. The document specifies what is not modeled: short-term TSRs (less than one year), redirected capacity, preempted non-firm reservations, counter-flows, and partial-path transactions.
hydro_read_through: The document does not name hydro or pumped storage explicitly. However, MISO's ESR energy-withdrawal study process directly determines how much capacity a pumped-storage facility can withdraw from the transmission system—a core revenue driver because it gates the energy PSH can buy to store. The revision clarifies that ESRs can access energy-withdrawal capacity through TSR, DPP/Surplus/Replacement/DER-AFS, or MTEP processes independently of whether a separate TSR is filed, and that the TSR process can supersede limits from prior studies. The light-load modeling basis (rather than peak-load) and the requirement that all ESRs in the study area be modeled as charging affect how much withdrawal capacity MISO will grant; PSH owners should monitor whether the modeling assumptions—especially the dispatch assumption and the out-year Light Load MTEP selection—reflect their operational needs and whether rollover-right treatment of redirected TSR requests (noted as pending NAESB approval) would affect long-term withdrawal certainty.

ai_summary: MISO presented the SUGAR automation platform deployed in February 2025 for steady-state system-impact studies in the Definitive Planning Process (DPP). SUGAR automates model building, power-flow analysis, and network-upgrade selection to comply with FERC Order 2023 strict timelines. Phase 1 study time compressed from ~93 days (2022 cycle) to 47 days (2023 cycle) to 54 days (2025 cycle); Phase 2 and 3 cycles are targeted at ≤54 business days. The platform includes a new Mitigation Library (pre-approved upgrades from prior cycles) to reduce stakeholder review burden and support alternative-mitigation submissions via response files. Ad-hoc group members (transmission owners, interconnection customers) must review draft models (6 business days), provide alternative mitigations (10 business days), and submit corrected/alternative proposals with response files (.idv) and slider diagrams. Temporary 5-business-day pre-review window begins in DPP-2023 Phase 2 (draft results estimated November 10, 2026; final report Q1 2027). MISO plans further enhancements: FERC-827 power-factor analysis, shared network-upgrade cataloging, improved voltage-mitigation reporting, and portal-based alternate-mitigation submission (target DPP26-PH1 onwards).
hydro_read_through: This document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage. However, hydro developers face queued interconnection requests subject to these study timelines and cost-mitigation processes. Faster study cycles and standardized mitigation libraries (drawing from past approved upgrades) reduce project-development cycle risk and cost uncertainty, which can benefit projects near the back of the queue. However, the shift to SUGAR-selected mitigations and the 5-business-day pre-review window mean interconnection customers must respond within tighter deadlines; hydro developers with limited engineering staff may find it harder to propose alternative mitigations if they cannot quickly build the required response files and slider diagrams. The expanded Mitigation Library also raises the bar for proposing a novel upgrade path—proof of cost-effectiveness versus library mitigations will be required.

ai_summary: MISO Market Subcommittee draft of Module D (Market Power Mitigation) presents revised conduct and impact thresholds for identifying economic withholding, physical withholding, and uneconomic production across Energy, Ancillary Services, and Planning Resource markets. Default Offers substitute a Reference Level (cost-based mitigation cap) when thresholds are exceeded and conduct causes substantial price impact. Penalty multipliers escalate from 1x to 3x for repeat violations within 18 months. ai_summary: On July 15, 2026, MISO deployed emergency resources (EEA 2) during a multi-day heat advisory across the Eastern Interconnect, with peak load driven by severe capacity margins in the North and Central regions. A software error prevented the pricing engine from registering the termination of Load Management Resources (LMRs) around 45 minutes into their deployment, causing real-time locational marginal prices to be set at elevated levels near the Emergency Offer Floor (~$1,000/MWh). MISO declared a Market Implementation Error on July 22, 2026, and recalculated prices per Module C Section 48.3 of the Tariff, resulting in $20 million reduction in seller credits to imports, $30 million reduction in generation dispatch-down charges, $10.5 million reduction in Price Volatility Make-Whole Payments, and $10.5 million reduction in Day Ahead Margin Assurance Payment (DAMAP) uplifts. The recalculation occurred when Ramp reserve resumed at 18:45, with STR reserve violations increasing the Spinning/Operating Reserve MCP by $60/MWh to incentivize deliverability. MISO is implementing processes to identify real-time pricing issues faster and test market inputs during emergency scenarios.

However, the incident illustrates how software errors in emergency pricing can inflate make-whole payments (DAMAP, PVMWP, RNU) that are meant to compensate day-ahead cleared capacity for real-time dispatch deviations—a mechanism that applies to all dispatchable resources. ai_summary: MISO presented analysis of applying Reserve Procurement Enhancement (RPE) logic to Regulation Reserve clearing in day-ahead and real-time markets to address deliverability failures. Today, Regulation Reserves are cleared based only on offers without regard to whether they can be delivered across transmission constraints; congestion frequently renders cleared reserves undeliverable. Enabling Reg-Up and Reg-Down post-deployment constraints on the Regional Directional Transfer (RDT) limit ensures cleared Regulation reserves are physically deliverable when deployed. A 06/02/2026 test case showed that enabling Reg-RPE on the South-to-N/C RDT reduced total production cost by less than 0.001%, separated regulation prices regionally ($16.41 in N/C vs. $13.45 in South), and improved overall dispatch efficiency. Next steps are to continue simulations validating the post-deployment constraint demand curve design and evaluate regulation performance rules, with redlines to Schedule 28-C expected.
hydro_read_through: The document does not name hydro or pumped-storage resources. Hydro and PSH are major suppliers of regulation services in MISO and other RTOs. Fixing regulation deliverability to reflect actual transmission constraints could improve the spatial granularity of regulation pricing (historically uniform across MISO) and reduce the cost of regulation procurement, but it may also penalize or require redispatch of resources that clear as regulation suppliers in constrained areas. How the demand-curve adjustment mechanism will work, and whether it produces tighter (cheaper) or looser (more expensive) regulation requirements at specific locations, depends on the pending simulations and tariff detail; the framework shown here applies to any regulation supplier meeting the locational test.

ai_summary: MISO's BPM-011 (Resource Adequacy) revision r35, effective September 30, 2026, comprehensively governs the qualification, accreditation, and settlement of Planning Resources used to meet seasonal reserve-margin requirements across the MISO footprint. The document specifies methodologies for calculating Seasonal Accredited Capacity (SAC) using a two-tiered weighting system based on Real-Time offered availability during Resource Adequacy (RA) Hours (the tightest 65 hours per Season plus emergency-event hours, capped at 25% operating margin) versus non-RA hours, with conversion to Zonal Resource Credits (ZRCs) for use in Planning Resource Auctions (PRA). Use-Limited Resources—a category encompassing conventional hydro and pumped-storage facilities—are subject to accreditation based on historical forced-outage rates and seasonal availability data, with provisions for class-average accreditation when resources lack 60 days of designated RAR history in a Season. The BPM also covers must-offer obligations, outage replacement rules (including the 31-day rule for extended outages), and treatment of long-term outages and catastrophic events.
hydro_read_through: Conventional hydro and pumped-storage plants registered as Schedule 53 resources in MISO will have their seasonal capacity value (SAC) determined by this accreditation formula, which emphasizes their availability during RA Hours—the periods of scarcest margin when hydro's ramp rate and flexibility are most valuable operationally but SAC is what determines their capacity-auction revenue. The two-tiered weighting means a hydro plant's winter SAC (when it typically has highest availability) will be weighed more heavily if the region's tightest margins occur in winter RA Hours; conversely, a plant with seasonal energy limitations must have sufficient Real-Time offer data over 3 years to avoid falling into class-average accreditation, which may understate seasonal capability. The SAC-to-ZRC conversion and subsequent auction clearing prices set the bulk of capacity revenue, so changes to how RA Hours are selected (currently MaxGen declarations plus the tightest 3% of hours below 25% margin threshold) and the Tier 1/Tier 2 weighting ratio will shift the sensitivity of hydro's capacity payment to operational scarcity.

ai_summary: MISO BPM-011 revision governs seasonal planning reserve margin (PRMR) requirements, capacity accreditation, and resource-adequacy compliance for MISO Market Participants. The document details the calculation of Seasonal Accredited Capacity (SAC) for all resource types, including a two-tiered methodology (Tier 1 Non-RA hours at 20% weight, Tier 2 RA hours at 80% weight) applied to resources' real-time offered availability over three-year lookback periods, with resource-class-level unit commitment power (UCAP) allocated proportionally to individual resources based on intermediate seasonal accredited capacity (ISAC). For Schedule 53/53A/53AA resources (conventional generation), SAC is calculated via detailed loss-of-load-expectation (LOLE) analysis methodology incorporating 30 years of correlated weather and load data and 65 critical hours per season capped at 1,950 hours per season. New resources or those with fewer than 60 days of real-time offered availability receive class-average accreditation based on their fuel type. Hybrid and co-located resources, electric storage resources, demand resources, and behind-the-meter generation each have specified qualification and accreditation pathways. The revision (effective date TBD per revision history) updates demand-resource qualifications, testing requirements, and accreditation processes to support the Planning Year 2026/2027 resource-adequacy cycle.

Run-of-river hydro is mentioned explicitly in the appendix reference structure (Appendix V), indicating it receives treatment distinct from dispatchable hydro; the document does not specify what that treatment is, but the appendix reference signals that MISO has adopted a separate accreditation path for variable hydro. The two-tier weighting (Tier 1 at 20%, Tier 2 at 80%) and the 1,950-hour seasonal cap mean hydro's seasonal capacity credit will reflect availability during peak-risk hours more heavily than off-peak hours, which should favor dispatchable units with flexible operations over intermittent or demand-constrained resources. Jointly owned units and combined-cycle plants receive detailed carve-outs addressing operational modeling choices; the extent to which run-of-river or pumped-storage operations are similarly modeled is not addressed in this excerpt.

ai_summary: MISO commissioned Energy & Environmental Economics (E3) to evaluate eight candidate reference technologies for Planning Year 2027–2028 and beyond. The reference technology standardizes the long-run cost of new entry and directly affects RBDC price caps, shapes, and offer-mitigation thresholds in MISO's Planning Resource Auction. Candidates include gas combustion turbines (Frame and Aero), combined-cycle gas turbines (F-Class and H-Class), 4-hour and 2-hour battery storage, co-located solar PV with 4-hour storage, and coal steam turbines. Evaluation uses quantitative metrics (gross and net CONE on both ICAP and UCAP bases, capacity accreditation under DLOL UCAP %) and qualitative criteria (feasibility, speed-to-build, market representation, forecast accuracy, stability). The study does not independently establish MISO's reference technology decision or set the CONE values MISO will use annually; it is an input for MISO's determination.

However, MISO's reference technology choice directly influences capacity-market revenue for all accredited resources, including storage. Storage candidates (including 4-hour and 2-hour batteries, and solar-plus-storage hybrids) are being evaluated alongside gas and coal, setting precedent for how MISO models and accredits storage resources in its capacity market. A reference technology's gross CONE becomes MISO's demand-curve price cap and feeds into offer-mitigation thresholds; if storage is selected and shows lower net CONE than conventional resources, it could suppress market prices and margins that currently compensate use-limited and peaking resources for seasonal scarcity. Conversely, how the study models storage accreditation (DLOL UCAP %) and energy-plus-ancillary-services margins will establish the framework MISO applies to all capacity resources, including potential PSH entrants.

Resource Classes include separate categories for Reservoir Hydro, Run-of-River Hydro, and Pumped Storage, each assigned a Resource Class-level UCAP derived from probabilistic LOLE analysis of availability and performance during Critical Hours (hours with margin ≤3% of load). Individual resource SAC is then determined as a pro-rata share of Resource Class UCAP based on Intermediate Seasonal Accredited Capacity (ISAC), calculated using a two-tier weighting (20% Tier 1 for non-RA hours, 80% Tier 2 for Resource Adequacy hours) applied to three years of Real-Time offered availability. Planned outage exemptions (Tier 1 and Tier 2) are conditioned on advance notice (120 days, or 31–14 days for Tier 1 with margin tests), with new rules effective December 1, 2026, zeroing availability for any resource offline with Start-Up Time plus Notification Time exceeding 24 hours or increasing such offers within 48 hours of the operating day. Indicative SAC results will be posted beginning September 1, 2024 for Planning Years 2025–2026 and thereafter; initial and final SAC postings are due December 15 and February 15 prior to each Planning Resource Auction, with disputes on ISAC due within 30 calendar days of initial posting.

The planned-outage exemption tiers, triggered by 120-day advance notice and maintenance-margin thresholds, and the new 24-hour start-up-time rule effective December 2026, will directly constrain when hydro can schedule maintenance without accreditation penalty. Since SAC determines capacity-market revenue in the Planning Resource Auction, the timing and mechanics of initial/final postings (December 15 and February 15) and dispute windows (30 days) are critical deadlines for hydro operators to challenge their accreditation before the auction.

ai_summary: MISO has formalized a four-phase Economic Reconfiguration process for Market Participants to request transmission-system topology changes intended to reduce congestion costs. Reconfiguration Requests must be submitted through the MISO Help Center at least thirty (30) days prior to the requested effective date; MISO will make reasonable efforts to grant or deny within seven (7) days of that date for timely submissions. Phase 1 screens requests against six criteria including a minimum 5% loading relief requirement and prohibition of radial load or stability impacts. Phase 2 requires Transmission Owners/Operators to conduct reliability assessments (steady-state and contingency analysis) and MISO to perform market evaluation; both must approve. Phase 3 implements granted requests via Operating Guides and CROW tickets. Phase 4 allows exit if the reconfiguration fails screening criteria, presents reliability risk, or no longer saves congestion costs. MISO will report the top 10 congested constraints at each Reliability Subcommittee meeting. The process applies across the MISO footprint and MISO expects to evaluate 3–5 requests per month.

The 5% minimum-relief threshold and the requirement that no "significant adverse market impacts" occur could constrain which reconfigurations reach implementation, potentially narrowing the avenues through which a hydro operator could itself propose or benefit from topology optimization. ai_summary: MISO's Loss of Load Expectation Working Group presented planned maintenance modeling methodology for use in SERVM and LOLE studies. Planned maintenance rates are derived from five years of GADS (Generator Availability Data System) historical data and applied at the resource level; existing resources receive unit-specific maintenance rates, while new resources with less than 3 months of seasonal outage data are assigned class-average rates. Maintenance schedules are optimized by stacking planned outage days with the lowest daily net load peaks across the simulation period. MISO uses an 80/20 maintenance distribution: 80% of planned maintenance is scheduled based on average peak net loads across all 30 weather years, while 20% reflects case-specific peak net load for each simulation iteration. The maintenance schedule is determined at the beginning of the study and remains fixed by weather year throughout the simulation.
hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage. However, MISO's planned maintenance modeling methodology is directly applicable to conventional hydro and PSH facilities as non-emergency, non-variable generation resources subject to GADS-based outage characterization. Since seasonal accreditation and resource adequacy depends on assumed availability profiles, the 80/20 scheduling algorithm and GADS-derived maintenance rates will determine how much seasonal capacity credit these resources receive in MISO's adequacy studies, which in turn affects their ability to clear accreditation thresholds and their revenue recognition during seasonal periods.

ai_summary: MISO's Loss of Load Expectation Working Group proposes replacing GDP-based load-forecast uncertainty assumptions with a distribution derived from historical variation in utility load-forecast submissions. The current GDP method has weakened over 15 years as electricity consumption has decoupled from economic growth due to efficiency improvements and sectoral shift, while future load growth is now driven by data-center expansion and electrification. The proposed methodology calculates the percent change in load forecasts across three years of Locational Resource Zone submissions on a zonal and seasonal basis, deriving a weighted mean of 0.201% and standard deviation of 2.48% to parameterize a normal distribution. The change increases the probability mass in the distribution tails and raises seasonal PRM% requirements: summer increases from 7.9% to 8.4%, fall from 11.6% to 12.3%, winter from 18.9% to 19.6%, and spring from 23.4% to 23.6% in the PY26-27 study.
hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydro or pumped storage. However, changes to MISO's load-forecast uncertainty assumptions and resulting reserve-margin requirements affect capacity adequacy requirements and the capacity revenue available to all dispatchable resources, including hydro. Higher seasonal PRM targets compress the energy-scarcity margin available to conventional generation and storage, potentially reducing energy-price signals during peak periods that hydro owners rely on for scarcity rents, while simultaneously tightening the adequacy envelope into which additional storage or fast-ramping capacity can be dispatched — shifting the strategic value of existing hydro's flexibility. The shift toward LSE-submitted forecasts also introduces data-center load growth (explicitly cited as a driver) as a formal input to resource adequacy, which is relevant to hydro owners assessing whether load growth will sustain scarcity value or whether the margin expansion will keep prices soft.

ai_summary: MISO proposes Flexible Large-load Interconnection and Transmission Service (FLITS), a framework allowing large loads to obtain interim or permanent non-firm network transmission service (NITS) while pursuing firm service upgrades. The proposal—developed under FERC show-cause order direction (195 FERC ¶ 61,212, 2026) with a filing deadline of November 16—permits large loads to curtail on-demand under predefined reliability conditions without economic compensation, excludes FLITS-served load from Auction Revenue Rights (ARR) entitlements and demand-response resource registration, and requires curtailment to zero MW within 30 minutes of instruction (without violating 30 MW/minute ramp limits for loads >900 MW). ai_summary: MISO has issued redlined updates to its pro forma Generator Interconnection Agreement (Appendix 6 to GIP, styled ZGIA) incorporating Order 2023 queue-reform language and new technical requirements. The document defines interconnection service types (Energy Resource vs. Network Resource), cost responsibility and study procedures, provisional and surplus interconnection pathways, and inverter-based resource (IBR) performance standards (IEEE 2800-2022 compliance for DPP-2022-Cycle and later generators, with staged applicability: DPP-2022 plants must meet Clauses 4 and 7; DPP-2023 and beyond must meet Clauses 5–6 and additional voltage/frequency ride-through and disturbance monitoring). Interconnection Customers requesting exceptions to IEEE 2800-2022 requirements must submit OEM documentation; GIAZGIAs signed or amended with inverter changes on or after January 1, 2025, are not eligible for exceptions to DPP-2022 requirements, and on or after January 1, 2026, for DPP-2023 requirements. The agreement governs facility modifications, surplus interconnection on existing plants via Energy Displacement Agreements, and monitoring obligations (DDR/PMU data for plants >20 MW, stored for 60 calendar days and available within 10 calendar days on request).

Conventional and run-of-river hydro seeking to interconnect or uprate in MISO would be classified under Energy Resource Interconnection Service (deliverable on as-available basis) or Network Resource Interconnection Service (firm transmission), and their cost allocation and study timeline depend on queue position and cluster assignment under GIP Sections 7–9 (not detailed here but referenced). Pumped-storage facilities would additionally face IEEE 2800-2022 ride-through and frequency-response requirements if entering as new IBR plants or undergoing equipment replacement; the progressive tightening of those rules (2025 and 2026 cutoff dates for exemption requests) means PSH upgrades deployed after those dates cannot claim exceptions based on equipment limitations alone. The surplus interconnection pathway (Appendix I) may allow a PSH plant to increase output at an existing site by displacing an incumbent facility's load, though the combined output must remain within the Interconnection Service limit and the incumbent retains all RAR obligations—a rule that directly constrains the revenue upside from adding or cycling storage capacity at an existing interconnection point.

ai_summary: MISO's Large Load Working Group tariff redlines revise Module E-1 and Schedule 53 governing seasonal accredited capacity (SAC) calculation and eligibility for behind-the-meter generation (BTMG) and load-modifying resources. Schedule 53 establishes a two-tiered weighting structure using Resource Adequacy Hours (RA Hours, targeting 65 per season and 260 annually based on historical maximum generation emergencies and low-margin periods) and non-RA Hours to calculate intermediate SAC values; Tier 1 and Tier 2 planned outage exemptions apply differently to each tier. The weighting shifts over time: for 2025–2026 and beyond, Tier 2 (RA Hours) receives 80% weight versus Tier 1 (non-RA Hours) at 20%. BTMG resources must demonstrate sustained four-hour energy production, capability to deploy at credited MW level for specified numbers of calls per season (5 in summer/winter, 3 in spring/fall), notification time ≤ 6 hours, and generator availability reporting; outages longer than 31 days trigger capacity-replacement obligations. Module E-1 redlines address transmission-loss grossing, deliverability of resources (including electric storage resources), forecasted demand identification timelines (November 1 submission deadline), and zonal deliverability charges for resources not in the same local resource zone as LSE demand. The document reflects draft status within an active working group; no vote date or next-step deadline is stated.
hydro_read_through: This document does not directly name hydropower or pumped storage, but MISO's SAC and capacity-market accreditation rules apply to all dispatchable generation including conventional hydro and PSH facilities operating in MISO's footprint. The shift toward 80% weighting on RA Hours (based on historical emergency and low-margin periods) from Tier 2 calculations means hydroelectric resources will be credited primarily on their availability during high-scarcity periods rather than average seasonal output; this raises the revenue value of plants with strong summer/winter performance but could penalize those with variable seasonal availability. The 31-day outage threshold for replacement obligations and the four-hour sustained-output requirement for load-modifying BTMG resources may constrain operational flexibility for reservoir-limited hydro or PSH facilities undergoing maintenance or experiencing low-water years. Deliverability rules and transmission-loss grossing affect how hydro exports from one LRZ are valued when serving load in another, and the November 1 demand-forecast deadline establishes the window in which hydro owners and load-serving entities must coordinate zonal requirements before the planning year.

ai_summary: Potomac Economics' Independent Market Monitor presents a February–June 2026 performance review of MISO South, finding the market remains competitive overall but identifying several design gaps. ai_summary: MISO has proposed the Load Addition Resource Study (LARS), a 120-day parallel study process that evaluates large load and associated generation together using aligned assumptions, rather than sequentially. The proposal requires a minimum load size of 250+ MW per study cycle, with up to 10 load-generation pairs per cycle; a $250,000 nonrefundable D1 application fee; and generation nameplate capped at 150% of identified load need. Generation must be geographically aligned to the load (same load resource zone but not co-located), have firm offtake agreements, and achieve commercial operation within 3 years. LARS outcomes include MTEP-approved transmission for reliable load withdrawal, allocation of generation injection rights (GIA), and a coordinated set of network upgrades. Entergy's presentation to the ERSC on August 7, 2026 supports the alignment concept but questions the 250 MW threshold basis, notes securitization requirements may exceed the proposed M2 deposit of $30,000/MW, and proposes relaxing the 150% nameplate cap when renewable energy or utility-scale battery energy storage systems are used to complement traditional generation.
hydro_read_through: The document does not name hydropower or pumped storage. However, LARS affects the strategic option of co-location and generation-serving-load models — a pathway where on-site or near-site generation (which could include small/medium hydro or pumped storage) serves a large, firm load with limited or no grid injection. The 120-day parallel study and streamlined GIA process could make such arrangements more economically viable by avoiding separate, cascading interconnection queues. The proposed 150% nameplate ceiling and the 'firm offtake agreement' requirement shape whether energy-limited resources like hydro fit the model. Entergy's request to raise the nameplate ceiling for renewable and BESS resources suggests the 150% rule may constrain resources with seasonal or variable output — a category that could include run-of-river or seasonal hydro if enrolled in such paired-load arrangements.

ai_summary: The MISO Resource Adequacy Subcommittee reports three major accreditation and capacity-planning reforms in progress. First, MISO announced in July that solar accreditation will remain unchanged using current fixed hours until DLOL (Demand-Limited Operating Limits) takes effect in Planning Year 2028/2029. Second, for offline resources, MISO is addressing concerns that resources have changed their lead times near emergency conditions while still receiving accreditation credit; three options are under consideration—reducing the maximum lead-time threshold from 24 to 12 hours, assigning zero availability to offline resources increasing lead time within 48 hours before an operating day, or a sliding-scale approach reducing availability 5% per hour above 4 hours to zero at 24 hours—with a FERC filing planned for October. Third, MISO has proposed a new PRMR (Planning Reserve Margin Requirement) allocation methodology allocating to Load Serving Entities based on actual demand during Tier 2 Resource Adequacy hours over the last three years, weighted by effective margins, with a FERC tariff filing planned by year-end for an effective date of Planning Year 2029/2030. The Loss of Load Expectation Working Group separately met in June to discuss wind profile enhancements for LOLE accreditation calculations and unprecedented load-growth pressures on load-forecast assumptions.
hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage directly, but addresses the core accreditation and capacity-adequacy mechanics that govern how all dispatchable resources—including conventional hydro and PSH—earn capacity revenue in MISO. The 24-hour lead-time rule and its proposed tightening affects offline units' accreditation treatment; hydro owners should monitor whether the three proposed alternatives would require faster-response commitments or devalue seasonal or maintenance-driven offline periods. The shift to DLOL and demand-weighted PRMR allocation in 2029/2030 will redefine the hours and conditions under which seasonal or variable hydro generation contributes to resource adequacy, potentially raising or lowering accreditation for run-of-river and seasonal-storage profiles depending on how those reformed hours align with hydro's output patterns.

ai_summary: MISO proposes a new Section 37A to its tariff establishing interconnection and operational reliability requirements for Large Load (defined as load of 50 MW or more associated with any facility or aggregation owned or coordinated by a single or group of entities). Computational Load (data-center and IT-equipment load) is subject to additional Phasor Measurement Unit, ride-through, and ramp-rate requirements. All Large Load must provide basic facility data, modeling, telemetry via ICCP (to be operational by September 1, 2027), load forecasts, and audit documentation to MISO. Computational Load must remain connected during voltage and frequency disturbances and meet transmission-provider-determined ramp limits. Transition provisions exempt Large Loads that achieved Service Commencement prior to the effective date, except upon a Qualified Change (modification increasing demand or repurposing the load). The Transmission Provider may require full compliance if material adverse reliability effects are determined. Failure to provide information may result in delayed Service Commencement, operational limitations, or disconnection.

However, the Large Load requirements establish technical and operational standards—PMU telemetry, ride-through performance, ramp-rate constraints, and demand forecasting—that MISO may extend to or use as precedent for other dispatchable and storage-like resources. The requirement for Computational Load to maintain stable ramp rates and ride-through capability mirrors flexibility and stability obligations hydro operators face; if applied to storage-as-load (behind-the-meter charging), or to distributed generation and battery resources, these standards would shape how quickly any co-located or aggregated resource can respond and how its output must be forecast, setting compatibility rules that affect hydro's ability to serve or compete with these loads. ai_summary: MISO has drafted tariff Section 37A establishing Interconnection Reliability Requirements for Large Load facilities (defined as 50 MW or more) with specific sub-requirements for Computational Load (25+ MW of IT equipment). Computational Load must comply with Phasor Measurement Unit installation, ride-through performance during voltage and frequency disturbances, and ramp-rate limits (up and down) during stable-state transitions. All Large Load must provide basic facility data, electrical models, real-time telemetry via ICCP, and day-ahead and real-time load forecasts by September 1, 2027 (or Service Commencement Date, whichever is later). Transition provisions exempt existing Large Load that achieved Service Commencement prior to the effective date, but any 25+ MW cumulative increase triggers full compliance. The Transmission Provider may require full compliance if material adverse reliability effects are identified. Audit rights permit verification of registration, modeling, metering, and settlements data retained for five years.

The ramp-rate and voltage-disturbance ride-through rules establish precedent for how dispatchable resources are required to behave during system stress, a model that could extend to synchronous hydro plants if MISO tightens grid-forming resource standards.

ai_summary: MISO is revising its Large Load Interconnection Reliability Requirements tariff to take effect November 1, 2027, establishing mandatory facility-data, modeling, telemetry, forecasting, and ride-through and ramp-rate requirements for loads ≥50 MW. The Business Practices Manual is to be developed June 2026–December 2026 to detail implementation.

ai_summary: MISO completed voltage-stability analysis for MTEP26 under two transfer scenarios: Manitoba Hydro/US Interface (export from Minnesota and North Dakota to Manitoba, 2031 winter, limiting voltage-stability transfer level 540 MW) and Illinois Import (MISO Classic to Illinois under Illinois' 2040 coal-retirement mandate, 2031 and 2036 summer peak). hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower resources by name; it addresses voltage stability as a transmission-constraint mechanism. Voltage-stability binding in Illinois Import scenarios driven by coal-unit retirement reflects loss of synchronous-machine reactive-power supply. Where synchronous coal units retire, voltage support must come from other sources—hydro and pumped-storage units are the primary existing synchronous resources in the footprint. Tighter voltage-stability constraints reduce maximum transfer limits into load pockets, which can reduce arbitrage revenue for generators selling into importing regions and may increase must-dispatch pressure in export regions where hydro assets are concentrated (particularly Manitoba interface scenarios). The worst-case vs. best-case spread (4,780 MW vs. 10,250 MW in 2031) shows how sensitive transfer capacity is to reactive-resource composition, raising the question whether MISO will compensate synchronous-resource owners for reactive-power provision as coal exits the system.

ai_summary: MISO proposes to exempt Electric Storage Resource (ESR) charging from transmission service requirements (TSR) when ESR transactions are offered with Economic dispatch status and provide grid services such as regulation, ramping, or energy-market participation—distinguishing economically-dispatched ESR from self-scheduled or traditional load. ESR charging with Self-Schedule dispatch status will continue to require TSR. The proposal aligns with FERC Order 841 and 841-A guidance that ESR providing grid services should not bear the same transmission charges as end-use load. MISO will move the proposal from the Planning Subcommittee to the PAC in August 2026, with a feedback deadline of August 7, 2026, and targets tariff filing by end of 2026. MISO will separately record and audit ESR charging and discharging to ensure operation continues as a grid service, with potential penalties including market removal for violation.

This framework enables co-located hydro and pumped-storage operations under state law, directly expanding the strategic options for hydro owners to serve large on-site loads (e.g., data centers) and avoid transmission congestion and market-power mitigation. title: 20260716 LLWG Item 06a Gen and Load Alignment Issue Acceptance

The proposal addresses a procedural bottleneck where signed Generator Interconnection Agreements (GIAs) are currently required before generation can be included in load studies, creating timing mismatches. MISO reports 27 GW of large load complete or under study in MTEP26, with 34 GW of newly-signed GIAs added in the past year, indicating rapid co-arrival of load and generation. For hydro owners, accelerated load-aligned transmission planning will expose more clearly which regions face generation scarcity (raising scarcity-pricing upside) and where existing hydro capacity becomes strategically constrained or critical to reliability — improving the business case for uprates, resource adequacy accreditation, and interregional export capability. title: 20260716 LLWG Item 06b Generation and Load Alignment Presentation
relevance_reason: MECHANISM: Accelerated interconnection and transmission study process for large loads with co-located generation (250+ MW threshold, 120-day combined study timeline) directly affects hydro/PSH revenue optionality—owners evaluating co-location, resource-adequacy coordination, and generation injection rights in ballpark of large industrial loads now face a faster, parallel study pathway that could reshape transmission-cost allocation and permit generation to serve load without full network injection, altering dispatch incentives and scarcity value.
ai_summary: MISO proposes a new streamlined process for studying large loads (250+ MW+) paired with associated generation in parallel, rather than sequentially, aiming to achieve MTEP approval and full study completion within 120 days (vs. 180+ days in current serial process). Outcomes include allocation of generation injection rights, transmission service for reliable load withdrawal, and optimized network upgrades; the proposal harmonizes with FERC's show-cause order (Paragraphs 114–118) on efficient infrastructure build to support large loads. The process imposes a $250,000 nonrefundable application fee per party, requires generation ≤150% of identified load need with firm offtake agreement, full site control through point of interconnection, and ability to reach commercial operation within 3 years; generation must transition to normal interconnection queue if load goes away. This is particularly relevant to pumped-storage and large hydro operators evaluating co-location with industrial or data-center loads—the faster study and clearer transmission-cost allocation could unlock new partnership models—and to all hydro owners tracking transmission-planning acceleration and the precedent it sets for generation-load nexus outside traditional firm-injection assumptions. Stakeholder feedback due July 30, 2026; tariff filing expected September 2026.

title: 20260716 LLWG Item 07b Non Firm Large Load

ai_summary: MISO proposes a Large Load Participation with non-firm Transmission option allowing data centers and other large loads to interconnect expeditiously without procuring firm transmission service, subject to curtailment under grid stress. The proposal touches resource adequacy (whether non-firm loads have capacity obligations), day-ahead/real-time energy and ancillary-service market participation, curtailment prioritization, and settlement—all of which reshape dispatch incentives and scarcity pricing that hydro relies on. title: 20260716 LLWG Item 07c BITS Proposal Alliant Energy
relevance_reason: BITS enables large loads to interconnect and ramp into service on an interim basis while transmission upgrades are constructed, directly affecting hydro's strategic options for co-located load service, behind-the-meter arrangements, and the economics of load growth as a driver of scarcity value.
ai_summary: Alliant Energy proposes Bridge Interim Transmission Service (BITS), a non-firm interim transmission product for large loads in MISO that allows service to begin once load interconnection studies are complete and local facilities are built, while required network upgrades are under construction—automatically converting to firm Network Integration Transmission Service (NITS) when upgrades finish. BITS requires load to have metering and telemetry in place, 24/7 contact availability, and ability to reduce load in 30 minutes if curtailed; loads are backed by accredited capacity resources and included in Module E forecasts. This removes a timing mismatch that has deterred large-load interconnection: hydro owners co-locating loads or offering behind-the-meter service can now ramp customers into service faster, capturing scarcity premiums from load growth without waiting years for transmission buildout. The proposal aligns with FERC's Large Load Show Cause Order (EL26-70) for MISO; Alliant seeks stakeholder feedback by August 7, 2026, and proposes FERC filing in Q4 2026 with implementation March 2027.

title: 20260716 LLWG Item 08 Firm Service Step Up (LLWG 2026 1) Draft Tariff

ai_summary: MISO is establishing a 'Firm Service Step Up' tariff to allow Large Load customers to secure incremental firm transmission service before full transmission upgrades are complete, in blocks of 25 MW minimum with in-service dates up to 36 months post-approval and aggregate capped at the full-load planning level. This accelerates data-center and industrial-load interconnection phasing, creating intermediate demand milestones that increase the certainty and stacking opportunities for hydro-based co-located or behind-the-meter load supply. Hydro owners (especially those in MISO footprint or considering it) should monitor MISO resource-adequacy and seasonal energy studies to assess whether accelerated load stepping raises scarcity rents during high-load, low-hydro periods, and whether co-location tariffs allow existing hydro to contract with stepping loads at intermediate thresholds.

title: 20260716 LLWG Item 09 Large Load Interconnection Reliability Requirements BPM Development
relevance_reason: MISO's proposed Large Load interconnection framework establishes reliability and operational requirements that directly affect interconnection obligations and grid-integration costs for dispatchable resources (including hydropower and pumped storage) co-located or competing for grid capacity with large industrial loads.
ai_summary: MISO is developing a new Large Load BPM-032 (Business Practices Manual) and related tariff framework to govern interconnection and operational reliability requirements for large load customers, with a hub-and-spoke implementation model where the Large Load BPM sets requirements and existing BPMs (BPM-020, BPM-013, BPM-031, BPM-025, BPM-002) supply supporting processes. The framework covers the full interconnection lifecycle from design through in-service operations, with initial focus on interconnection reliability and operational requirements; future phases will address stability assessment, oscillation, PMU, and compliance monitoring. MISO's Tariff filing is targeted for July 2026, and the BPM portfolio is scheduled for finalization by October 1, 2026, with LLWG review cycles on August 27 (first draft) and mid-September (near-final). For hydro and PSH owners, this matters because large industrial loads competing for interconnection queue positions, transmission capacity, and grid reliability resources (particularly voltage support and ride-through capability) may face new facility-data, modeling, and operational verification requirements that shift cost allocation or delay service commencement—affecting the economics of co-located or adjacent hydro/PSH interconnections and increasing modeling/compliance burden on existing hydro plants if brought into Large Load validation scopes.

title: 20260716 MUG Item 08 Large Loads Operating Modeling Requirements.pdf

ai_summary: MISO establishes detailed network and commercial modeling requirements for large load facilities (those where a single breaker opening/closing changes load by >50 MW), requiring explicit device-level representation of generators, battery-energy storage systems, and demand-response resources rather than aggregation. Behind-the-meter generation ≥5 MW must be individually metered and modeled; generation at large-load facilities can participate in markets via traditional GIA, pseudo market generation, or ZGIA (zero-injection generation interconnection), with dispatch instructions flowing through MISO's centralized mechanism. Large loads must establish separate CPNodes (pricing/settlement nodes) to prevent load-distribution skew between day-ahead and real-time models. This directly affects hydro owners with co-located generation or storage at large industrial facilities—they face clearer rules on whether plant-level generation participates in MISO markets or remains behind-the-meter, and how storage (BESS) and ramp-support devices are metered and dispatched. Feedback is due Monday, July 31, 2026.

title: New Issue - Generation and Load Alignment

For hydro owners, coordinated load-generation planning affects both the pace and location of transmission expansion (raising or constraining hydro export capability) and the visibility of load-driven scarcity that drives energy and capacity revenues; misalignment between load forecasting and generation planning can also distort queue discipline and interconnection costs, which cascade to existing hydro deliverability and valuation.

title: New Issue - Non Firm Large Load

MECHANISM: Non-firm load participation raises two direct concerns for hydro owners. First, if non-firm large loads are NOT counted toward resource-adequacy requirements (or counted with heavy discounts), the RA bar for other resources including hydro rises, while loads receiving scarcity benefit bear no capacity obligation — this inverts normal cost-allocation. Second, if non-firm loads ARE curtailed preferentially during scarcity events, hydro operators face reduced dispatch value in real-time scarcity periods, since the non-firm load absorbs the curtailment instead of pushing higher locational prices. MISO's design choices on RA treatment and curtailment-dispatch rules will determine whether non-firm loads are free-riders on hydro's scarcity value or are appropriately penalized. This affects all hydro in MISO, particularly reservoir and run-of-river operators in tight seasonal periods.

Feedback on Future scenarios is due June 17, 2026; solutions will be developed in 2027, making this the foundational study for MISO transmission expansion over the next decade.

Hydro and PSH developers in MISO—especially those pursuing modular or multi-party transmission solutions—will face revised upgrade-cost responsibility rules and faster application processing; the timing of FERC filings and portal releases will compress the compliance window for projects already in queue or filed under prior rules.

title: 20260709 MSC Item 02c DERWG Status Report.pdf
