No comment deadline or vote date is stated in this status report.

title: 20260709 MSC Item 03 Liaison Report.pdf
relevance_reason: MECHANISM: Multiple items touch hydro/PSH revenue and obligations — ancillary-services pricing (Regulation and Up Ramp Capability demand curves), reserve deliverability for DA/RT markets, and transmission seams management affecting interregional hydro dispatch and revenue.
ai_summary: MISO filed tariff revisions (ER26-2705-000, effective date August 4, 2026) to update demand curves for Regulation, Spinning Reserves, and Up Ramp Capability (URC) in response to rapid solar penetration and net-load ramping stress. Regulation and Spinning curves are being simplified to a single $98/MWh value, and the URC cap rises to $96/MWh to strengthen market signals during tight conditions. Separately, MISO is advancing 'Enhance Reserve Deliverability for DA and RT Markets' (MSC-2026-2) with most stakeholder feedback supportive, and pursuing updates to the Freeze Date congestion-management construct along MISO seams (jointly with PJM, SPP) to improve interregional coordination. These changes directly affect the price and procurement of flexibility and ramping products hydro supplies; URC and Regulation are primary revenue streams for dispatchable hydro and pumped storage. No comment deadline is stated for the demand-curve filing beyond FERC's statutory review.

title: 20260709 MSC Item 04a FERC Status Report.pdf
relevance_reason: MISO's demand curve updates for regulation, spinning reserves, and up-ramp capability directly affect the ancillary-services revenue hydro operators earn; the co-located resource dispatch rule affects strategic dispatch options for hybrid and co-located hydro; and uninstructed deviation settlement changes alter operational compliance obligations and economic incentives for all dispatchable units including hydro.
ai_summary: MISO filed three tariff changes: (1) Demand Curve update (ER26-2705-000, effective August 4, 2026) revising the demand curves for Regulation and Spinning Reserves and the Up Ramp Capability product in Day-Ahead and Real-Time Markets — hydro's core ancillary-service revenue streams. (2) Interconnection Service Limit Constraint for Co-located Resources (ER26-1915-000, filed 3/25/26, amended 6/11/26 for later implementation) allowing co-located resources to dispatch more efficiently within their interconnection limits — relevant to owners of hybrid hydro-solar or hydro-wind plants seeking optimized dispatch. (3) Uninstructed Deviation Settlement Charges (ER26-1521-000, accepted by FERC 5/29/26, effective 6/1/26) modifying settlement rules to incentivize reduction of uninstructed deviations — affects all dispatchable units including hydro by changing the economic penalty structure for unscheduled output. Ancillary-service demand curves are particularly material to large, responsive generators; co-located rules widen strategic options for mixed-renewable portfolios; uninstructed-deviation incentives reshape operational discipline across all hydro plants.

title: 20260709 MSC Item 04c ARR FTR TCM Quarterly Results.pdf
relevance_reason: ARR/FTR transmission revenue allocation and congestion-rent distribution directly affects hydro's transmission-dependent revenue stream and capacity value in MISO.
ai_summary: MISO reports quarterly Transmission Customer Metric (TCM) results measuring what portion of day-ahead congestion revenue is returned to transmission customers via ARR/FTR credits versus retained by non-transmission customers. The 2025–2026 planning year shows 60% TCM, with 2026–2027 at 95% (partial-year data through June 29, 2026). The metric tracks total DA congestion revenue ($1.845B in 2025–2026), splits between transmission-customer returns ($1.102B) and non-transmission-customer revenue ($743M). Seasonal variation is substantial: winter 2025 TCM was 50%, while summer 2024 peaked at 92%. This directly impacts reservoir and pumped-storage hydro located in congested zones—a higher TCM means more congestion rent flows back to hydro owners with ARRs, improving revenue from transmission-constrained dispatch; lower TCM diverts that rent elsewhere. The metric has trended upward since 2020 lows (55% in 2020–2021), suggesting improving transmission-customer treatment, but shows high volatility by season and year.

title: 20260709 MSC Item 06 IMM 2025 State of the Market Recommendations.pdf
relevance_reason: Independent Market Monitor recommendations on capacity accreditation, emergency-range penalties, storage dispatch optimization, real-time capacity products, and interchange optimization directly affect hydro and PSH revenue through RA/accreditation rules, ancillary-service and reserve payments, and real-time energy pricing mechanisms.
stakeholders: David Patton, PhD (MISO Independent Market Monitor (Potomac Economics))
ai_summary: MISO's IMM presented 2025 State of the Market findings and six new recommendations to the Market Subcommittee on July 9, 2026. Key proposals affecting hydro and PSH include: (1) improved capacity accreditation with corrections to maintenance-margin calculations and modified off-control unit treatment (2025-5); (2) penalties on units failing to provide emergency output, with estimated impact of $5.6M on coal and $12M on gas/oil emergency-range capacity payments (2025-6); (3) reduced make-whole and reserve payments for deviating resources to strengthen dispatch-following incentives (2025-2); and (4) revival of existing recommendations for a real-time capacity product for 2–4 hour start resources (2020-1) and look-ahead dispatch optimization for storage management (2021-4). The report also flags 26.6 GW of projected load additions by 2030 and evening ramp demands up 50% year-over-year, driven by solar growth. No comment deadline or vote date is stated in this summary document, but the recommendations are now before the Market Subcommittee for consideration of tariff filing. Hydro and PSH owners benefit from tighter accreditation rules that reduce overstated capacity claims by competitors, from enhanced real-time products that play to their flexibility, and from optimization of storage dispatch timing; they face potential penalties if emergency-range claims are overstated.

title: 20260709 MSC Item 07 IMM Quarterly Report.pdf
relevance_reason: IMM quarterly market-monitor report documents energy price formation volatility, storage resource participation and dispatch efficiency, contingency reserve shortages, capacity accreditation methodology, and interchange optimization affecting real-time pricing—all directly material to hydro revenue and PSH dispatch strategy.
ai_summary: Potomac Economics' Spring 2026 IMM quarterly report to MISO Market Subcommittee (July 9, 2026) identifies rising evening net-load ramp demand (averaging 15 GW between 3–7 pm, up 45% year-over-year), 20 shortage-pricing intervals (nearly double prior year), and 187 intervals with negative system-wide prices as solar penetration increases. Energy Storage Resources (ESRs) now comprise 1.3 GW capacity, setting system and local prices in 5% and 16% of intervals respectively and providing 28% of regulation; a software flaw caused 7% ESR unavailability when outside state-of-charge limits, dispatching units inefficiently (e.g., above-max ESRs discharging into negative-price hours, below-min ESRs charging at >$200/MWh), now addressed with a July software fix. The report recommends optimizing MISO–SPP/PJM interchange through alternate real-time dispatch cases to lower volatility and average energy prices by ≥$2/MWh (saving >$40 million/year), and shifting existing-solar accreditation from 2–5 pm (68% summer) to 4–7 pm (∼50%) to correct over-crediting that artificially suppressed 2026 PRA clearing prices and reduced summer bids by $240/MW-day. Hydro and PSH owners should track storage accreditation methodology changes and price-volatility patterns as ESR fleet grows; the interchange optimization recommendation indicates MISO may adopt real-time co-optimization mechanics that would affect locational value and ramping-product revenue.

title: 20260709 MSC Item 08 2026 Biennial Review of MSC Inactive Issues on MISO Dashboard.pdf
relevance_reason: Storage-as-transmission asset (MSC-2020-1) and hybrid resource participation rules (MSC-2020-3) are among nine inactive issues under biennial review; both directly affect PSH participation models and revenue-recognition pathways, though both remain deprioritized for 2026.
ai_summary: MISO's 2026 biennial review recommends keeping all nine inactive Market Subcommittee issues in inactive status, including MSC-2020-1 (Using Storage as a Transmission Asset to Provide Market Services) and MSC-2020-3 (Enhanced Hybrid Resource Participation Model). Both issues were placed inactive in December 2022 and remain deprioritized due to competing initiatives—MSC-2020-3 is contingent on separate hybrid-resource work (MSC-2020-2) for which MISO has requested a delayed implementation date beyond June 2026. This preserves the current treatment of PSH and co-located hydro-storage hybrids under baseline participation rules rather than advancing alternative frameworks that could unlock additional revenue streams or operational flexibility. The next biennial review is scheduled for 2028, meaning no near-term market-design changes are anticipated for storage or hybrid resources in MISO.

title: 20260709 MSC Item 08 Improve Market Monitoring and Mitigation (MSC-2026-5)_IMM Module D Stakeholder Feedback.pdf
relevance_reason: MISO's Independent Market Monitor proposes revisions to market-monitoring and mitigation rules (Module D) that directly touch offer validation, commitment-cost caps during tight conditions, and reference-level development for demand-response resources — mechanisms that affect how dispatchable and use-limited resources (including hydropower and PSH) are mitigated and priced in real-time and emergency conditions.
stakeholders: Carrie Milton (Potomac Economics (MISO Independent Market Monitor))
ai_summary: The MISO Independent Market Monitor (Potomac Economics) presented stakeholder feedback on proposed Module D revisions to market-monitoring authority, duty-of-candor requirements, transmission withholding surveillance, and cost caps on startup/no-load offers during emergency-energy events and tight conditions. Key findings: Entergy and OMS MWG support IMM verification and capping of startup and no-load costs during emergencies (addressing very high offers submitted during winter storms not otherwise validated under tariff); the IMM is developing clarified authority to assess reference levels for demand-response and validate opportunity-cost components of startup offers (including costs from regulatory or emissions-based start restrictions). Redlined tariff language addressing stakeholder concerns on duty of candor scope, transmission "full capability" definition, and rule clarity is expected. Most affected are generators offering into tight/emergency conditions and demand-response resources used to validate reference levels; no vote date is stated.

title: 20260709 MSC Item 09 2026 Biennial Review of MSC Inactive Issues on MISO Dashboard.pdf
relevance_reason: MISO's biennial review of inactive market-design issues includes three proposals directly touching hydro and PSH revenue and participation: storage-as-transmission (MSC-2020-1), hybrid-resource participation (MSC-2020-3), and uncertainty products (MSC-2021-9), all held inactive pending other work — their eventual reactivation will reshape how PSH and hybrid hydro participate in MISO's markets.
ai_summary: MISO's 2026 biennial review recommends keeping nine market-design issues inactive, including three with direct hydro impact: MSC-2020-1 (Using Storage as a Transmission Asset to Provide Market Services), MSC-2020-3 (Enhanced Hybrid Resource Participation Model), and MSC-2021-9 (Uncertainty Product in DA, RT, AS). All three remain inactive due to other competing priorities and contingencies—MSC-2020-3 explicitly waits on completion of a separate hybrid-resource initiative (MSC-2020-2) for which MISO requested a delayed implementation beyond June 2026. MSC-2020-1 has been inactive since December 2022; MSC-2021-9 was reactivated in February 2024 but returned to inactive status in November 2024. These issues, once active, would expand PSH's ability to offer grid services beyond energy and ancillary services, unlock hybrid participation in MISO's markets, and introduce flexibility products that could shift PSH's revenue sources—but no work is scheduled before the next biennial review in 2028.

title: 20260709 MSC Item 09 MSC Issue Status Change Recommendations.pdf
relevance_reason: The document addresses the Uninstructed Deviation Enhancement (UDE) Flag, which touches settlement rules and dispatch compliance affecting how hydro and other dispatchable resources are charged or credited for deviations from dispatch instructions—a direct obligation and settlement mechanism for hydro operators.
ai_summary: MISO implemented the Uninstructed Deviation Enhancement (UDE) Flag in November 2025, with settlement enhancements becoming effective June 1, 2026. The MSC recommends closing this issue (MSC-2024-7) as Completed. The UDE flag modifies how deviations from dispatch instructions are metered and settled; hydro and other dispatchable resources must now comply with revised settlement rules that took effect June 1, 2026, affecting how they are charged or credited for off-dispatch performance. The mechanism is live; no further stakeholder action is requested, but operators should verify their settlement systems align with the June 1, 2026 rules.

title: 20260709 MSC Item 11 FTR-ARR Market Enhancements (MSC-2025-5).pdf
relevance_reason: MISO is evaluating the Auction Revenue Right (ARR) nomination and Financial Transmission Rights (FTR) allocation process, which directly affects how transmission-hedging revenue flows to generation owners, including hydropower and pumped-storage facilities that rely on point-to-point FTR positions for congestion hedging and revenue certainty.
ai_summary: MISO is conducting a holistic review of its ARR/FTR market under FERC Order 681/681-A compliance constraints, with focus on the ARR nomination process (Reference Year, definition of baseload supply resources), changes to the allocation of ARRs into monthly MPMA auctions, and improvements to transmission-outage reporting incentives. The current ARR allocation uses a fixed Reference Year tied to historical transmission usage to balance stability against gaming and accords long-term (10-year rollover) financial rights to Load Serving Entities for power supply hedging; MISO is evaluating whether the Reference Year, RSP definition, or tariff execution rules should be modified, while ensuring full funding of existing LTTRs and no introduction of new gaming opportunities. MISO requests stakeholder feedback by July 23, 2026, and will present next steps and proposed outage-reporting mechanisms at the August MSC meeting. Most exposed are generation owners (particularly hydropower and storage) whose ARR holdings and FTR self-scheduling optionality depend on stable path valuations; changes to Reference Year or baseload definitions could shift which generation types retain long-term transmission-hedge access.

title: 20260709 MSC Item 12 Enhance Reserve Deliverability for DA and RT Market (MSC-2026-2).pdf
relevance_reason: MISO's Regulation reserve market performance and clearing mechanism directly affects hydro and pumped-storage revenue from ancillary services (the largest and most volatile reserve product in MISO), the treatment of battery entry into Regulation markets, and potential automation of performance-based disqualification rules that could reshape how dispatchable and storage resources compete for reserve procurement.
ai_summary: MISO staff presents an analysis of Regulation reserve clearing and performance deterioration: Regulation requirements roughly doubled on July 1, 2024 (to ~800 MW base), Regulation reserve prices rose 53% and mileage prices 71% year-over-year in 2025, yet non-performance penalties reached 31% of total Regulation revenue by 2025, with gas resource penalties rising more than 2x year-over-year. The document identifies that (1) Regulation performance is assessed only in settlement, after-the-fact, with no automated real-time feedback loop to disqualify poor performers (unlike offline Supplemental and STR); and (2) coal and gas performance has deteriorated while batteries have entered as significant Regulation suppliers. MISO staff indicate they are evaluating options to improve real-time clearing and performance monitoring, with next steps to follow. Pumped-storage operators should monitor this closely because: (i) rising Regulation prices increase PSH revenue exposure to that product, but (ii) potential automation of performance testing and real-time disqualification could advantage faster-ramping technologies (batteries) and penalize PSH and conventional hydro more heavily if response-time or consistency standards are tightened without accounting for hydro's multi-hour operational flexibility constraints.

title: 20260709 MSC Item 13 Evaluation of Updates to Congestion Management and TCDCs (MSC-2026-6).pdf
relevance_reason: MISO is evaluating transmission constraint demand curves (TCDCs) and congestion management during reserve shortages, which directly affects how dispatch and pricing decisions treat dispatchable generation—a core revenue mechanism for hydro—and how make-whole payments (DAMAP) are triggered when congestion and reserve scarcity interact.
ai_summary: MISO is evaluating updates to transmission constraint demand curves (TCDCs), which cap the shadow prices the market will pay to enforce network constraints, with particular focus on how undersized TCDCs interact with operating-reserve shortages to cause manual redispatches and Day-Ahead Marginal Assurance Payment (DAMAP) uplift. The document illustrates how reserve scarcity can overwhelm congestion signals, forcing resources down post-facto and triggering make-whole payments (e.g., Winter Storm Elliott example). MISO is considering expanding TCDC breakpoints, adding steps that increase during reserve shortages, and adjusting weighting between base and contingent constraints; a feedback request and implementation plan will be shared later in 2026. Dispatchable generators (including reservoir hydro) are most exposed: when reserves are scarce, high MEC penalties can force dispatch back to EcoMax despite binding constraints, then manual redispatch down creates the DAMAP liability. Hydro owners should track this work because enhanced TCDCs or dynamic reserve-shortage scaling could improve real-time economic dispatch and reduce the frequency of out-of-market corrections.

title: 20260709 MSC Item 13a DAMAP Reduction Total - New Issue Introduction (MSC-2026-7).pdf
relevance_reason: DAMAP (Day-Ahead Margin Assurance Payment) and RSG Distribution calculations directly affect revenue sufficiency and make-whole payments for dispatchable units including hydro; overstated Reduction Totals suppress adjusted DA schedules and thus unit revenue when derated or manually redispatched.
ai_summary: MISO proposes correcting the Day-Ahead Margin Assurance Payment (DAMAP) Reduction Total calculation, which currently overstates the sum of cleared day-ahead products by double-counting MWs shared across multiple products, resulting in artificially suppressed adjusted DA schedules for derated or manually redispatched units. The fix would base Reduction Totals on physical unit limitations rather than product sums, and would also correct a similar defect in Revenue Sufficiency Guarantee (RSG) Distribution. Both changes require tariff filings; MSC-2026-7 has been introduced for adoption at the July 9, 2026 Market Subcommittee meeting. Any hydro or pumped-storage unit that experiences deratings, manual redispatch, or forced outages would receive more accurate (and typically higher) make-whole compensation under the corrected formulas.

title: 20260709 MSC Item 13b DAMAP Reduction Total - Presentation (MSC-2026-7).pdf
relevance_reason: DAMAP Reduction Total calculation directly affects how derated and manually re-dispatched hydro and storage units are compensated for lost ancillary-service revenue, and the change alters the baseline against which their schedule adjustments are measured.
ai_summary: MISO proposes to revise the Day-Ahead Margin Assurance Payment (DAMAP) Reduction Total calculation for derated and manually re-dispatched units, replacing a simple sum-of-cleared-products approach with constraint-based clearing values that reflect physical MW-sharing limits between regulation, contingency reserves, ramp capability, and short-term reserves. Currently, the sum method can overstate total cleared MWs (since ancillary-service MWs can be shared with energy), leading to larger schedule reductions than physical capability warrants; the proposed method uses the maximum of two DART constraint combinations to more accurately cap the Reduction Total. MISO also proposes a parallel change to one Real-Time Revenue Sufficiency Guarantee distribution component (DDC_NDL_CAP_VOL) using the same constraint logic. Stakeholder feedback is due July 24, 2026, with a target Q3 2026 filing and 60-day effective date. The change most directly affects dispatchable hydro, pumped storage, and other use-limited resources that routinely clear multiple ancillary services alongside energy.

title: 20260709 MSC Item 14a DAMAP Reduction Total - New Issue Introduction (MSC-2026-7).pdf
relevance_reason: DAMAP and RSG calculations affect the adjusted day-ahead schedules and revenue guarantees for derated or manually re-dispatched units, which directly impacts revenue sufficiency and dispatch accuracy for dispatchable hydropower and pumped-storage resources.
ai_summary: MISO proposes to correct the Day-Ahead Margin Assurance Payment (DAMAP) Reduction Total calculation, which currently overstates reductions by summing MWs across shared products when units are derated or manually re-dispatched. The correction would base the reduction on physical unit limitations instead, yielding more accurate adjusted day-ahead schedules and affecting the Revenue Sufficiency Guarantee (RSG) Distribution calculation as well. Both changes require a tariff filing; the Market Subcommittee is adopting this as a new issue (MSC-2026-7) for proceeding to tariff modification.

title: 20260709 MSC Item 14b DAMAP Reduction Total (MSC-2026-7)_redlines.docx

ai_summary: MISO proposes revised rules for allocating Real-Time Revenue Sufficiency Guarantee (RRSG) Constraint Management Charges to electric storage resources, distinguishing treatment by day-ahead and real-time commitment status (Charge, Discharge, Available, Continuous). title: 20260709 MSC Item 14b DAMAP Reduction Total - Presentation (MSC-2026-7).pdf

ai_summary: MISO proposes to change how the Day-Ahead Margin Assurance Payment (DAMAP) Reduction Total is calculated for derated and manually re-dispatched units, replacing a summation of all cleared day-ahead products (Energy + Regulation + Contingency Reserves + Ramp + Short-Term Reserve) with the maximum of two DART constraint-clearing values that reflect which products can physically share megawatts. The current method potentially overstates the Reduction Total by double-counting shared MWs across products, resulting in lower adjusted day-ahead schedules for affected units; the proposed method aligns the reduction calculation with actual physical constraints that limit product combinations during day-ahead clearing. MISO also proposes a conforming change to one Revenue Sufficiency Guarantee Distribution component (DDC_NDL_CAP_VOL). Stakeholder feedback is due July 24, 2026, with a target FERC filing in Q3 2026 and effective date 60 days thereafter. This principally affects dispatchable thermal and hydroelectric units that regularly clear ancillary services alongside energy, and pumped-storage facilities that rely on accurate product-stacking calculations for profit optimization.

This matters to hydro owners because DLOL methodologies (which use observed loss-of-load events to define accreditation windows) are being adopted to address the divergence between fixed-hour accreditation and actual system scarcity; hydro's own accreditation framework may face similar pressure to move from traditional ELCC windows toward performance-driven models, and precedents set for solar will inform how flexibility and run-of-river resources are credited in MISO resource adequacy.

title: 20260708 RASC Item 06 External Resources Accreditation (RASC-2024-5 and 2019-2).pdf
relevance_reason: MISO is reforming accreditation methodology for external resources (pseudo-tied and non-pseudo-tied), which directly affects how external hydropower (including pumped storage participating across seams) receives capacity-value accreditation and participates in the Planning Resource Auction—a core revenue and participation mechanism for hydro owners exporting into MISO or participating via external-resource schedules.
ai_summary: MISO proposes to accredit pseudo-tied external resources using Schedule 53A (real-time offer data, 3-year lookback, 80/20 weighting between Tier 2 RA and Tier 1 non-RA hours) and non-pseudo-tied external resources using day-ahead e-Tag availability (same weighting, no outage exemptions, 3-year lookback). MISO is also eliminating the Use-Limited Resources category, redirecting accreditation of all use-limited assets (including run-of-river and storage hydro) into the Schedule 53A and Schedule 53B frameworks. The proposal shifts external hydro accreditation away from ad-hoc techniques toward seasonal-availability-aligned methods, but non-pseudo-tied resources (which may include many Northwest hydro exports) lose outage exemptions and rely on day-ahead e-Tag offers rather than real-time operational data—potentially reducing accreditation for resources whose actual availability exceeds their day-ahead self-commitments. Stakeholder comments are due July 26, 2026; MISO targets FERC filing in Q4 2026 or Q1 2027 with effective date Planning Year 2029/30 or beyond. Most exposed: pumped storage and run-of-river hydro exporting from adjacent balancing authorities via external-resource schedules; large reservoir hydro with seasonal energy constraints that may be miscaptured by day-ahead e-Tag methodology.

title: 20260708 RASC Item 07 24 Hour Lead Time in Accreditation (RASC-2026-1).pdf
relevance_reason: MISO proposes three alternative rules for how offline resources' capacity accreditation should be calculated based on lead time, which directly affects how thermal and hydro peaking units can be credited toward resource-adequacy showings during emergencies — the key revenue mechanism for dispatchable generation.
ai_summary: MISO proposes three solutions to close a perceived gap in its 24-hour lead-time accreditation rule for offline resources. The problem: thermal generators increased their start-time lead times approaching Winter Storms Fern, Enzo, and Heather, rendering 3.1 GW unavailable for commitment in the Day-Ahead Market and Forward Reliability Assessment Commitment (FRAC) processes while still receiving full accreditation value, despite contributing to emergency deployment of LMRs. Solution 1 (12-hour max lead time) aligns offline-resource accreditation with the Operating Margin calculation but risks uneconomic commitments. Solution 2 (zero availability for lead-time increases within 48 hours of the operating day) would penalize changes near emergencies but allow longer-lead resources to participate in multi-day FRAC. Solution 3 (sliding scale: full availability at 4 hours, declining 5% per hour to zero at 24+ hours) offers graduated incentives. MISO will select a recommended solution in August 2026, file revised tariff at FERC in October 2026. Stakeholders should comment by July 22, 2026. Pumped-storage and conventional-hydro operators should monitor because the same accreditation rules govern their RA value; any tightening of lead-time rules that penalizes start-time flexibility, or that creates asymmetries between thermal and hydro accreditation, could compress the capacity credit PSH and peaking hydro claim during peak-scarcity periods.

title: 20260708 RASC Item 08 PRMR Allocation (RASC-2020-4 and 2019-2).pdf
relevance_reason: MECHANISM: MISO's shift from forecasted load (CPDf) to three-year-lookback settled load for Planning Reserve Margin Requirement (PRMR) allocation changes how reserve obligations are assigned to Load Serving Entities, directly affecting the revenue adequacy and resource-procurement obligations of hydro and PSH owners whose output and strategic flexibility are valued in MISO's resource-adequacy and Planning Resource Auction frameworks.
ai_summary: MISO proposes replacing Coincident Peak Demand forecast (CPDf)-based PRMR allocation with a Resource Adequacy Hour Demand (RAHD) metric using three-year-lookback settled load during Tier 2 RA hours, weighted by effective margin. The proposal aligns PRMR allocation with MISO's updated Resource Accreditation reform and the DLOL framework, tying reserve requirements to actual historical load behavior during highest-risk hours rather than peak forecasts. Hydro and PSH operators benefit when this mechanism improves accuracy of LSE reserve obligations: precise allocation signals encourage load-serving entities to procure capacity-constrained products (like the ramping and storage flexibility hydro and pumped storage supply) at times of actual scarcity rather than all-hours forecasts. MISO requests stakeholder feedback by July 24, 2026, with initial tariff redlines due in August 2026, final redlines in September 2026, and FERC filing targeted for end of 2026.

Operators in hydro-rich neighboring RTOs (e.g., PJM members with hydro capacity, or DSOs considering MISO seams) should track whether MISO's congestion profile shifts—persistent binding on M2M corridors may signal interregional transmission expansion opportunity or pressure for storage-as-transmission alternatives.

title: 20260701 Markets Committee of the BOD Item 04 State of the Market Presentation.pdf
relevance_reason: MISO's 2025 State of the Market report addresses capacity accreditation reform (marginal DLOL methodology), reserve and frequency response incentives, congestion pricing and transmission management, virtual market liquidity effects on energy pricing, large load interconnection impacts, and renewable resource integration challenges—each directly affecting hydro and PSH revenue, strategic positioning, and system value in a 26.6 GW load-growth scenario.
stakeholders: David Patton, PhD (MISO Independent Market Monitor (Potomac Economics))
ai_summary: MISO's Independent Market Monitor presented findings from the 2025 State of the Market report showing all-in prices rose 67% to $53/MWh, driven by natural gas cost increases and capacity-market reforms. Key findings for hydro owners: (1) MISO transitioned to a reliability-based demand curve in capacity markets and reformed resource accreditation to reflect resources' marginal contribution to reliability in riskiest hours—shifting value from solar/wind with declining accreditation to dispatchable resources, including hydro; (2) shortage-pricing reforms in Fall 2025 improved energy and ancillary-service price signals, and MISO filed recommended penalties to improve incentive for units to follow dispatch setpoints; (3) real-time congestion costs rose 23% to $2.2B, driven partly by conservative transmission ratings and MISO's manual re-dispatch—highlighting transmission constraints that affect hydro deliverability; (4) MISO projects 26.6 GW load additions by 2030 (3.1–5.1% CAGR), with guidance that co-located generation and load should not avoid capacity or transmission costs, and siting at weak network locations should be non-firm pending upgrades—affecting co-location economics and interconnection strategy; (5) renewable penetration peaked at 45.7% in 2025, creating ramp-demand volatility and voltage-support constraints that favor dispatchable resources and storage; (6) marginal accreditation for new renewables is falling sharply, making continued investment in dispatchable generation essential—directly elevating the system value of existing hydro and PSH in MISO's reliability planning.

meeting_title: Markets Committee of the Board of Directors - July 1, 2026
title: 20260701 Markets Committee of the BOD Item 04 State of the Market Report.pdf
relevance_reason: State of the market report covering MISO energy and ancillary services pricing, resource adequacy trends, transmission congestion, virtual market activity, and recommended market reforms that affect hydro revenue, capacity accreditation, and dispatch performance.
ai_summary: Potomac Economics' 2025 State of the Market Report for MISO examines energy price formation, ancillary services markets, capacity adequacy, transmission congestion, and resource operations across the year, with a forward-looking section on future market needs as wind/solar penetration rises and net-load ramps accelerate. Key findings include uplift costs in real-time markets, changes in MISO's generating capacity mix, congestion dynamics on key transfer constraints, and seasonal adequacy challenges highlighted by 2025 load-shed events and transmission emergencies in MISO South. The report's recommendations (Section X) propose reforms to energy pricing, operating reserves, ramping products, transmission congestion management, and capacity market design — with particular relevance to resource adequacy rules and scarcity-pricing mechanisms that directly influence dispatchable and storage resource revenues and obligations. Most exposed: all MISO hydro and pumped-storage owners subject to MISO's capacity and ancillary services accreditation, and those exposed to real-time pricing and make-whole payment volatility during tight-supply periods.

title: 20260629 LLWG Item 01b Agenda.pdf
relevance_reason: Large Load Working Group agenda addresses co-located load-and-generation registration, interconnection reliability, and operational requirements that directly affect hydro's strategic options for serving large loads and co-location arrangements, plus hydro's obligations for operational reliability and dispatch coordination.
ai_summary: MISO's Large Load Working Group (LLWG) is meeting June 29, 2026, to address market participation rules for co-located load and generation (item 6: Zero-Injection GIA under PAC-2024-2B), interconnection reliability requirements (LLWG-2026-3), large-load telemetry/PMU requirements (LLWG-2026-4C), operational forecasting requirements (LLWG-2026-4A), and reserve product enhancements (LLWG-2026-2). The co-location and zero-injection items directly enable hydro owners to serve large loads behind the meter or as bundled resources, expanding revenue and strategic flexibility; the interconnection and operational requirements impose new compliance obligations on dispatchable generation (including hydropower) serving large loads. Next LLWG meeting is July 16, 2026. No voting or comment deadlines are stated in this agenda.

title: 20260629 LLWG Item 01c Action Items.pdf
relevance_reason: Large-load interconnection and co-located load affect hydro's strategic positioning in energy markets and scarcity value; this action-items document flags active MISO work on large-load firm service that could shape transmission access and revenue opportunities for hydro.
ai_summary: MISO's Large Load Working Group issued feedback requests on June 10, 2026 (closed) for the Large Load Firm Service Step Up proposal (LLWG-2026-1), with comments originally due June 24. The proposal addresses how MISO accommodates large-load customers seeking firm service, a mechanism that intersects hydro's role in providing dispatchable energy and flexibility to serve new demand. Large-load firm-service design can shift the value of hydro by changing transmission constraints, scarcity pricing, and the premium for flexible supply — particularly for pumped-storage operators positioned to serve or compete with large loads. The document provides no detail on the proposal's substance, status, or next steps.

title: 20260629 LLWG Item 01c Minutes 20260610.pdf
relevance_reason: MISO is developing Zero-Injection Generator Interconnection Agreements (ZGIAs) to enable co-located load-and-generation market participation, which directly affects hydro and pumped-storage strategic options for hybrid/co-located resource models and load-following services.
stakeholders: Chris Plante (MISO Large Load Working Group)
Werner Roth (MISO Large Load Working Group)
ai_summary: MISO is advancing a Zero-Injection GIA (ZGIA) framework to permit market participation and registration of co-located load and generation resources, with draft tariff language posted and a planned FERC filing at end of June 2026. The proposal follows six months of collaborative stakeholder input and includes interconnection process, market participation, and registration mechanics. For hydro and pumped-storage owners, ZGIAs create a participation pathway for co-located load (e.g., data centers, industrial hydro-adjacent facilities) to be served behind-the-meter or via dedicated interconnection without exporting net energy to the grid, potentially increasing asset utilization and revenue optionality for hybrid facilities and enabling PSH charging load registration. The framework is near completion; the June filing will trigger FERC review and any final stakeholder feedback window.

title: 20260629 LLWG Item 01d Management Plan.pdf
relevance_reason: This MISO working group management plan addresses large-load integration, co-located generation/load, and operational reliability requirements that directly affect hydro and pumped-storage participation options, interconnection pathways, and reserve-product design.
ai_summary: MISO's Large Load Working Group (LLWG) is tracking six active workstreams through Q4 2026 that reshape how large loads and co-located resources (including hydro-paired load) participate in MISO markets. Key items include: (1) Large Load Firm Service Step Up (LLWG-2026-1) and reserve-product enhancements (LLWG-2026-2), which will define capacity/reserve accreditation and service-level requirements for flexible resources attached to large loads; (2) Interconnection reliability requirements (LLWG-2026-3) and operational-reliability workstreams (LLWG-2026-4A/B/C covering forecasting, network models, and PMU/telemetry) that establish must-offer and real-time operational standards for co-located assets; and (3) Market participation rules for zero-injection GIAs (PAC-2024-4B), affecting how hydro or storage can register co-located load without serving the MISO grid. The June 29, 2026 meeting will surface a tentative FERC action and initial reserve-enhancement evaluation results; final tariff redlines and recommendations are scheduled for August and November 2026. Pumped-storage operators and conventional hydro owners considering co-location or large-load service opportunities need to monitor reserve-product design and the zero-injection GIA interpretation, as these will determine whether co-located capacity can stack ancillary-service revenues or will be constrained by MISO operational requirements.

title: 20260629 LLWG Item 04 Liaison Report.pdf
relevance_reason: MISO's Large Load Working Group is developing interconnection frameworks, co-located resource rules (ZGIA), and reserve product enhancements that directly affect how pumped-storage and conventional hydropower can participate in markets and operate at existing or new facility locations; operational requirements for large loads including ride-through and stability control establish precedent for dispatchable resource standards.
ai_summary: MISO is pursuing a three-phase framework for rapid large-load integration: Connect (120-day GIA completion), Transition (flexible service options including firm step-up), and Ensure Long-Term Reliability (real-time coordination and reserve product enhancements). The ZGIA (zero-injection GIA) tariff language covers market participation, resource adequacy treatment, ride-through, and stability requirements for co-located generation and load; initial proposal was filed with FERC in June 2026, with a non-firm service option and firm service step-up option timeline influenced by FERC show-cause order review (target July 2026 filing). Co-located resource rules and the firm service step-up option create new pathways for PSH and hydro to participate in MISO markets with flexible injection/withdrawal capability, while operational reliability requirements (SCADA telemetry, PMU standards, dynamic reserve preparedness) establish obligations that will apply to dispatchable and storage-like resources. The Steering Committee special meeting on July 7, 2026, will determine the forum for continued ZGIA discussion and review LLWG charter.

title: 20260629 LLWG Item 05 Legal Review of Show Cause Order Presentation.pdf
relevance_reason: FERC Show Cause Order directs MISO to redesign interconnection processes and transmission service offerings for large co-located generation and load, which directly affects how hydropower and pumped-storage facilities can interconnect, participate in co-location arrangements, and be studied for network impacts—a strategic option under interconnection and deliverability rules.
ai_summary: FERC issued a Show Cause Order (June 18, 2026, Docket EL26-70-000) directing MISO to revise its tariff to accommodate large loads through tailored interconnection processes for electrically proximate and co-located generation-load pairs, transmission service studies that reflect limited network scope, and transparency mechanisms for upgrade costs. MISO proposes a Zone Generation Interconnection Agreement (ZGIA) service type and expedited study process, but must reconcile its approach with FERC's specific requirements around interim/permanent service options, remote disconnection capability, and escalating readiness milestones. MISO's informational report is due July 18, 2026, with abeyance request August 2, 2026, and compliance filing August 17, 2026 (absent abeyance)—this timeline affects whether pumped-storage and other hydro facilities seeking co-location or electrically proximate generation arrangements will face revised study procedures and may open faster interconnection pathways for hydro behind large-load nodes.

title: 20260629 LLWG Item 06 Market Participation and Registration of Co Located Load and Generation (PAC 2024 4B)
relevance_reason: MISO's Zero-Injection GIA (ZGIA) framework directly affects co-located generation and load registration, which creates new revenue and settlement rules for hydropower and storage resources operating at or near large industrial loads, and establishes precedent for how RTOs treat behind-the-meter or tightly co-located hybrid resources.
ai_summary: MISO proposes to require Zero-Injection GIAs (generation interconnection agreements where generation is co-located with large industrial loads) whose associated load exceeds the Large Load threshold to register as market resources. Grandfathered ZGIAs already accepted by FERC are exempt. MISO proposes no time limit on ZGIAs and will clarify that loads are firm NITS loads paying gross transmission charges. Market registration will ensure both load and generation volumes are reported separately for accurate ancillary-service charge allocation, affecting settlement and LMP exposure. This proposal responds to FERC's recent Show Cause Order. Stakeholder feedback is due July 15, 2026, with tariff filing expected July 2026. The mechanism matters most to pumped-storage operators and conventional hydro owners considering co-location with or service to large loads (data centers, manufacturing, etc.); the registration and metering rules will determine whether co-located generation can capture locational price signals or is treated as internal to the load node.

title: 20260629 LLWG Item 07 Draft MISO Large Load Interconnection Requirement Technical Compendium
relevance_reason: Large load interconnection and operational requirements directly affect hydro's strategic options for co-location, load-following capability valuation, and transmission/grid-stability service revenue through emerging demand for ramp, ride-through, and dynamic-performance capabilities that hydro uniquely supplies.
ai_summary: MISO has published a Large Load Interconnection Reliability Requirements technical compendium establishing interconnection standards for rapid-growth transmission-connected loads (data centers, AI computing, etc.), with four requirement categories: data/telemetry/forecasting; ramp management; voltage/frequency ride-through; and stability assessment. The framework defines minimum disturbance-performance expectations and dynamic-response capabilities that large loads must meet. This expands MISO's valuation of ramping, frequency support, and voltage stability — services hydro suppliers have historically dominated — and opens strategic pathways for hydro co-location with large loads and behind-the-meter service delivery. The document establishes technical requirements that may inform future MISO ancillary-services procurement and reserve-adequacy modeling as load volatility and grid-stability demands increase; hydro owners should monitor whether MISO translates these reliability needs into new product definitions or accreditation adjustments that reward fast-response, high-ramp-capability resources.

title: 20260629 LLWG Item 07 Large Load Interconnection Reliability Requirements (LLWG 2026 3)
relevance_reason: Large load interconnection requirements and their operational reliability mandates (remote disconnect, ramp-rate controls, ride-through, telemetry/PMU) directly constrain how co-located loads (data centers, AI/HPC) can interact with the transmission system and may affect hydro's ability to serve or coordinate with these loads, plus set a precedent for how RTOs will require dispatchable resources to respond to fast-ramping demand.
ai_summary: MISO is filing revised Tariff language by end of July 2026 to impose interconnection reliability requirements on large loads (≥50 MW new, ≥25 MW cumulative increase) and computational loads (≥1 MW of data-center-type digital demand), implementing FERC's show-cause order. Requirements include basic facility data, modeling, hourly forecasts, telemetry, and PMU data; computational loads face additional phasor measurement, ride-through (voltage/frequency), and ramp-rate controls; MISO will install and charge customers for remote disconnect equipment and control systems. A transitional provision exempts loads with service commencement before 11/1/2027 from ramp and ride-through requirements for their lifetime unless they upgrade by ≥25 MW after 10/1/2026. This affects hydro owners because (1) it establishes a co-location precedent — large loads are now defined as discrete withdrawal points, creating opportunities for hydro to site behind-the-meter generation and enter direct load-service arrangements; (2) the ramp-rate and ride-through enforcement on computational loads (AI, crypto, HPC) creates a demand-side flexibility requirement that could be partially satisfied by hybrid hydro-storage systems and (3) the remote-disconnect and PMU mandates on loads set operational-control expectations that may extend to dispatchable generation. Stakeholders expressed concerns about applicability, transition, and specific language; feedback has influenced the revised Tariff language.

title: 20260629 LLWG Item 08a Large Load Telemetry and PMU Requirements (LLWG 2026 4C)
relevance_reason: MISO's telemetry and PMU requirements for large loads will impose new operational compliance obligations on hydropower and storage facilities co-located with or behind the same point of interconnection as computational loads, and may affect dispatch visibility and real-time market participation for generation resources at large-load sites.
ai_summary: MISO proposes mandatory real-time SCADA telemetry (MW, MVAR, breaker status via ICCP) for all large loads and generation resources ≥20 MVA sharing the same point of interconnection, plus PMU installation (sampling at 60 Hz minimum in IEEE C37.118 format) at computational large loads before service commencement. Generation behind the large load's POI cannot be netted with load and must stream individual telemetry including state-of-charge data for battery or storage devices, and control-mode telemetry for market-participating generators. MISO requests feedback by July 13, 2026, with detailed requirements to be drafted in Business Practice Manuals. Pumped-storage facilities and conventional hydro units co-located at large-load sites (especially data-center campuses) will face new capital costs (PMU installation and ICCP comms) and operational constraints (non-netting, continuous dispatch visibility, reduced operational flexibility).

title: 20260629 LLWG Item 08b Large Load Operational Forecast Requirements (LLWG 2026 4A)
relevance_reason: Large load forecasting requirements directly affect hydro's operational flexibility value and dispatch obligations, and the rule design (monitoring, incentives, settlement potential) may establish precedent for how variable/dispatchable resources' forecast accuracy is treated in MISO's commitment and real-time dispatch processes.
ai_summary: MISO proposes to require large loads (data centers, industrial facilities, campuses) to submit short-term operational forecasts at hourly (next 1–168 hours) and 5-minute (next 6 hours) granularities, feeding into MISO's Multi-Day/Next-Day/Intraday reliability commitment and look-ahead commitment/real-time dispatch processes. Forecasts are submitted at the Commercial Pricing (CP) node level by the Tariff Customer; MISO will monitor timeliness and accuracy against telemetered actual load and is considering incentive mechanisms (ranging from escalation to settlement-based penalties). Status: requirements finalized for LLWG feedback by July 13, 2026; accuracy incentives and BPM implementation to follow. For hydro operators, the mechanism is load-side variability management: large loads add volatile demand that MISO's standard weather/calendar forecasts cannot capture; if these forecasts are inaccurate, MISO's commitment stack and reserve procurement tighten or loosen unpredictably, affecting the scarcity signals and ramping/flexibility value hydro receives in real-time and look-ahead markets. The settlement-based penalty option (SPP precedent cited) could create a parallel market-discipline framework applied to demand-side forecast accuracy, potentially informing future treatment of hydro forecast errors and opportunity-cost offers.

title: 20260629 LLWG Item 09 Large Load Reserve Product Enhancements (LLWG 2026 2)
relevance_reason: MISO's revised methodology for quantifying reserve requirements (Regulation Reserve, Ramp Capability, Short-Term Reserve) directly affects how uncertainty and variability from large loads are valued in reserve-product pricing and procurement — a core revenue stream for hydro and pumped storage, which are traditional suppliers of all three products.
ai_summary: MISO has established a dynamic reserve requirement methodology that quantifies net uncertainty and derives seasonal reserve requirements for Regulation Reserve (4 sec–5 min timeframe), Ramp Capability Product (10 min), and Short-Term Reserve (30 min–3 hr), with requirements varying by season, region, and time of day. Large loads exhibiting non-conforming behavior (volatile industrial or storage-adjacent profiles) were evaluated as a source of net-load and tie-line uncertainty; however, MISO's correlation analysis (sampling February–November 2025) found weak or negligible relationships between non-conforming load profiles and reserve-product uncertainty requirements across all three products, suggesting existing large loads have limited impact on reserve sizing to date. MISO will continue to monitor uncertainty patterns periodically and revise reserve methodologies if non-conforming load impact reaches criticality. Stakeholder feedback (six respondents, May 2026) was mostly supportive, and further engagement will occur at the Large Load Working Group.

title: 20260629 LLWG Item 09 Reserve Product Enhancement (LLWG 2026 2) Feedback Response (20260514)
relevance_reason: MISO is evaluating reserve product enhancements and regulation requirements to manage load variability from large data-center and computational loads, which directly affects how much regulation and ramping reserve MISO procures and prices — the demand curve for these products that conventional hydro and pumped storage depend on for revenue.
ai_summary: MISO is developing reserve product enhancements to accommodate fast ramp rates and variability from large loads (data centers, computational facilities), with focus on regulation (4-second dispatch cycle, 5-minute deployment) and contingency-reserve upward and downward directions. Stakeholder feedback from six participants—mostly supportive of MISO's approach—pushed MISO to evaluate whether existing initiatives (RSC-2024-1/2, MSC-2026-1) already suffice before adding new products, and to allocate reserve costs to the loads driving demand rather than socializing them. MISO commits to reserve-enhancement evaluation updates and cost-allocation recommendations at July or August 2026 and later in 2026 LLWG meetings. The mechanism: larger, more variable loads will increase MISO's procurement of regulation and ramping reserves; if MISO adds new reserve products or expands regulation requirements, traditional hydro and PSH owners will face higher competition for those product revenues and greater uncertainty in which resources are called upon to provide regulation—particularly affecting resources with ramp-rate and regulation-eligibility constraints.

title: 20260716 LLWG Item 01c Minutes 20260610.pdf
relevance_reason: MISO's Zero-Injection GIA (ZGIA) proposal directly affects how co-located generation and load can participate in markets and be registered—a strategic option for hydro owners seeking to site generation with load, and a novel participation pathway that may extend to small hydro and hybrid resources under Order 2222 principles.
stakeholders: Chris Plante (MISO Large Load Working Group)
ai_summary: MISO is developing a Zero-Injection Generator Interconnection Agreement (ZGIA) framework to enable market participation and registration of co-located load and generation. The proposal reflects six months of stakeholder input and is nearing a tariff filing at end of June 2026, with draft language and Planning Advisory Committee feedback still being incorporated. The framework adapts existing interconnection processes (surplus, replacement, ERAS) to zero-injection scenarios. For hydro owners, ZGIAs represent a new pathway to co-locate generation with large industrial load—potentially raising MW value by shifting pricing exposure, enabling behind-the-meter hydro dispatch, and avoiding transmission constraints; most relevant to pumped-storage operators and small hydro seeking high-load-density sites. Comment deadlines and detailed tariff language appear in related filings (PAC-2024-2B, LLWG-2026-3, LLWG-2026-2) due May 26–June 4, 2026.

The agenda includes refreshers on seasonal LOLE targets, LOLE load-modeling results, capacity and outage-year assumptions, and wind-profile enhancements. Substantively: LOLE targets and load forecasts drive which resources are needed for RA compliance and how scarcity is priced; hydro's accreditation (seasonal and annual ELCC/UCAP) and the timing of peak-scarcity events are set within these models. Wind-profile enhancements may shift the seasonal shape of reserve requirements, changing when hydro's flexibility commands the highest value. Next meeting is August 11, 2026; the working group is requesting feedback on several items (load modeling, capacity assumptions, wind profiles), though no formal comment deadline is stated in this agenda.

meeting_title: Loss of Load Expectation Working Group (LOLEWG) - June 23, 2026
title: 20260623 LOLEWG Item 01c Minutes 20260202.pdf
relevance_reason: MISO's Loss of Load Expectation (LOLE) study and Reliability Based Demand Curves (RBDCs) directly inform capacity market accreditation and resource-adequacy requirements that affect how much capacity hydropower and pumped storage can sell into MISO's Planning Resource Auction.
ai_summary: MISO presented PY 2026-2027 Marginal Reliability Impact (MRI) curves and preliminary Reliability Based Demand Curves (RBDCs) showing systemwide summer LOLE risk as highest, but subregional variation (North/Central region peaks in summer; South region peaks in winter, a seasonal shift from prior year). MISO confirmed battery-storage modeling will use 'even loss methodology' and is implementing an enhanced wind-profile model for the PY 2027-2028 LOLE study (near-term), with long-term coordination toward consistent renewable profiles across all planning studies. The wind-profile refinement showed preliminary no material change to LOLE outcomes. These LOLE and RBDC outputs flow directly into MISO's capacity accreditation framework and Planning Resource Auction parameters; seasonal subregional shifts in reliability risk can reset the demand curves that cap how much capacity owners—including hydro and pumped storage—can bid and clear at given prices. Next LOLEWG meeting is June 23, 2026.

title: 20260623 LOLEWG Item 01d Management Plan.pdf
relevance_reason: MISO's Loss of Load Expectation (LOLE) analysis directly determines Planning Reserve Margin (PRM) requirements, zonal Local Reliability Requirements (LRR), and Capacity Import/Export Limits (CIL/CEL) — all foundational inputs to MISO's capacity accreditation, seasonal adequacy assessment, and locational pricing signals that drive hydro revenue and participation incentives.
ai_summary: MISO's Loss of Load Expectation Working Group (LOLEWG) manages the LOLE analysis that calculates Planning Reserve Margin requirements, zonal Local Reliability Requirements, and Capacity Import/Export Limits per Module E-1 of the tariff, conforming to ERO and Regional Entity standards. The group held five meetings in 2025 (average 154 participants) and has scheduled work in 2026–2027 including annual wind/solar capacity-credit reviews, LOLE load modeling for PY2027–2028, planned-maintenance modeling, seasonal LOLE targets, and updates to CIL/CEL calculations. These LOLE-derived parameters feed into MISO's capacity accreditation framework and seasonal adequacy mechanisms; changes to load modeling assumptions, wind/solar profiles, or maintenance treatment directly affect the reserve margins and locational signals that determine how much capacity MISO needs from hydro assets and at what premium scarcity pricing may emerge, influencing both RA accreditation levels and energy-market scarcity incentives for dispatchable hydro.

committee: Loss of Load Expectation Working Group
meeting_title: Loss of Load Expectation Working Group (LOLEWG) - June 23, 2026
title: 20260623 LOLEWG Item 03 Refresher on Seasonal LOLE Targets.pdf
relevance_reason: MISO's seasonal LOLE framework affects how hydro and other dispatchable resources are accredited in capacity adequacy studies and shapes seasonal RA requirements that determine hydro's reliability value and revenue exposure across quarters.
ai_summary: MISO adopted a seasonal LOLE (Loss of Load Expectation) construct in 2023–2024, replacing a single annual 0.1 days/year target with per-season minima of 0.01 days/year. The framework accounts for seasonal variation in peak load (winter mornings, overnight cold events), forced-outage rates (thermal units fail more in extreme cold/heat), planned maintenance clustering (spring/fall), and ELCC values for wind and solar, which differ materially by season. MISO runs an annual LOLE study first, then upwardly adjusts any season falling below 0.01 days/year by adding perfect or proxy units. This document presents the construct as positioned between PJM's simple annual PRMR% approach and ISO-NE's proposed monthly granularity, and includes historical LOLE splits (PY25–26 all summer risk; PY26–27 split summer/winter/spring; PY29–30 nearly even summer/winter) showing how seasonal requirements dampen year-to-year volatility. Hydro operators are most affected because seasonal accreditation directly determines their RA contribution value in each quarter—winter peaking and spring outage windows matter independently rather than being smoothed into a summer-anchored requirement—and because the tariff filing referenced as of June 1, 2026 (adding a perfect positive unit to the LOLE algorithm) may change the study's outcome.

committee: Loss of Load Expectation Working Group
meeting_title: Loss of Load Expectation Working Group (LOLEWG) - June 23, 2026
title: 20260623 LOLEWG Item 04 LOLE Load Modeling Process and Results.pdf
relevance_reason: MISO's Loss of Load Expectation (LOLE) study drives resource-adequacy requirements and seasonal capacity accreditation for all dispatchable units including hydro; unprecedented load growth and forecast-uncertainty revisions directly affect the capacity value and RA showing requirements hydro operators must meet, and seasonal peak-demand modeling shapes winter/spring reliability signals that influence hydro dispatch and scarcity pricing.
ai_summary: MISO's Loss of Load Expectation Working Group is revising its load modeling process and load-forecast uncertainty assumptions for Planning Year 2027–2028, noting that actual loads have deviated from LOLE projections by 4% in shoulder seasons—exceeding current uncertainty bands. MISO is automating the load-development process (replacing NeuroShell with Histogram Gradient Boosting), standardizing extreme-temperature thresholds, and proposing to expand load-forecast error bands (e.g., from ±2% to a range including +3% to +4%) to reflect data-center and electrification-driven load growth. The key mechanism is that higher projected load peaks and wider uncertainty distributions increase the probability of scarcity conditions in LOLE runs, raising capacity-accreditation requirements for all dispatchable resources and making seasonal hydro availability more valuable in winter and shoulder months. MISO is requesting stakeholder feedback on model inputs and uncertainty-assumption options through July 7, 2026, via the Feedback Tool at misoenergy.org.

committee: Loss of Load Expectation Working Group
meeting_title: Loss of Load Expectation Working Group (LOLEWG) - June 23, 2026
title: 20260623 LOLEWG Item 05 CIL CEL Model and Input File Overview.pdf
relevance_reason: CIL/CEL study directly affects hydro's capacity accreditation and zone-to-zone transfer limits under MISO's Planning Resource Auction, which determines how much capacity hydro can export across Local Resource Zones and thus what cleared capacity and locational revenue it receives.
ai_summary: MISO is conducting Capacity Import Limit (CIL) and Capacity Export Limit (CEL) studies for Planning Year 2027-2028 across four seasons (Summer 2027, Fall 2027, Winter 2027-2028, Spring 2028). CIL/CEL values constrain capacity transfers between MISO's Local Resource Zones in the Planning Resource Auction and are calculated using transfer-capability analyses that redispatch conventional generators and wind/solar (wind and solar are curtailed, not ramped up). The study uses PSSE power-flow models and contingency files now posted on ShareFile for stakeholder review. MISO requests stakeholder feedback on input files by July 7, 2026, with preliminary results expected in September 2026 and final values in October 2026. For hydro operators, tighter CIL/CEL values reduce their zone's ability to export capacity—lowering locational RA value and export revenue—while looser limits enhance those streams; the redispatch methodology's treatment of hydro as curtailable (not dispatchable) may understate the transfer capability available when hydro can flex output. Most exposed are multi-zone hydro fleets and pumped storage units in export-constrained Local Resource Zones.

committee: Loss of Load Expectation Working Group
meeting_title: Loss of Load Expectation Working Group (LOLEWG) - June 23, 2026
title: 20260623 LOLEWG Item 06 Capacity and Outyear Model Assumptions.pdf
relevance_reason: MISO's Loss of Load Expectation (LOLE) model determines resource adequacy requirements and capacity accreditation thresholds that directly affect hydro and storage revenue through capacity-market clearing prices and RA obligation sizing.
ai_summary: MISO's Loss of Load Expectation Working Group has updated capacity assumptions for the PY 2027-2028 LOLE study, making two key changes: (1) resource retirements from OMS-MISO Survey data will no longer be modeled in outyear LOLE projections—only retirements with approved Attachment Y filings will be reflected—and (2) ERAS resources will now be included in the model based on their Application In-Service date rather than earlier assumptions. These changes affect which resources are counted toward resource adequacy in MISO's planning year, directly influencing the capacity margin and thus the magnitude of capacity-market clearing prices and RA accreditation values for all dispatchable resources including hydro. The shift away from retirement-survey data means retiring units will be assumed available longer in the outyear, potentially depressing LOLE and lowering RA scarcity signals, while ERAS (Energy Resource Aggregation System) inclusion may improve visibility of emerging resources in adequacy. No comment deadline or vote date is specified in this working-group presentation.

committee: Loss of Load Expectation Working Group
meeting_title: Loss of Load Expectation Working Group (LOLEWG) - June 23, 2026
title: 20260623 LOLEWG Item 07 Wind Profile Enhancement Update.pdf
relevance_reason: MISO's enhanced wind-profile methodology changes how wind and storage resources are accredited in ELCC and DLOL frameworks, directly affecting capacity-value revenue for dispatchable resources including pumped storage competing in MISO's resource-adequacy market.
ai_summary: MISO is adopting enhanced meteorology-driven wind profiles for its PY2027–2028 Loss of Load Expectation (LOLE) studies, replacing status-quo profiles with 30-year synthetic data that better capture low-wind conditions and seasonal variability. The new profiles increase wind ELCC values (especially in Spring, rising from 19.3% to 43.8%), but also shift the distribution of critical-event durations by season, causing storage DLOL accreditation to rise significantly in Fall (+12.7 percentage points) while falling in Winter and Spring (−11.2% and −20.0% respectively). Thermal resources' accreditation is affected primarily by shifts in which maintenance-outage hours overlap with newly identified critical hours. MISO plans to move forward with the enhanced profiles subject to final review and will maintain a hybrid approach (synthetic pre-2012, observed post-2012). This directly reshapes the seasonal accreditation profile for pumped-storage hydro competing in MISO's capacity market, particularly for four-hour-plus storage duration valuations.

ai_summary: MISO and PJM propose to retire the Coordinated Transaction Scheduling (CTS) product—a coordinated interchange optimization tool approved by FERC in 2016 and launched in 2017—due to minimal usage, underperformance ($740k in annual savings vs. $17–72M projected), and high migration costs ($1.4M to migrate to the new Market Clearing Engine, $0.8M to maintain over 5 years). Stakeholders submitted mixed feedback: some requested a modern replacement (e.g., SPP's Inter-Market Optimization) before retirement to avoid operational gaps, while others supported retirement given CTS inefficiencies. MISO responds that other interchange products (Fixed, Cleared Day-Ahead, and Dynamic schedules) already offer more granular, real-time scheduling (adjustable to 20 minutes before interval vs. 75 minutes for CTS), and MISO is open to pursuing replacement products with PJM and SPP after retirement. MISO and PJM intend to coordinate tariff and Joint Operating Agreement filings later in 2026 to remove CTS. Hydro owners on or serving the MISO-PJM interface lose a tool for optimizing interchange pricing and may see reduced locational value signals for flexibility; replacements under discussion are not yet defined.

title: 20260623 MISO-PJM JCM Item 03 MISO Interchange Ramp Rules Update.pdf

ai_summary: MISO is eliminating restrictions on interchange ramp calculations for day-ahead market submissions, effective Q3 2026. Previously, MISO enforced limits of ±1000 MW on increased imports/decreased exports and +500 MW on increased exports/decreased imports, enforced via the Ramp Reservation System (RRS) for quarterly schedule changes. Removing these caps increases the scheduling flexibility available to hydro and other resources moving power across the MISO-PJM interface, allowing larger and more frequent interchange adjustments without pre-reservation denials. This particularly benefits reservoir-based hydropower and pumped storage that rely on schedule flexibility to optimize operations across interregional pricing signals; the change reduces a non-price scheduling constraint that previously limited their ability to respond to real-time conditions. Implementation is targeted for Q3 2026.

The proposal addresses interconnection planning (using familiar surplus/replacement/ERAS processes), resource adequacy accreditation (ZGIA resources offset only their associated local load's capacity obligation, accredited under current MISO rulesets and eligible for zonal resource credits limited by Schedule 53 Direct Loss of Load accreditation or local load obligation), market registration (independent metering and telemetry required; market resources must maintain offer limits ≤ local load demand; MISO will monitor injections and consider charges for overage), and transmission planning (ZGIA included as Non-Transmission Alternative in MTEP). Draft tariff language has been posted; formal feedback is requested from the PAC (pending) and LLWG (June 10, 2026), with a FERC filing planned for late June 2026. Most exposed are owners of on-site generation (including small hydro or pumped storage sited at industrial or utility facilities) seeking to participate as co-located resources or hybrid assets; the framework clarifies accreditation caps and injection limits that will govern revenue from capacity and energy markets.

title: 20260610 LLWG Item 06 Large Load Interconnection Reliability Requirements Presentation (LLWG-2026-3).pdf
relevance_reason: Large load interconnection requirements directly affect hydropower and pumped-storage operators' strategic options for co-located load development, their transmission deliverability, and may impose new operational modeling/telemetry/ramp obligations on facilities with computational loads or adjacent generation.
ai_summary: MISO is finalizing tariff language for Large Load Interconnection Reliability Requirements, targeting a June 30, 2026 filing. The framework distinguishes between Computational Loads (digitally driven, requiring advanced modeling, PMU, ramp, and ride-through requirements) and Non-Computational Loads (baseline data and telemetry only), with applicability triggered at 50 MW or expansions of 25+ MW. For hydro owners, this matters because (1) co-located data centers, cryptocurrency mining, and HPC workloads with which hydro may be sited or co-operate are now subject to detailed telemetry, PMU, dynamic modeling, and forecasting requirements that will flow upstream to the interconnecting hydro facility; (2) large-load definition and transition provisions now allow flexibility for in-flight projects, creating windows for strategic positioning; and (3) the distinction between computational and non-computational behavior may allow run-of-river or variable hydro paired with load to avoid some advanced-modeling burdens if properly characterized. Stakeholder feedback significantly shaped the revised language, particularly on applicability date, transition timelines, and load-type distinctions.

title: 20260610 LLWG Item 06 MISO Large Load Interconnection Reliability Requirements_Technical Compendium Draft.pdf
relevance_reason: Large-load interconnection reliability requirements establish grid-performance and operational-readiness obligations that will affect hydropower's ability to maintain system stability during rapid load-consumption changes and disturbances, and may constrain hydro's operational flexibility or impose new coordination/telemetry burdens; also signals that MISO's rapid load growth (data centers, AI computing) creates scarcity conditions that raise the market value of existing hydro's dispatchability and ramping capability.
ai_summary: MISO published a technical compendium establishing reliability requirements for large transmission-connected loads (data centers, AI computing, crypto mining) that are growing rapidly across its footprint. The framework mandates telemetry and PMU requirements, data/modeling disclosures, short-term load forecasting, ramp-rate limits, voltage and frequency ride-through standards, and transient-stability and oscillation assessments for new large loads. This affects hydro owners in two ways: (1) large-load behavior—rapid changes in power consumption and sudden disconnections during disturbances—will drive more volatile and unpredictable demand patterns that hydropower must balance in real time, potentially increasing the operational value of hydro's ramping and regulation services; and (2) ride-through and stability rules imposed on loads may shift grid-stability burdens away from demand-side and back onto traditional generation (including hydro), creating new obligations for synchronous units. The document does not indicate a comment deadline or vote schedule; it appears to be a draft technical standard (marked as compendium draft) with stakeholder-engagement appendix noted but not shown in excerpt.

title: 20260610 LLWG Item 07 Firm Service Step Up Study Process.pdf
relevance_reason: Large load interconnection and interim service step-up procedures materially affect hydro's strategic options for co-located load participation, transmission deliverability, and resource-adequacy obligations, and establish precedent for how RTOs structure partial-service pathways that could extend to storage and other dispatchable resources.
ai_summary: MISO is formalizing a Firm Service Step Up process to allow large load customers to begin service on partial load blocks before full transmission upgrades are complete, using only interim available capacity. The process requires each partial load addition to pass NERC TPL-001 reliability studies (90-day cycle, quarterly submissions, first-ready-first-served prioritization) and mandates that the load-serving entity procure generation capacity in MISO's Planning Resource Auction to cover the interim load. Approved partial loads become effective at the start of the planning year and persist until the full load interconnection is operational; service is revoked if a load block fails to energize within 90 days of its approved date. For hydro and pumped-storage operators, this is strategically relevant: (1) co-located hydro can now supply large-load customers incrementally rather than waiting for full transmission readiness, shortening payback and improving investment returns; (2) the requirement that interim loads participate in the PRA means the resource-adequacy framework now extends to partial-service loads, establishing that generation must be procured at each step, a model that could define how storage and other flexible resources are accredited in segmented operations; (3) hydro deliverability and transmission-constraint management now explicitly account for multiple overlapping interim-service blocks, which affects zonal scarcity pricing and ramping-reserve demand. MISO requests stakeholder feedback on the prioritization methodology, submission granularity, study frequency, and generation-availability accounting by Monday, June 24, 2026, with tariff language to follow in August.

title: 20260610 PSC Item 01b Agenda

The first item signals MISO's shift toward lifting GIA restrictions that have historically constrained PSH charging-mode operations and revenue capture. The second embeds storage (including PSH) into the transmission planning baseline, potentially improving the visibility of storage's contribution to reliability and the case for new transmission or storage-backed reliability solutions. Both are scheduled for discussion at the June 10, 2026 meeting; no explicit vote or comment deadline is stated in this agenda.

title: 20260610 PSC Item 01c Minutes 20260429

ai_summary: MISO proposed updates to BPM-015 (Business Practice Manual) to remove storage charging limitations in generator interconnection agreements (PAC-2024-3), replacing the Shoulder off-peak charging case with a Light Load charging case and limiting charging study phases to II and III of the Definitive Planning Process.
