The changes do not affect DPP cycles already underway and are expected to begin with DPP-26 if approved by year-end; feedback is due May 20, 2026, and MISO will introduce language to the Planning Advisory Committee in Q3. Pumped-storage operators should scrutinize how Light Load charging assumptions affect their accreditation and cost allocation during interconnection studies, particularly for projects already queued or in mid-study phases.

title: 20260610 PSC Item 01d Management Plan
relevance_reason: TRANSMISSION PLANNING: The PSC oversees MISO's MTEP reliability planning, transfer-capability analysis, and multi-year transmission projects that directly affect deliverability and revenue for hydro generators; storage-charging transmission service requirements (PAC-2023-2) and removal of storage-charging limitations in grid interconnection agreements (PAC-2024-3) materially alter the operational and economic constraints on pumped-storage hydro.
ai_summary: MISO's Planning Subcommittee manages the Multi-Year Transmission Evaluation Process (MTEP) and reliability assessments across 2026–2027, with recurring quarterly reviews of approved transmission projects, voltage stability, and transfer-capability analyses. Two active initiatives directly affect storage and hydro: PAC-2023-2 (Transmission Service Requirements for Charging Electric Storage Resources from the Grid) and PAC-2024-3 (Removing Storage Charging Limitations in GIAs) are under discussion at the June 10, 2026 meeting and scheduled for final review through Q3 2026. PAC-2024-3 removes contractual caps on charging volume in generator interconnection agreements, potentially unlocking incremental pumped-storage dispatch and charging flexibility; PAC-2023-2 addresses how the grid must serve charging load, affecting cost allocation and dispatch freedom for PSH. The PSC's four quarterly cycles through 2027 include dispatch-model assumption reviews and sensitivity studies that will incorporate updated wind/solar forecasts and storage assumptions, shaping the transmission baseline against which hydro's operational value and export capability are evaluated.

title: 20260610 PSC Item 02 Liaison Report
relevance_reason: MECHANISM: Storage charging treatment in interconnection studies and transmission planning directly affects PSH (and battery) participation economics; removal of charging limitations in GIAs and model changes to Phase 3 injection studies signal MISO's evolving approach to how stored-energy resources are studied and integrated into grid planning, with downstream impact on PSH project viability and cost allocation.
ai_summary: MISO has decided to remove storage charging limitations in Phase 3 of its Distributed Generation Proposal (DPP), shifting the modeling approach from SH to LL methodology to include battery charging in interconnection studies; however, MISO will not remove charging constraints in Phase 1 of DPP. This decision elevates to the Planning Advisory Committee (PAC). The change directly affects how pumped-storage hydro and battery resources model their charging footprint in interconnection impact assessments, potentially lowering their study costs and revealing more favorable network impacts when charging is explicitly accounted for. Additionally, MISO posted feedback responses confirming its Annual Review of Dispatch Wind/Solar Assumptions and Transmission Cost Estimation Guide for MTEP26, which will inform transmission expansion studies and affect whether existing hydropower resources receive congestion-relief value or face new constraint headroom requirements. Pumped-storage projects seeking interconnection approval and existing PSH facilities relying on congestion revenue should monitor the PAC review timeline and MTEP27/DPP2027 modeling implementation.

title: 20260610 PSC Item 03a Modeling Update - Planning Process
relevance_reason: MISO's multi-year planning model series (MISO26, 2026 ERAG MMWG) underpins resource-adequacy studies, transmission expansion, and seasonal energy-adequacy analyses that directly affect hydro revenue projections, ELCC accreditation, and deliverability planning.
ai_summary: MISO Planning Modeling team has completed the 2025 ERAG Multiregional Modeling Working Group (MMWG) series and is advancing the 2026 and MISO26 series, which serve as the backbone for NERC transmission planning (TPL) and MISO's Planning Resource Auction (resource-adequacy) studies. The MISO26 power-flow models are on track for June 2026 submission to MMWG, with final Pass 4 models released April 1, 2026; dynamics models use PSSE v35.6.4 and include summer-peak, light-load, and shoulder-load cases across 2026, 2030, and 2035 horizons, with wind and solar capacity-credit penetrations specified for each case. These model series are the inputs to seasonal energy-adequacy studies and transmission needs assessment that determine whether existing hydro plants' RA contributions (ELCC values) and transmission-delivered energy values remain stable or erode under future generation mixes; changes to model structure or resource assumptions in future years (e.g., solar saturation levels, minimum-load scenarios) cascade into accreditation and planning-reserve-margin calculations.

title: 20260610 PSC Item 05 Removing Storage Limitations in GIAs (PAC 2024 3)
relevance_reason: MISO is modifying generation interconnection study procedures for storage charging analysis, which directly affects how pumped-storage hydro interconnection impacts and cost allocations are evaluated in the DPP process.
ai_summary: MISO proposes to replace the 'Summer Shoulder' charging scenario with a 'Light Load' charging scenario in generation interconnection (DPP) studies, effective DPP 2026 (pending approval by December 2026). The Light Load model represents early-morning hours at 45–65% loading, continuing to evaluate both storage charging and injection of queued generation across all three DPP phases. This change affects how network upgrades triggered by storage charging are identified and cost-allocated; PSH developers will now see upgrades tied to morning charging rather than shoulder-period charging, potentially altering which interconnection service categories bear upgrade costs. The mechanism matters because interconnection study procedures determine whether PSH charging access is operationally feasible and cost-justified; shifting the charging scenario from shoulder to light load could reduce or defer upgrade requirements, lowering interconnection costs for PSH projects. Most exposed are pumped-storage developers in the queue; MISO requests feedback by July 15, 2026 (PAC meeting) on the proposed BPM-015 language, with legal review and posting of updated BPMs targeted for Q4 2026.

title: 20260610 PSC Item 06 MTEP Reliability Sensitivities of NERC TPL
relevance_reason: MTEP scenario changes affecting transmission planning reliability assessment directly impact the operational and dispatch conditions under which hydro resources are modeled for interconnection, deliverability, and resource-adequacy accreditation purposes.
ai_summary: MISO proposes to replace the 2-year Light Load, 0% wind planning sensitivity with a 2-year Winter Peak, low wind case (0% solar, wind TBD but below 67%) in its MTEP reliability sensitivities to better reflect winter operating conditions and stress the transmission system under NERC TPL compliance. The change affects how MISO models generation dispatch and transmission adequacy in planning studies used for both MTEP and generator interconnection (DPP), ERAS, and surplus-service reviews. Stakeholder feedback is due June 26, 2026, before BPM-020 and the Planning Modeling Manual are updated for MTEP27. Hydro owners should consider whether the winter-peak dispatch assumptions (low solar, lower wind) accurately represent the seasonal value and dispatch patterns of their resources in MISO's planning studies, particularly regarding accreditation in seasonal resource-adequacy analyses and interconnection deliverability assessments.

title: 20260609 IPWG Item 01c Minutes 20260428.pdf

ai_summary: MISO's Interconnection Process Working Group meeting on April 28, 2026, covered three interconnection-related initiatives affecting all generators: (1) Expedited Resource Addition Study (ERAS) program has 53 of 68 allowed projects active, with Cycles 1–2 complete and Cycle 3 ongoing; (2) Surplus Interconnection and Generator Replacement rules received FERC approval April 14, 2026, with new $150,000 study-deposit amounts effective immediately, and BPM-015 redlines pending finalization; (3) IBR Performance, Modeling, and Conformance (PAC-2024-2) is developing system-strength screening for electromagnetic-transient (EMT) studies to target weak-grid interconnection cases as IBR penetration grows. For hydro and PSH, the Surplus Interconnection approval and revised deposit structure directly lowers barriers to uprates and replacement generation at existing hydroelectric sites; ERAS eligibility and study-cycle progression affect delivery timelines for new run-of-river and reservoir projects. IBR modeling requirements (June 1, 2026, deadline) impose conformance obligations on synchronous machines co-located or competing for queue position, though hydro's synchronous generator status may exempt traditional plants from inverter-specific rules. Feedback on Attachment GGG MHVDC improvements was due May 12, 2026; stakeholders should track the June 2026 BPM posting and Q3–Q4 FERC filings.

title: 20260609 IPWG Item 02 Liaison Report.pdf

ai_summary: MISO reports progress on Attachment GGG improvements (PAC-2024-6) addressing cost-recovery clarifications for Necessary vs. Network upgrades, with stakeholder feedback incorporated and PAC review pending. The DPP 2026 cycle has an application deadline of September 10, 2026, with a $7,600 application fee (recalculated triennially for inflation); study-cycle kick-off is December 9, 2026. MISO's restructured Resource Planning Team consolidates interconnection project management, DPP studies, ERAS studies, and tariff administration, with new roles in surplus interconnection and replacement-generation queuing. Hydro and PSH owners in MISO should flag the September 10 DPP deadline and monitor Attachment GGG clarifications on how Network-upgrade costs are recovered when their projects trigger system improvements.

title: 20260609 IPWG Item 03b DPP Study Schedule.pdf

ai_summary: MISO's Distributed Project Portfolio Study Schedule (version 5/1/2026) shows systematic delays across multiple study cycles through 2027, driven primarily by stability-model audits, transmission-operator (TO) mitigation delays from Ameren, PPI, and NIPSCO, and cascading effects from the 2022 Phase 2 cycle. DPP cycles are progressing through DPP 2 and DPP 3 phases with GIA execution dates extending into 2027; for example, DPP-2022 Central (121 projects, 23,908 MW) is delayed 3–7 calendar days monthly due to stability analysis and mitigation delays. The schedule notes that MISO's Reduced GIP Timeline (effective March 15, 2022) applies to all active cycles, and final reports post 15 business days before completion dates. For hydro and storage interconnection customers, these delays directly extend the time to GIA execution and commercial operation; projects queued in 2021–2025 cycles should monitor their specific region (Central, East ATC/ITC, South, West) and track whether stability or TO-mitigation bottlenecks are the binding constraint on their advancement.

title: 20260609 IPWG Item 04 Att GGG (PAC-2024-6)_redlines.pdf

The document defines the terms, scope, and procedural framework for entities seeking to interconnect merchant HVDC transmission lines to MISO's transmission system, including definitions of Connection Facilities, Network Upgrades, Injection Rights, and cost-allocation mechanisms (Common Use Upgrades, Multi-Party Facilities Construction Agreements). While the excerpt provided contains only definitions and scope language (effective July 19, 2018), redlines indicate updates are under review. Hydro owners and independent power producers using HVDC interconnection for long-distance export of generation—particularly from low-hydropower-density regions into MISO or across MISO seams—are directly affected by the study timelines, upgrade cost-sharing rules, and injection-rights certification procedures these procedures establish.

title: 20260609 IPWG Item 04 Attachment GGG Improvements (PAC-2024-6).pdf
relevance_reason: MISO's clarifications to the MHVDC interconnection procedure (Attachment GGG) affect how non-MISO generation, including hydropower and pumped-storage resources, can interconnect and inject power into MISO — touching deliverability, interconnection pathways, and the cost-recovery treatment of network upgrades that directly impact project economics.
ai_summary: MISO proposes final tariff and business-practice-manual changes to Attachment GGG (MHVDC Interconnection Procedure) to clarify the Module B transmission-service injection pathway as an alternative to Attachment X external Network Resource Interconnection Service, distinguish between Necessary Upgrades and Network Upgrades cost recovery, and update the Multi-Party Facility Construction Agreement. Stakeholders in the April 28 IPWG meeting expressed general support but raised concerns about the scope of Necessary Upgrades in connection studies and cost-recovery pathways for Module B versus Attachment X. MISO plans to file the first tariff change to FERC within 30 days (introducing Limited Operations provisions and clarifying injection/withdrawal-rights scope) and a second filing in Q3–Q4 2026 (updating application forms and clarifying Module B as injection-only, not restricted to External NRIS). Most affected are outside generators—including remote hydropower and pumped-storage facilities seeking to export into MISO—for whom these pathway and cost-allocation rules determine interconnection feasibility and return on investment.

title: 20260609 IPWG Item 05 GI Portal Product Update.pdf
relevance_reason: MISO's interconnection queue portal automation directly affects how hydropower and other generators apply for interconnection service and queue position, touching both the interconnection-queue obligation and the strategic timing/cost of interconnection entry.
ai_summary: MISO launched the Generation Interconnection Application Automation (GIAA) portal in November 2025 and is executing incremental releases (April, May 2026, with July/September/November 2026 planned) to improve application processing automation, data migration from the legacy Grid Unity system, and user experience. The portal now supports Surplus and Replacement applications, Inverter-Based Resource (IBR) uploads, and expanded transformer and Point of Interconnection voltage-level fields. Known issues include file-size limitations, lack of project-list sorting/filtering, and unclear user-type account options—problems that can slow application review or create friction for interconnection customers (generators including hydro and pumped-storage developers). A dedicated product team was established March 1, 2026, with ongoing focus on bug resolution and data cleanup from the legacy system. Generators relying on timely queue processing should monitor the portal's usability and watch for the next release cycle (tentatively July 18, 2026) to assess whether validation and automated-review improvements reduce application review delays.

title: 20260608 MISO-PJM IPSAC Agenda
relevance_reason: MISO-PJM interregional transmission planning and FERC Order 1920 implementation directly affect hydro deliverability, interregional transfer capability, and market-seam governance—all strategic options for hydro owners operating across or exporting from the MISO-PJM footprint.
ai_summary: The MISO-PJM IPSAC agenda covers three topics: (1) a Targeted Market Efficiency Project Study update, (2) MISO-PJM FERC Order 1920 compliance progress, and (3) interregional transmission planning status. FERC Order 1920 requires improved interregional coordination and transmission planning between RTOs; implementation here affects how hydro resources in or serving the MISO-PJM seam can compete for capacity, how interregional energy flows are priced and scheduled, and whether transmission constraints limit hydro export capability. The June 8 meeting includes verbal reports on these items with no public comment period advertised in this agenda, but the transmission-planning update and Order 1920 progress are material to hydro owners evaluating long-term positioning in the MISO-PJM region and to any with portfolio exposure across the seam.

title: 20260608 MISO-PJM IPSAC Item 01 TMEP Study Update
relevance_reason: TMEP (Transmission and Market Enhancement Projects) study identifies and evaluates interregional transmission solutions between MISO and PJM, directly affecting the deliverability and revenue opportunity for hydro and storage resources at the seam.
ai_summary: MISO and PJM are conducting a coordinated Transmission and Market Enhancement Projects (TMEP) study to address ~$681 million in persistent congestion on Market-to-Market flowgates between the two RTOs (2024–2025 data). The study, initiated following a March 13, 2026 Issues Review IPSAC decision, will evaluate 23 flowgate candidates and assess whether non-transmission solutions (operator adjustments, market redesigns, or asset-owner flexibility) can relieve binding constraints more cost-effectively than capital projects. Study steps run June–November 2026, with outcomes informing which interregional bottlenecks impede hydro export capability and which may be solvable via operational or market changes rather than new wires. For hydro owners with resources near the MISO-PJM seam, the study outcomes determine whether transmission constraints limiting their revenue will be addressed via infrastructure investment, demand-response/flexibility products, or remain as persistent opportunity costs. The next IPSAC meeting is scheduled for August 17, 2026.

title: 20260608 MISO-PJM IPSAC Item 02 FERC Order 1920 Interregional Compliance _UPDATED
relevance_reason: FERC Order 1920 interregional long-term transmission planning compliance will reshape how MISO and PJM coordinate on transmission expansion, directly affecting interregional deliverability of hydro and pumped-storage resources and their strategic transmission-planning participation opportunities.
ai_summary: MISO and PJM are implementing FERC Order 1920/1920-A through two-phase compliance: Phase 1 (regional planning, MISO June 12, 2026; PJM Dec. 12, 2025) and Phase 2 (interregional coordination, due Dec. 12, 2026). The RTOs assert their existing long-term regional planning processes (MISO LRTP, PJM Long-Term Planning) and interregional procedures are generally compliant; key reforms include explicit long-term transmission-needs posting, joint evaluation of interregional facilities, and allowance for any entity to propose interregional projects within regional planning processes. Stakeholder review (redlines July–August 2026, regional committee engagement through October–November 2026) precedes the December 2026 FERC filing. For hydro owners, interregional facility eligibility and transparent cost-benefit evaluation of cross-regional transmission solutions directly affect how PSH and reservoir hydro assets can be sited and valued for export; the expanded entity-proposal rights create a formal pathway for hydro interests to nominate interregional transmission solutions to meet long-term needs, with December 12, 2026 as the RTO filing deadline and stakeholder feedback windows in July–October 2026.

title: 20260608 MISO-PJM IPSAC Item 03 Interregional Transmission Planning Status Update
relevance_reason: Interregional transmission planning between MISO and PJM directly affects hydro and PSH deliverability, interregional transfer capability, and strategic options for resources sited in or serving both RTOs, particularly regarding long-range adequacy, benefit-metric development for transmission that may indirectly influence scarcity pricing and capacity accreditation frameworks.
ai_summary: MISO and PJM are jointly developing an expanded interregional transmission planning framework to overcome structural limitations in their Joint Operating Agreement's ability to identify and evaluate interregional solutions, with emphasis on long-range scenario-driven benefit identification under FERC Order 1920. They are stress-testing three benefit metrics (reliability, production-cost, and extreme-weather benefits) through an Interregional Transmission Coordinated Study (ITCS), with a compliance filing expected in Q4 2026 and ongoing coordination of planning assumptions and horizons across MTEP/RTEP cycles. This effort is material to hydro and PSH owners in the MISO-PJM seam because transmission expansion projects evaluated under the new framework could alter interregional transfer limits, change the economic value of storage flexibility across the seam, and shape how long-duration or seasonal hydro resource adequacy is credited in joint reliability studies — owners should monitor the Q4 2026 filing and the benefit-metric definitions MISO and PJM adopt, as they may reframe how interregional hydro exports and PSH cyclic operation are valued in future planning.

title: 20260604 OMS-MISO Survey Results Workshop Presentation.pdf
relevance_reason: MISO's 2026 OMS-MISO Survey establishes seasonal resource-accreditation (SAC) forecasts and transitions to Direct Loss of Load (DLOL) methodology for capacity accreditation starting PY 2028/29, directly affecting how hydropower and pumped storage are credited toward resource adequacy and capacity revenue.
ai_summary: MISO's 2026 OMS-MISO Survey projects 15.0 GW/yr of summer capacity additions and 12.4 GW/yr of winter additions over the next five years, with 99.5% participation from resource owners. The region is implementing a transition to Direct Loss of Load (DLOL) accreditation methodology targeted for PY 2028/29, which will value resources based on their contribution during highest-risk hours rather than peak load hours — a shift designed to better capture storage and flexible resources' reliability value when weather and load patterns decouple traditional peaks from risk periods. This methodology change affects how pumped-storage hydro and hydropower are credited in MISO's capacity market, potentially altering their accreditation values and RA-revenue implications; seasonal accreditation also shows winter becoming the critical season as the resource mix evolves, raising strategic value of winter-capable dispatchable resources like hydro.

For pumped-storage operators specifically, the document does not address PSH as a separate resource class; PSH paired with conventional hydro retains the Large Hydro treatment (100%), but the accreditation methodology's focus on production-profile overlap with solvable LOLE hours may not capture the full flexibility value of rechargeable storage.

stakeholders: Marguerite Wells (Alliance for Clean Energy New York)
ai_summary: Alliance for Clean Energy New York appeals the Operating Committee's August 17, 2026 approval of the Transition Cluster Study 2024 Report, challenging National Grid's Short Circuit Ratio (SCR)-based transmission upgrades and cost allocations assigned to Inverter-Based Resources. ai_summary: Con Edison comments on NYISO's proposed Transmission Security Limit (TSL) calculation methodology, which was modified at the November 20, 2025 ESPWG meeting to include generator outages resulting from transmission outages (9300 code events) in derating factors used to determine TSL floor. Con Edison argues that inclusion of planned transmission outages inflates summer capacity requirements unnecessarily; NYISO's June 22, 2026 review showed that more than half of winter and a small portion of summer 9300 code events were due to planned transmission work. Con Edison proposes either removing planned 9300 code events prior to EFORD calculation (consistent with exclusion of planned generator maintenance) or using summer-only outage rates, arguing that the 2025 TSL changes alone significantly increased locational capacity requirements (LCRs) and drove price spikes in May and June 2026 without attracting new dispatchable resource applications.
hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydro directly. However, TSL calculation methodology determines the capacity requirement floor that sets locational capacity market prices — hydro and other capacity-accredited resources depend on those prices for revenue. Overly conservative outage assumptions increase capacity prices paid by load-serving entities and may benefit incumbent generators with existing plants but constrain the economic case for new capacity investment. If NYISO adopts a more granular (summer-focused or planned-outage-excised) TSL methodology, the resulting lower capacity requirements could moderate the price signal available to hydro units for seasonal accreditation, whereas maintaining annual conservative assumptions keeps prices higher.

ai_summary: NYISO's 2026 Reliability Needs Assessment (RNA) base case, presented September 1, 2026 to the Electric System Planning Working Group, projects that New York's resource adequacy will exceed the Loss-of-Load-Expectation criterion starting in 2033, with deficiencies of approximately 200 MW in 2033 growing to greater than 1,800 MW by 2036. Key drivers include approximately 2,700 MW of large load projects, planned retirement of 517 MW of NYPA small gas plants (after 2030), and approximately 2,600 MW of aging generation risk. Transmission-security analyses identify NYC deficient by approximately 400 MW (2032) growing to over 1,800 MW (2036), and Lower Hudson Valley deficient by approximately 130 MW (2032) growing to over 1,900 MW (2036)—primarily exacerbated by the Gowanus and Narrows barges unavailability and NYPA retirements. The analysis shows these deficiencies are not primarily internal-transmission-constrained but rather a statewide supply-sufficiency issue; approximately 1,850 MW of additional perfect capacity would be required statewide to meet criterion if distributed proportionally. The report is under stakeholder review prior to defining Reliability Needs in the draft RNA report, with final board approval planned for November 2026.
hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped-storage facilities directly. However, NYISO's RNA base case projects a statewide resource deficiency of 1,800+ MW by 2036 driven by load growth, generation retirement, and aging-unit attrition—a structural scarcity that will trigger resource adequacy and transmission-security Reliability Needs. These Needs typically lead to capacity-market adjustments, accreditation changes, preferred-resource portfolios favoring dispatchable and flexible supply, and possibly long-term service agreements or alternative-procurement mechanisms (including energy-storage mandates) that reshape market value across load zones. For conventional hydro with geographic and seasonal flexibility advantages, and for pumped-storage assets with both energy-storage capability and fast-ramping capacity, this scarcity environment creates both revenue opportunity (higher RA prices, potential RMR or emergency-service calls) and strategic risk (pressure to modify operations, potential must-offer or seasonal-availability requirements if selected into resource portfolios). The aging-generation risk noted (2,600 MW) may also trigger fleet-replacement or mothballing decisions that alter transmission topology and interregional transfer capability—factors affecting hydro's export value from upstate to downstate load centers.

ai_summary: NYISO filed a proposal responding to FERC's June 2026 Show Cause Order (EL26-69) on large and co-located load integration. The Bulk Electric Large Load (BELL) study framework defines procedures for projects ≥50 MW at a single point of interconnection, including a 90-day Resource Adequacy and Modeling Period (RAMP) and 90-day System Impact Study (SIS) to determine Firm and Non-Firm Withdrawal Service eligibility. Large loads without associated generation receive Non-Firm Withdrawal Service; those with co-located or Partner Resources may receive Firm Withdrawal Service if resource-adequacy impact is ≤25 MW de minimis or if flexible load can mitigate larger impacts. Application fees ($10,000) and study deposits ($100k–$300k depending on project size) are required. The process includes optional pre-application ($5,000 per POI), validation of integration requests on a rolling basis, transmission security analysis to identify required Network Upgrades, and a Facilities Study phase. NYISO presented this on 1 September 2026 to ESPWG/TPAS/ICAPWG with a Section 205 tariff filing due by 16 November 2026.
hydro_read_through: This document does not mention hydropower or pumped-storage facilities. However, it establishes the framework by which new large loads will be assessed for firm transmission withdrawal rights in New York, which directly affects hydro generators' ability to sell energy and capacity into a resource-adequate market and influences dispatch economics in tight supply conditions. Partner Resources and co-located generation in the BELL process may include storage (battery and potentially longer-duration storage); the resource-adequacy methodology—in which flexible load is reduced before emergency operating procedures—signals how storage and dispatchable generation trade off against unserved load. The interconnection-queue and network-upgrade cost-allocation mechanics here may also create opportunities or costs for hydro retrofits or uprates at existing facilities competing for capacity to serve new loads.

ai_summary: NYISO's Load Forecasting Task Force presented the 2026 peak dates and times used in ICAP-market certification, and the schedule for 2027–2028 Installed Reserve Margin (IRM) and 2027 Summer Installed Capacity (ICAP) forecasts. The IRM forecast uses weather-normalized transmission-district peaks and Regional Load Growth Factors (RLGFs) derived from the 2026 Gold Book and Moody's Analytics August 2026 economic data, plus large-load projections submitted by transmission owners by September 10, 2026. Preliminary RLGFs are based on 2026 forecasts and will be finalized unless transmission owners submit updates by September 18, 2026. The ICAP forecast incorporates final weather adjustments, demand-response impacts, behind-the-meter net-generation resource peak-load impacts, and proportional transmission-loss allocation across transmission districts, with zonal and locality peak outputs feeding minimum capacity-procurement requirements. Forecast schedules and responsible-party assignments are shown for release through summer 2027.
hydro_read_through: Load forecasting directly determines NYISO's installed reserve margin (IRM) and locational capacity requirements (LCR), which set the baseline demand for all resource-accreditation studies and capacity-procurement rules. Hydro's seasonal and daily accreditation depend critically on these peak forecasts; growing load (especially large-load interconnections like data centers) increases peak demand and the scarcity premium available to dispatchable resources during those peak windows, raising hydro's energy and capacity revenue. The inclusion of behind-the-meter net generation and demand-response impacts in the forecast shows NYISO accounting for distributed resources that may displace traditional peak-hour contributions, affecting how much accredited capacity the market needs from conventional hydro plants. Transmission-loss allocation across zones also influences locational marginal prices and the economic signals hydro receives for serving constrained areas.

ai_summary: NYISO Installed Capacity Manual, version 18.0, effective July 7, 2026, with Committee Acceptance on June 18, 2026 by the BIC. This is a draft manual documenting incremental edits to NYISO's capacity market rules governing minimum capacity requirements, UCAP calculation for all resource types, auction structure and clearing, demand curves, capacity accreditation resource classes (CARCs), capacity accreditation factors (CAFs), and peak-load-window definitions. Recent revisions (v. 13.0, effective May 1, 2025) removed all references to Capacity Limited Resources (CLRs) and established a new Section 7 describing the annual process for assigning capacity accreditation resource classes and CAFs to ICAP suppliers starting in May 2024. Key rule areas include Energy Duration Limitations and Duration Adjustment Factors (sunsetting as of May 1, 2024), DMNC (Demonstrated Maximum Net Capacity) test procedures with ambient-weather adjustments, bidding requirements at Normal Upper Operating Limit, treatment of DER aggregations and co-located storage resources, and external capacity import rights and deliverability rights. The manual addresses storage participation models via sections on co-located storage resources and their UCAP calculation. The document was prepared by NYISO Capacity Market Products at 10 Krey Boulevard, Rensselaer, NY 12144, (518) 356-6060, www.nyiso.com.
hydro_read_through: Although the manual never names hydropower or pumped storage, it directly governs the capacity accreditation methodology and seasonal peak-load windows by which all non-energy-limited dispatchable resources—including conventional hydro and run-of-river plants—derive their capacity value and thereby their auction revenue. The June 2024 removal of all CLR references and the May 2024 sunset of Duration Adjustment Factors represent a structural shift in how seasonal availability is credited: hydro owners must track what the annual CARC/CAF assignment process produces to determine their accreditation in each capability year. Co-located storage and DER aggregation rules now embedded in the manual affect pumped-storage participation pathways and small-hydro aggregation feasibility. Any change to DMNC test conditions, ambient adjustments, or bidding-limit exemptions (v. 12.0 and v. 13.0 modifications) will touch the reservoir of capacity data hydro facilities must submit and the terms under which their tested capacity translates to cleared UCAP in auctions.

ai_summary: NYISO proposes incremental revisions to the ICAP Manual to implement seasonal minimum capacity requirements and ICAP demand-curve changes for the 2027–2028 capability year, building on Winter Reliability Capacity Enhancements rules accepted by FERC on June 26, 2026 and effective June 28, 2026. The revisions redefine Load-Serving Entity capacity obligations using seasonal minimum requirements (rather than a single annual obligation), clarify customer-switching adjustment procedures, and adjust the ICAP demand curve's Winter Level of Excess (WLOEz) term by replacing the "Winter 2026–2027 Capability Period" reference with "April 2027 Obligation Procurement Period" for the 2027–2028 winter period. The NYISO is targeting approval at the September 16, 2026 Business Issues Committee meeting.
hydro_read_through: Although the document does not mention hydro or pumped storage directly, seasonal capacity requirements and demand-curve adjustments are core revenue mechanisms for capacity-limited resources. Conventional hydro and PSH resources operate under energy-limitation constraints that make their seasonal availability highly variable; moving from a single annual NYCA minimum requirement to seasonal minimums (higher in winter scarcity, lower in summer abundance) could increase winter capacity accreditation revenue for seasonal units while reducing summer obligations — a material shift in the shape of annual capacity revenue for use-limited resources. The demand-curve adjustment (redefining the WLOEz term for 2027–2028) will reset the scarcity pricing and procurement surplus calculation that drives capacity-clearing prices; how that curve is calibrated affects the price signal PSH and seasonal hydro receive for winter peak availability.

relevance_reason: NYISO's Demand Curve Reset (DCR) process and methodology directly establish the capacity market framework within which all resources—including conventional hydro and pumped-storage facilities—compete and earn capacity revenue; changes to proxy unit selection, cost-to-build assumptions, financial parameters (ATWACC), and demand-curve structure alter the annual profitability and investment signals for every capacity-accredited resource in the market.

ai_summary: NYISO is proposing targeted enhancements to its ICAP Demand Curve Reset (DCR) process. Key proposals include: (1) maintaining the current tariff definition of proxy-unit screening criteria with no narrowing; (2) adopting EIA overnight capital-cost data as the initial benchmark for all proxy technologies, with tariff modification to require the independent DCR consultant to review national sources; (3) expanding the consultant's scope to assess and account for proxy unit residual value at the end of the amortization period; (4) indexing certain financial parameters (Cost of Debt, Tax Rate, Risk-Free Rate) annually while keeping Equity Beta, Debt-to-Equity Ratio, and Equity Premium fixed for each reset period; (5) using the Handy-Whitman Index to escalate construction materials, generator costs, and labor costs in annual updates; and (6) adopting a new combined-kink demand curve structure with parameters determined either formulaically in tariff or actively discussed during each DCR, moving away from a single straight-line curve. The project goal is to develop complete market design with corresponding tariff updates by the end of 2026.
hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydro or pumped-storage facilities. However, NYISO's DCR process sets the demand curve and proxy unit that directly determine the capacity-market clearing price and price slope faced by all resources, including conventional hydro and PSH. ai_summary: NYISO's Balancing Intermittency project deploys Uncertainty Reserve Requirements (URR) at the end of August 2026 to account for forecast uncertainty in Net Load (load net of Behind-The-Meter Solar), Land-Based Wind, Offshore Wind, and Front-of-The-Meter Solar. The URR is a 24-hour requirement calculated before the Day-Ahead Market and procured in addition to existing reserve requirements. Historical forecast error metrics are calculated automatically after the first week of January using the prior calendar year's data, internally reviewed and validated, and posted by April 1 each year; the same set of metrics remains in use until the next annual update. FERC accepted the design in July 2025 (Docket ER25-1998), and manual revisions were approved by stakeholders in July 2026. The composite URR calculation uses mean and standard deviation of forecast errors across resource categories and applies a z-score (1.645 for the 95th percentile) to derive the requirement.

title: 5 FERC 205 Clean up Edits for DER
relevance_reason: The document cleans up DER (distributed energy resource) and aggregation tariff language in NYISO's MST and OATT following the sunsetting of DADRP/DSASP programs, which affects the market participation pathway and offer rules for aggregated DER resources—a precedent-setting mechanism for how order-agnostic resources (including small hydro and distributed hydro assets under aggregation rules) can participate and be mitigated.

ai_summary: NYISO presents cleanup tariff revisions removing outdated references to the DADRP and DSASP demand-side programs following their sunset, and correcting related errors in the MST and OATT. Key changes include: removal of "Demand Reduction Provider" and "DSASP Provider" language throughout MST 13; consolidation of demand-side and aggregation reference-level rules by folding Aggregations into MST 23.7.3 and sunsetting the special process in MST 23.7.4 (which previously exempted demand-side resources from cost-based reference-level requirements); clarification that BTM:NG Resources, LESRs, Energy Storage Resources, and Aggregations are excluded from Minimum Generation Bid submission; and various grammatical corrections and reinstatements of accidentally deleted BPCG cost-recovery language. The revisions are scheduled for NYISO Board approval in August or September 2026, followed by a Section 205 FERC filing.
hydro_read_through: Although this document does not mention hydro or pumped storage directly, it establishes the tariff framework governing how aggregated distributed generation—including small run-of-river or distributed hydro assets—participates in NYISO's market and are subject to mitigation rules. The consolidation of Aggregations into a single reference-level pathway (MST 23.7.3) means distributed hydro in aggregations will now use cost-based reference levels like other resources, rather than the prior demand-side exemption; this changes the opportunity-cost offer development that small-hydro aggregators must prepare. The clarification that Aggregations cannot submit Minimum Generation Bid further constrains how aggregated hydro flexibility can be bid into the dispatch stack.

ai_summary: NYISO's Q1 2026 State of Market Review (authored by Potomac Economics MMU) analyzes energy and capacity market outcomes, with focus on the January 24–February 9 cold spell. Key findings: (1) All-in energy prices ranged $101–$135/MWh across regions, up 5–48% year-over-year; hydro generation averaged 2.64 GW and set prices as a marginal fuel in 26% of intervals. (2) Out-of-market commitments were extensive: SRE commitments on 14 days and SCR activations on 8 days, driven partly by oil-inventory management rather than minimum reserve requirements; 580 MW of pumped-storage capacity was excluded from NYISO's SRE adequacy evaluation. (3) Market power mitigation: SRE-committed gas generators generated ~$80M in uplift during the cold spell, with fuel costs under investigation; generators with delayed startup times on dual-fuel units were flagged for potential physical withholding. (4) Outage scheduling: 1.2 GW of firm-fuel capacity was on scheduled outages during the cold spell, with ~800 MW on non-recallable outages lasting ≥3 months; MMU recommends NYISO limit firm-fuel units from scheduling such outages during peak winter. (5) Capacity market: spot prices $6.25/kW-month in NYC (down 23% YoY), $3.37/kW-month Rest of State (up 30% YoY); prices driven by ICAP requirement changes and administrative parameters rather than supply reductions. No formal vote or comment deadline stated; document is published June 2026 for 2026-Q1 outcomes.
hydro_read_through: Hydro owners should note three direct revenue and operational impacts: (1) Pumped-storage units were systematically undercounted (580 MW excluded) in NYISO's real-time SRE adequacy assessment, which means the ISO committed expensive gas units instead of tapping cheaper storage, compressing storage arbitrage value and suppressing energy prices; this exclusion should be corrected to let PSH compete fairly in reliability procurement. (2) The report documents how out-of-market actions and SRE commitments during scarcity depress energy prices while inflating uplift, shifting margin from energy-market winners (including low-cost hydro) to OOM recipients — this is a long-standing hydro complaint that the data here validate quantitatively. (3) The restriction on outage scheduling for firm-fuel units reflects a broader principle (reliability and dispatch precedence for dispatchable resources) that could tighten scheduling windows for any unit with low inventory risk, including run-of-river and seasonal hydro; conversely, relaxing outage rules for firm-fuel generators without symmetry would advantage gas over hydro.

ai_summary: NYISO requires gas/fuel-oil generators electing the Firm Fuel Capacity Accreditation Resource Class to submit elections by August 1, 2026 for the 2027–2028 capability year and to maintain fuel-supply documentation by December 1 to satisfy a Firm Fuel Performance Availability Requirement (eight consecutive hours of operation daily during the December–February winter period, within a 56-hour-per-7-day rolling constraint). Generators must bid their elected firm MW in the day-ahead market, respond to supplemental resource evaluations, and notify NYISO within five business days of any change to fuel-supply agreements. Failure to maintain fuel, bid the firm capacity, or meet documentation requirements triggers annual firm-fuel sanctions and settlement adjustments, with FERC referral possible for false claims or misleading data. Proposed outage-scheduling changes would require resources to return to service within three days during winter and summer peak periods (exempt for non-firm-accredited units during winter). The document is a technical overview and monitoring framework for participants; no vote or action item is scheduled.

More broadly, the accreditation, must-bid, notification, and sanction framework establishes precedent for how NYISO polices capacity resource performance and commitment. Conventional hydro (not reliant on fuel oil or gas) would not participate directly, but if NYISO were to extend similar accreditation or performance-assurance rules to non-fuel-limited resources, the enforcement mechanics shown here—rolling availability targets, bid requirements, ex-post settlement adjustments—would define the model.

ai_summary: NYISO proposes revisions to its ICAP Manual to implement the Winter Reliability Capacity Enhancements tariff provisions, which became effective June 28, 2026. The revisions establish seasonal (summer and winter) NYCA minimum capacity requirements, seasonal locational minimum requirements, and revised ICAP demand curves with separate zero-crossing-point and level-of-excess parameters for each season, replacing the previous summer-to-winter and winter-to-summer conversion ratios. Revisions also implement seasonal elections for Unforced Capacity Deliverability Rights (UDRs) and External-to-Rest-of-State Deliverability Rights (EDRs) with accompanying must-offer requirements. Hydro owners in NYISO must respond to the seasonal minimum-requirement structure and the revised demand-curve parameters that now have independent winter parameters rather than ratios applied to summer values; this changes how their winter capacity can be monetized and whether their winter availability translates to matching winter-peak capacity credit. The mandatory UDR/EDR elections with must-offer requirements also constrain hydro's ability to withhold external-import capacity optionality if it relies on external deliverability rights for compliance.

ai_summary: NYISO has published modeling guidelines for projects entering cluster study under Attachment HH of the OATT. Projects must submit one-line diagrams with detailed electrical component data, steady-state models (PSSE 35.6.4 .sav/.raw/.idv/.sld files), short-circuit models (ASPEN 15.9 .olr/.chf files), and dynamic models (PSSE 35.6.4 .dyr files using standard library models or documented exceptions). Usability tests include 20-second flat-run tests at nominal and reactive-power-limit conditions, 9-cycle three-phase fault ride-through tests at two short-circuit ratios (SCR=3 and SCR=10), and short-circuit criteria requiring non-tripping performance for single-phase, two-phase, and three-phase faults. Projects must also satisfy NERC PRC-024 protection settings, transmission operator (LIPA and Con Edison) specific fault ride-through and reactive power capability requirements, and primary frequency response droop and deadband criteria. Where modeling data is inconsistent with the validated Interconnection Request, the request is the data of record.
hydro_read_through: This document does not mention hydro directly but establishes mandatory modeling and testing standards that apply to all generator and storage projects entering NYISO's interconnection queue, including hydro and pumped-storage facilities. Hydro operators must ensure dynamic models capture ride-through behavior, frequency response capabilities, and reactive-power injection characteristics at specified fault levels and short-circuit ratios to pass usability testing before cluster study advancement. The requirement that projects not trip during fault events and meet specific VCCS and frequency-response parameters will affect project design and control-system development, potentially requiring equipment upgrades or detailed transient modeling for conventional hydro units.

ai_summary: NYISO's 2026 RNA presents preliminary base-case results for years 2030–2036 showing statewide resource-adequacy LOLE violations beginning in 2033 (0.115 event-days/year) and worsening to 0.596 event-days/year by 2036. Key drivers include approximately 2,700 MW of proposed large-load additions by 2036, planned retirement of 517 MW of NYPA small gas plants after 2030, and approximately 2,600 MW of aging-generation risk. NYC transmission security margins are deficient by ~130 MW in 2031, growing to over 1,800 MW by 2036; Lower Hudson Valley shows ~300 MW deficiency in 2032 growing to over 2,000 MW by 2036, primarily following NYPA small-plant retirement and unavailability of Gowanus and Narrows barges. Statewide, approximately 1,850 MW of compensatory capacity would be required to meet the adequacy criterion if distributed proportionally across zones. The RNA study timeline shows draft report and stakeholder review in September, with final approvals scheduled for October–November 2026.
hydro_read_through: Long-duration resource scarcity—driven by load growth, retirements, and aging risks—raises the energy and capacity value of all available dispatchable generation including conventional hydro and pumped-storage resources. The NYC and Lower Hudson Valley locational deficiencies, which persist even accounting for emergency assistance and operating procedures, suggest that resources capable of serving those constrained zones will attract higher locational revenues in capacity and energy markets. Hydro owners should monitor whether these identified needs drive either accelerated investment in new resources (raising competition) or preferential accreditation/valuation of flexible, available capacity in the deficient zones (raising hydro value).

ai_summary: NYISO issued procedures responding to FERC's June 2026 Show Cause Order on large load integration. The procedures establish two new interconnection pathways: Bulk Electric Large Load (BELL) for loads ≥50 MW at voltages >69 kV, and Bulk Operating Load Tracking (BOLT) for loads 10–50 MW. BELL includes a 90-day screening and modeling period, 90-day system impact study, and alternative upgrades evaluation; loads may take firm withdrawal service (no curtailment restrictions) or non-firm withdrawal service (subject to $200/MWh mandatory bid cap curtailment). Co-located loads with generation at the same point of interconnection can net injection and withdrawal, though FERC directed elimination of cross-subsidy by requiring gross-demand charging for regulation and black-start service. Transmission customer must provide hourly load forecasts, real-time telemetry, and accept remote-disconnect capability and ramp-rate constraints. Large loads may partner with proposed generators in the same capacity region to mitigate resource-adequacy impacts. NYISO's compliance filing deadline is August 17, 2026, but may request an abeyance extending it to November 16, 2026. Written feedback requested by July 27, 2026.
hydro_read_through: The document does not name hydro or pumped-storage resources. However, the order has direct implications: (1) non-firm withdrawal service with a $200/MWh mandatory bid cap creates a new curtailment product that will compete for scarcity rents with ancillary services and energy revenue from conventional and pumped-storage resources during tight conditions; (2) the requirement that co-located loads be charged on a gross-demand basis for regulation and black-start eliminates a netting opportunity that may have previously allowed hybrid or adjacent generation to offset costs, establishing precedent for how NYISO treats co-located and adjacent resources more broadly; and (3) the firm versus non-firm distinction allocates transmission rights based on resource adequacy screening, which may pressure legacy generation (including existing hydro plants serving regional adequacy) if load growth accelerates faster than modeled. The operational requirements (ramp rates, ride-through, remote disconnect) are general rules applied to large loads; they set the operational bar for grid-following devices and may inform future standards for synchronous and energy-limited resources.

title: 03b IPPNY Comments on NYISO Demand Curve Reset Methodology Improvement Project

stakeholders: Richard Bratton (Independent Power Producers of New York, Inc. (IPPNY))
ai_summary: IPPNY, representing 80% of New York generation, submits comments on NYISO's preliminary DCR improvements, urging four changes: (1) require proxy units to meet firm-fuel winter-availability requirements (minimum 8 hours daily operation December–February, or 56 hours on-site fuel storage); (2) adjust the Level of Excess to close the gap between market and planning assumptions; (3) shift the zero-crossing point (ZCP) of capacity demand curves rightward to reduce price volatility with small supply changes; and (4) improve annual escalation factors for financial parameters while retaining the quadrennial reset cycle, using New York-specific data for cost-of-debt and market-return indices. The core grievance is that NYISO's 2022 switch to a 2-hour battery as proxy unit excluded firm-fuel costs needed for winter reliability, causing capacity prices to fall below levels needed to retain or invest in generation — a signal deficiency that IPPNY argues has induced retirements and underinvests in reliability. Status: IPPNY feedback on preliminary recommendations; no vote or implementation date stated. Most exposed are any hydro/PSH operators relying on NYISO capacity-market revenues for cost recovery, particularly if they have winter firm-fuel capability that the battery-proxy ignores.

title: 3 ICAP Demand Curve Reset (DCR) Process and Methodology Improvements

ai_summary: NYISO is redesigning its Installed Capacity (ICAP) demand curve reset (DCR) process and cost-to-build methodology, with initial recommendations evaluated against reliability-based valuation, transparency, investment efficiency, and ease of administration. Key proposals include: using EIA overnight capital cost data to streamline cost-to-build estimates (rather than consultant-driven bottom-up approaches), codifying proxy-unit screening criteria to increase predictability, implementing more frequent indexed updates to financial parameters, and adjusting demand curve structures (kinked curves, zero-crossing informed by Minimum Reliability Index). The document is an interim presentation (July 1, 2026) building to an initial concept proposal in August and a complete market design with tariff updates by year-end. For hydro and pumped-storage owners, changes to CONE inputs and proxy-unit definitions directly affect capacity accreditation values and the price signal that drives the DCR clearing price—hydro's primary revenue mechanism in NYISO; any shift toward faster reset cycles or non-consultant methodologies could increase or decrease the accuracy of cost-to-build estimates that anchor their capacity payments, and technology-prescriptive proxy choices (e.g., mandating a gas turbine) would exclude alternative dispatch profiles that might better reflect hydro's actual value.

ai_summary: LIPA proposes an FY2027 NYISO Market Project to amend ICAP Manual §4.9.3.2(iii) to create a durable eligibility pathway for ISO-NE capacity imports to Zone K, addressing a collision between ISO-NE's planned elimination of the Capacity Export Through Import-Constrained Zones (CETICZ) mechanism and NYISO's categorical disqualification of resources in zones separated from the NYCA by constrained zones. Under current Path B rules, Cross Sound Cable (HVDC) and Northport–Norwalk Harbor Cable imports from Rest-of-Pool are automatically disqualified whenever Connecticut is modeled as an ICZ, regardless of actual price separation, and ISO-NE's transition to a prompt (1-month-ahead) capacity auction removes the ~3-year forward visibility that previously allowed hedging of this risk. LIPA seeks rolling documentation rules, seasonal CSO-netting stabilization, and grandfathering of existing contracts to preserve external ICAP eligibility and multi-year contracting certainty, noting that NYISO already accepts PJM imports under facility-level deliverability tests rather than categorical zonal exclusions. relevance_reason: NYISO's 20-year System & Resource Outlook directly informs transmission-constrained deliverability of hydro and zero-emissions resources, identifies congestion chokepoints (Central East, Northern New York) where hydro exports and firm capacity face transmission limits, and shapes long-term resource-adequacy strategy affecting hydro's strategic siting and revenue opportunity.
ai_summary: NYISO's 2025–2044 System & Resource Outlook, presented to the Management Committee on June 24, 2026, projects 20-year system conditions, demand, generation mix, and transmission congestion across New York. Key findings emphasize that transmission capability increasingly determines whether new resources can serve load, and identify the Central East interface and Northern New York as targeted upgrade opportunities for bulk transmission to enable zero-emissions and firm-capacity development. The Outlook recommends establishing a path for firm, dispatchable capacity (including potential hydrogen-based generation) to provide grid services alongside renewables, coordinating resource additions and retirements to avoid tightening system conditions, and enhancing dynamic voltage support across Central East. Hydro owners in New York and the region exporting into NYISO should track the final Outlook (Board approval scheduled for July 2026) because transmission constraints identified here directly govern where new hydro projects achieve economic deliverability, and the emphasis on firm capacity and operational flexibility reaffirms hydro's strategic value in a high-renewable future—but only if interconnection and transmission planning prioritize hydro access.

title: 8 MMU Outlook Review
relevance_reason: NYISO Market Monitoring Unit analysis of renewable curtailment, storage economics, and energy price signals directly affects hydro and pumped-storage revenue via Index REC/Storage Credit structures, technology and nodal discounts on LBMP, and the value of storage-based curtailment mitigation.
stakeholders: Joe Coscia (Potomac Economics / NYISO Market Monitoring Unit)
Pallas LeeVanSchaick (Potomac Economics / NYISO Market Monitoring Unit)
ai_summary: NYISO's Market Monitoring Unit analyzed the 2025–2044 System & Resource Outlook to evaluate how market signals guide renewable and storage investment. Key finding: energy storage becomes cost-effective for curtailment mitigation only as wind and solar penetration increases and marginal curtailment rates rise; under the Index Storage Credit structure, storage has strong incentives to locate where curtailment risk is highest, but may be unprofitable near profitable renewable sites. The MMU also identifies nodal and technology discounts (differences between zonal average LBMP and generation-weighted LBMP at renewable sites), which reduce wind and solar net revenues below Index REC strike prices—a signal that affects both the competitiveness of all-renewable portfolios and the relative value of storage as a complementary product. For pumped-storage owners, this analysis quantifies the regional and temporal distribution of curtailment opportunities and implied net revenue costs of storage across three policy scenarios (Contract Case 2030, 100×44 High Load 2035, 95×44 Baseline Load 2035), directly informing where PSH investment is most economically justified under NYISO market rules.

title: 04 Geospatial Modeling of EV Load Impacts at National Grid
relevance_reason: Load growth from EV electrification drives demand forecasting inputs to NYISO's resource-adequacy and operational-planning processes, which directly affect hydro's strategic value and dispatch scheduling; co-located load and feeder-level demand patterns also inform transmission and storage deployment decisions that touch hydro assets and deliverability.
ai_summary: National Grid's Load Forecasting & Analytics team presented geospatial modeling methods to forecast electric-vehicle load impacts on NYISO's distribution and transmission network at feeder and system levels through 2035+. The work integrates EV adoption propensity models (driven by socioeconomics, vehicle-registration data, program enrollment) with vehicle-specific charging profiles (light-duty, medium/heavy-duty, transit/school bus) to project unconstrained load impacts by location and time. The presentation outlined a hybrid allocation approach (census-tract and parcel-level granularity for subsets like depot-based MHDVs and queued storage/PV) and flagged ongoing challenges in data integration, propensity-model robustness, and governance consistency. No near-term policy decision or vote was announced, but this forecasting framework feeds NYISO's system-planning and resource-adequacy studies—which determine seasonal reserve requirements, transmission expansion triggers, and the scarcity value of dispatchable hydro and PSH.

title: 2 Improving Capacity Accreditation and Resource Adequacy Modeling
relevance_reason: MECHANISM: NYISO is evaluating alternative capacity accreditation methodologies (moving from LOLE to Expected Unserved Energy) that will directly affect how hydropower and pumped-storage resources are credited toward resource adequacy requirements and capacity payments, with implications for accreditation factors (CAFs) and UCAP contributions across different resource classes.
ai_summary: NYISO is conducting a study to increase transparency in resource adequacy modeling and evaluate whether Expected Unserved Energy (EUE)—a magnitude-based metric capturing duration and depth of capacity shortfalls—should replace or supplement the traditional 1-day-in-10-years LOLE criterion for calculating Capacity Accreditation Factors (CAFs). The CAF determines how much Unforced Capacity (UCAP) each resource can provide; EUE would capture reliability contributions differently across resource types, particularly affecting hydro's seasonal contribution and ability to mitigate prolonged weather events as NYISO's winter-risk profile increases (4.4 GW of intermittent resources expected in five years). NYISO has engaged GE to model CAF sensitivity under EUE scenarios and assess accreditation stability; the study is due to complete in 2026, with broader stakeholder assessment of which methodology better reflects NYISO's evolving resource mix to follow.

title: 3 External SRE Opportunity Cost & Penalty
relevance_reason: NYISO proposes to cap opportunity-cost recovery for external ICAP suppliers (including hydropower and storage) called for emergency service, and to add FERC referral penalties for non-compliance — changes that directly affect how external hydro and PSH can recover costs when required to respond to emergency calls, and the penalties they face for non-compliance.
ai_summary: NYISO proposes two changes to external ICAP supplier obligations during System Reserve Events (SREs): (1) cap opportunity-cost recovery at the applicable proxy-generator-bus LBMP minus ATC interface congestion, eliminating pass-through of revenues external resources could earn in neighboring control areas; (2) retain existing ICAP Shortfall Penalties for SRE non-response but add FERC referral threat if an external supplier delivers to another control area while failing to meet its NYISO energy obligation. The proposal reframes opportunity costs as compensation for NYISO's mandatory -$1,000/MWh bidding requirement, aligning external treatment closer to internal reliability suppliers. Next step: NYISO will return to ICAPWG/MIWG with draft tariff and manual language following stakeholder feedback. For external hydro and PSH owners operating at NYISO seams, this eliminates the option to recover the full spread between NYISO and neighboring-market prices during an SRE call, while the FERC referral adds reputational/regulatory risk to non-compliance.

title: 3 External SRE Opportunity Cost & Penalty - Revised
relevance_reason: NYISO proposal to cap opportunity-cost recovery and strengthen defection penalties for external ICAP suppliers affects how hydro and other dispatchable resources located outside NY (notably in PJM or ISO-NE) value their NYISO capacity obligations and manage the trade-off between NYISO SRE calls and higher-priced neighboring-market opportunities — a direct revenue and strategic participation lever for multi-region hydro portfolios.
ai_summary: NYISO proposes to cap opportunity-cost recovery for external ICAP suppliers responding to Supplemental Resource Evaluations (SREs) at the applicable proxy-bus LBMP, excluding ATC interface congestion, and to add FERC referral as a sanction for suppliers that defect to sell energy elsewhere during an SRE obligation. Currently, external suppliers can claim any opportunity costs; the proposal aligns external cost recovery more closely to internal reliability-commitment rules (startup, minimum generation) and removes the subsidy for selling at neighboring-market prices. Status: draft for ICAPWG/MIWG discussion; next step is stakeholder feedback and return with tariff/manual language (no deadline stated). External ICAP suppliers — especially multi-region hydropower and gas operators serving NYISO capacity markets from PJM, ISO-NE, or IESO — face lower opportunity-cost compensation in high-priced hours in neighboring control areas, reducing the financial benefit of maintaining NYISO ICAP obligations; simultaneously, the threat of FERC referral for non-compliance strengthens the incentive to answer SREs even when outside-market prices spike.

title: 4 Balancing Intermittency: Manual Updates
relevance_reason: MECHANISM: Uncertainty Reserve Requirements (URR) design directly affects hydro's revenue from ancillary services and flexibility products; URR adds new locational reserve requirements calculated for Net Load, Wind, and Solar forecast uncertainty, requiring hydro and other dispatchable resources to supply additional reserves on top of existing requirements, with deployment in August 2026.
ai_summary: NYISO is implementing Uncertainty Reserve Requirements (URR)—a new 24-hour reserve product to account for forecast uncertainty in Net Load, Land-Based Wind, Offshore Wind, and Front-of-Meter Solar. The URR design was accepted by FERC in July 2025 (ER25-1998) and is scheduled for August 2026 deployment. NYISO has incorporated stakeholder feedback from June 2nd meeting and updated the Ancillary Services Manual and a new Locational Reserve Requirements document; notably, the Long Island 30-minute total reserve requirement will vary from 270 MW (off-peak) to 540 MW (on-peak). These additional, locational reserve requirements create new demand for the ramping and flexibility services that hydropower traditionally supplies, raising the value of flexible hydro capacity during high-uncertainty periods (high wind/solar variability). All resources—including hydro and pumped storage—will be obligated to contribute to URR supply. Stakeholder vote scheduled for July 15–16, 2026, at BIC and OC meetings; deployment begins August 2026.

title: 4a Locational Reserves Requirements
relevance_reason: NYISO locational reserve requirements define the operating-reserve products (spinning, 10-minute, 30-minute) that hydropower and pumped-storage units are eligible to supply, and establish locational and magnitude thresholds that affect their reserve-procurement revenue and dispatch obligations.
ai_summary: NYISO specifies locational reserve requirements across five zones (NYCA, EAST, SENY, NYC, LI) for three reserve products: spinning reserve (most restrictive, synchronous units only), 10-minute non-synchronized reserve, and 30-minute reserve. NYCA requires 655 MW spinning and 1,310 MW 10-minute total; EAST requires 330 MW spinning and 1,200 MW 10-minute; SENY requires 1,300–1,800 MW 30-minute (varying by hour, reduced to zero during thunderstorm alerts); NYC and LI have localized requirements of 625–1,250 MW and 120–540 MW respectively. Hydropower and pumped-storage units eligible for spinning reserve (synchronous generation) are the primary suppliers of the 655 MW NYCA spinning requirement and regional spinning reserves; conventional hydro can also supply 10-minute and 30-minute reserves. The document does not indicate a pending vote or comment deadline but establishes the baseline rules governing reserve accreditation and revenue eligibility for reservoir hydro and PSH in New York.

title: 4b Draft Ancillary Services Manual redline

The manual includes new or revised sections on energy storage resources' reactive power testing (3.6.5), synchronous condenser testing (3.6.3), HVDC VSC technology (3.6.4), and regulation service performance audits (4.11.3). The document is in draft for discussion; it was accepted by BIC on 04/15/2026 and OC on 04/16/2026, with an effective date of 05/01/2026. Hydro and pumped-storage operators must track revisions to regulation demand curves (4.8), performance adjustment rules (4.5–4.6), and resource qualification thresholds (4.11), as these directly affect the value of regulation and reserve services — historically hydro's largest ancillary-service revenue source in NYISO. The manual's treatment of energy storage resources in reactive power testing and performance frameworks may also signal NYISO's direction on storage parity rules relevant to pumped-storage PSH participation.

title: 5 Transmission Security Background
relevance_reason: NYISO's derating-factor methodology and transmission-security-assessment practices directly affect ICAP accreditation for all generators including hydropower, and the document addresses seasonal EFORd calculations and limited-control run-of-river hydro treatment in capacity-adequacy studies.
ai_summary: NYISO staff present transmission-security assessment background and derating-factor recommendations for the Installed Capacity market, including treatment of seasonal forced outage rates (EFORd) for thermal units and reference to run-of-river hydro derating under ICAP Manual Attachment N. The document identifies a methodological gap: 5-year seasonal EFORd averages understate zonal derating factors by roughly 2% compared to 5-year continuous EFORd, and NYISO recommends developing an automated tool to support multi-year continuous seasonal EFORd calculations. The implications for hydro are indirect but material—derating factors determine Locational Minimum Installed Capacity Requirements (LCRs) that shape the ICAP demand curve and pricing hydro and other resources bid into. Run-of-river resources are explicitly noted as following Attachment N methodology, though the document does not propose changes to that treatment in this June 2026 working-group meeting.

title: 6 Seasonal TSL Floor Kick Off
relevance_reason: NYISO's seasonal TSL floor methodology directly affects ICAP accreditation and capacity requirements for all resources including hydro and storage, with implications for winter peak conditions and derating factors for limited-control run-of-river hydro.
ai_summary: NYISO is implementing seasonal Transmission Security Limit (TSL) floor values as part of its Winter Reliability Capacity Enhancements proposal (filed with FERC February 18, 2026, Docket ER26-1431, effective date requested June 28, 2026, for 2027-2028 capability year onward). The seasonal methodology will replace annual calculations with winter- and summer-specific peak loads, bulk transmission limits, equipment ratings, and derating factors. Critically, NYISO proposes to include winter performance data for Limited Control Run of River hydro resources in the seasonal derating factor calculation and will establish winter-specific Special Case Resource (SCR) enrollment, which raises the ICAP addback component. The document indicates that 5-year derating factors will consider winter EFORd for thermal units and seasonal adjustments for intermittent and run-of-river hydro per updated ICAP Manual Attachment N (revised June 2026), and that seasonal External Unforced Deliverability Rights (UDR) elections would be implemented starting 2027-2028. Pumped storage and battery-based energy storage resources (ESRs) currently face no specific UCAP duration-limit adjustment in the TSL floor calculation, though the document notes ESRs are modeled in resource adequacy with full availability subject to duration limits. Run-of-river hydro owners should monitor the winter derating factor methodology to understand how winter-season performance data may reduce their seasonal ICAP accreditation; reservoir and pumped-storage operators should track the seasonal UDR election framework and any future ESR adjustments proposed.

title: 2 Winter Reliability Capacity Enhancements – Seasonal UDR/EDR Elections and Must Offer Requirement: Proposed ICAP Manual and Attachment Revisions
relevance_reason: NYISO establishes seasonal must-offer requirements and penalties for holders of External Unforced Capacity Deliverability Rights (UDRs) and External-to-Rest of State Deliverability Rights (EDRs), which directly affects how external capacity—including hydropower—can be exported from and must be offered to meet NYCA obligations, and creates an enforcement mechanism (penalty methodology in new Attachment Q) that changes an owner's compliance exposure and dispatch obligations.
ai_summary: NYISO is implementing seasonal elections for External UDRs and EDRs starting May 1, 2027 (2027–2028 Capability Year), with elections due August 1, 2026. Holders of External UDRs or EDRs must submit distinct seasonal elections (one for Summer, one for Winter) to return capacity to the NYCA, or face a must-offer requirement: capacity not returned must be offered in each ICAP Spot Market Auction or certified to meet LSE minimum UCAP requirements, and failure triggers a penalty calculated using Market Clearing Price and a new Attachment Q methodology converting ICAP to UCAP. This reshapes the options available to external capacity owners (including hydro exporters to NYCA) by forcing them to commit seasonally to either export or domestic service, with financial penalties for non-compliance; pumped-storage and reservoir hydro operators holding external rights into New York will need to evaluate seasonal dispatch strategies against the penalty risk. The proposal was filed with FERC in Docket No. ER26-1431 with requested effective date June 28, 2026; ICAP Manual revisions become effective one business day after the 10-day appeal period if approved (by July 7, 2026 absent appeal or FERC rejection).

title: 2a Draft ICAP Manual

Sections 4.1.1 and 4.1.4 detail Energy Duration Limitations and Duration Adjustment Factors for installed-capacity suppliers and co-located storage; Section 4.2 governs Demonstrated Maximum Net Capability (DMNC) testing that determines hydro's accredited capacity; and Section 4.4 establishes monthly operating-data reporting requirements (including intermittent power resources and energy-limited resources). The document is in draft for discussion at the Business Issues Committee (BIC) meeting on June 18, 2026, following circulation at the June 9, 2026 ICAPWG meeting (yellow-highlighted changes noted). Hydro and PSH owners need to review the updated duration-adjustment methodology, DMNC test procedures, and state-of-charge rules for co-located storage to confirm accreditation treatment and compliance deadlines.

title: 03 Operations Report - May 2026
relevance_reason: Monthly operational metrics tracking NYISO generation mix, hydro/pumped-storage capacity and availability, intermittent resource forecasting, curtailment, and transmission constraints that directly affect hydro dispatch and revenue opportunities.
ai_summary: NYISO's May 2026 operations report shows hydro (including pumped-storage hydro) at 6,324 MW nameplate capacity, comprising 12% of NYCA generation resources. The report tracks month-to-month generation mix, day-ahead market capacity unavailable in real-time (broken by fuel type including hydro), wind and solar curtailment by transmission constraint, net load ramps, and reserve activations. Two new transmission projects (Smart Path Connect and additional 345 kV facilities) came online in May, and the Champlain Hudson Power Express merchant transmission facility entered the real-time energy market on 5/13, potentially improving deliverability for hydro exports. title: 05a Summer 2026 Operations Study - Presentation

ai_summary: NYISO's Summer 2026 operations study reports 1,225 MW of generation retirements (including large thermal units like Danskammer 532 MW and Narrows 352 MW) offset by 225 MW of solar and storage additions. These changes redistribute flows and alter interface thermal limits: Total East interface limit decreased 125 MW, UPNY-ConEd increased 250 MW, UPNY-SENY increased 225 MW, and Moses South increased 250 MW. The study's status is a June 2026 presentation update to the Operating Committee; no forward deadlines are stated. For hydro owners, the net effect is mixed: retirement of thermal generation reduces dispatchable competition and may elevate real-time energy prices and ramping value, while the HVDC and transmission upgrades improve northern import capability and may compress NY price separations, affecting both in-state dispatchable hydro revenue and Northwest-to-NY export economics. Pumped-storage operators should monitor how the reduced Moses South thermal limits and increased UPNY interfaces change the voltage-support and frequency-response service opportunities in those zones.
