relevance_reason: NYISO's renewable pocket analysis identifies transmission constraints affecting hydro deliverability in northern and western New York; hydro resources compete with wind and solar for shared transmission paths, directly impacting energy-delivery value and strategic interconnection/transmission planning.
ai_summary: NYISO's 2025–2044 System & Resource Outlook Appendix J analyzes renewable generation pockets and finds that hydro resources in Pockets W and X (western and northern New York) face rising curtailment and congestion in high-penetration renewable scenarios. Pocket X1 (St. Lawrence hydro corridor) exhibits the second-highest congestion among all pockets; hydro curtails before wind and solar because hydro is ineligible for Tier 1 RECs and therefore carries no negative-bid cost in the production-cost model, putting it at a competitive disadvantage when transmission is constrained. The analysis is draft (dated June 10, 2026 BIC) and used to inform longer-range transmission-upgrade planning; approved Phase 1 and Phase 2 transmission projects in Northern New York (Smart Path Connect) are expected to alleviate some congestion, but Policy Case scenarios with 13–35 GW of additional land-based renewable capacity by 2035 will intensify resource-concentration pressures on hydro energy deliverability.

title: 9 Order No. 1920 Long-Term Regional Transmission Planning
relevance_reason: FERC Order 1920 transmission planning and cost allocation framework directly affects hydro deliverability, interconnection, and strategic transmission expansion that determines whether existing and new hydro resources can reach markets; long-term scenarios and resource-mix assumptions will drive transmission investment decisions that enable or constrain hydro export capability.
ai_summary: NYISO is implementing FERC Order 1920 (and subsequent clarifications 1920-A and 1920-B) through a redesigned Long-Term Transmission Planning Process that expands the 20-year planning horizon, incorporates New York Department of Public Service scenario input, and establishes an ex ante cost-allocation methodology for selected transmission projects. The process creates a new Catalog of Transmission Expansion Opportunities, solicits private-sector project proposals competing against NYISO baseline solutions using seven FERC-mandated benefit metrics (avoided reliability facilities, LOLE reduction, production cost savings, reduced losses, outage-congestion mitigation, extreme-weather resilience, and capacity benefits), and gates selection through NYPSC declaration of Long-Term Transmission Needs before cost recovery is allocated. The framework directly affects where transmission investment flows: hydro owners in New York face a new, longer-term planning horizon and competing non-wires alternatives that may or may not prioritize inter-area hydro exports versus local reliability; the cost-allocation methodology (details not yet finalized) determines whether transmission enabling hydro delivery is socialized regionally or assigned to specific beneficiaries. The compliance mechanics are active — NYISO Board approval of the planning structure is imminent, and the first Outlook cycle and PSC filings will begin shortly thereafter.

This reframes deliverability-rights holders' compliance posture: seasonal elections create a new obligation to commit or forfeit, converting a flexible holding into a binary choice with penalties. Pumped storage and large reservoir hydro holding external rights face the most direct impact; small hydro with external positions must track August elections and ensure compliance or incur monthly penalties.

title: 2 DER Market Enhancements
relevance_reason: DER aggregation participation rules directly affect small hydropower owners' ability to participate in NYISO markets under Order 2222 frameworks; the DADSR concept and proposed telemetry/accreditation changes alter the strategic options and compliance burden for hydro resources enrolled in DER aggregations.
ai_summary: NYISO proposes a Day-Ahead Demand-Side Resource (DADSR) variant within its existing DER & Aggregation participation model, designed to accommodate DSR with longer start-up times and limited real-time flexibility. DADSR would bid day-ahead, lock to a fixed real-time schedule, and be ineligible for operating reserves or regulation service; it would qualify for ICAP participation with 2–24-hour energy duration limitations and potentially reduced telemetry requirements (6-second with 30-second scan rates for sub-1 MW facilities versus current standards for 1+ MW). Small hydropower and run-of-river resources enrolled in DER aggregations face a strategic choice: participation under current DER rules (with full telemetry/ancillary-service obligations) or under DADSR (simpler telemetry, day-ahead certainty, but loss of regulation/reserve revenue and real-time flexibility upside). ai_summary: NYISO proposes revisions to ICAP Manual Attachment N to implement seasonal (summer and winter) translation factors for intermittent resources and limited-control run-of-river hydro, replacing the current summer-only methodology. The change responds to observed winter Loss of Load Expectation (LOLE) beginning in the 2026–2027 IRM study and supports the Winter Reliability Capacity Enhancements proposal (filed with FERC 2/18/2026, target implementation 5/1/2027 for the 2027–2028 Capability Year). The proposal also corrects the availability-factor formula to apply proper weighted averaging, aligning calculation with current implementation in IRM, LCR, and deliverability studies. For run-of-river hydro owners, this means winter availability will now drive a separate winter UCAP translation factor based on December–February production patterns weighted by winter LOLE distribution, potentially improving winter accreditation if winter production is high relative to winter scarcity hours, or reducing it if winter is a dry season; the revision will be presented to the Business Issue Committee on 6/10/2026.

ai_summary: NYISO is finalizing manual revisions to implement its Uncertainty Reserve Requirement (URR), a new 24-hour reserve product designed to hedge forecast uncertainty for net load, land-based wind, offshore wind, and front-of-meter solar. The design was accepted by FERC in July 2025 (ER25-1998) and is scheduled for deployment in August 2026. The updated manuals clarify URR calculation methodology (incorporated in new Attachment D to the Ancillary Services Manual), specify that URR can be met using 30-Minute Reserve in the day-ahead market, introduce locational demand curves with a new Long Island requirement row (270 MW and 540 MW separately), and refine operating-capacity accounting for seasonal differences. Stakeholder votes are scheduled for June 10–11, 2026 (BIC and OC); comments can be submitted at the June 4 SOAS meeting. For hydro owners, URR creates both a revenue opportunity (new procurement of a flexibility product hydro naturally supplies) and a compliance obligation (must-offer rules in the 30-minute reserve product that backs URR); pumped-storage facilities are particularly positioned to capture value from locational reserve requirements, especially on Long Island where the demand curve now explicitly separates 270 MW and 540 MW tiers.

title: 6 2025 State of the Market Report

stakeholders: Joe Coscia (NYISO Market Monitoring Unit / Potomac Economics)
ai_summary: NYISO's Market Monitoring Unit (Potomac Economics) identifies structural gaps in the capacity market that undervalue reliability contributions and distort investment incentives. Key findings: (1) demand curves based on 2-hour battery cost understate Net CONE, risking premature retirements even as load grows; (2) seasonal incentives are misaligned—firm fuel/UDR elections locked 16 months in advance don't respond to winter market prices, and elected capacity for 2026/27 (15.2 GW) exceeds planning assumptions (12.3 GW), creating cost-allocation risk; (3) transmission security is undercompensated—downstate LCRs increasingly bind at floor, overpaying bottled generation (SCRs, large units) and underpaying non-firm gas units while creating $74M annual inefficiency post-CHPE. Recommendations filed or pending include raising the demand-curve floor (Rec. 2025-1a), moving seasonal-election deadlines closer to winter (Rec. 2022-2), introducing locational CAFs (Rec. 2025-2), and expanding capacity zones. These touch pumped-storage accreditation (2-hour battery CONE undermines longer-duration PSH value), seasonal energy adequacy (firm fuel elections timing), and locational value recognition (hydro deliverability and transmission-security contribution). No formal comment deadline is stated in this highlights presentation, but the full 2025 SOM Report (posted May 19, 2026) and tariff filing ER26-1431 are the operative documents.

title: 3 Automatic ICAP Surplus Offers
relevance_reason: MECHANISM: NYISO is revising the ICAP market's surplus-offer rules to automatically resell capacity that load-serving entities and ICAP suppliers procure but do not need, at zero-dollar bids. For hydropower and storage owners selling capacity into NYISO's ICAP market—whether as primary capacity suppliers or via bilateral trades—this rule removes their option to withhold surplus capacity and directly affects the monetization path and price realization for unsold UCAP.
ai_summary: NYISO proposes a new tariff section (5.14.4) that automatically submits zero-dollar offers for any Unforced Capacity (UCAP) surplus held by load-serving entities, ICAP suppliers, and ICAP marketers after the monthly certification deadline, effective May 1, 2027 (Board approval and FERC filing required). Currently, surplus UCAP often goes unoffered, potentially raising market-clearing prices; the automatic zero-dollar offer guarantees resale at the auction clearing price. Hydropower and pumped-storage owners—particularly those acquiring capacity via bilateral trades or selling excess UCAP—will face mandatory resale of any certified surplus, eliminating the ability to withhold capacity or negotiate off-market prices for unexpectedly available MW; however, capacity associated with a physical transmission interface (PTID) and 'unoffered MW' remain subject to physical-withholding rules and are excluded from automatic resale.

title: 3a MST 5.14 redline
relevance_reason: ICAP capacity-market accreditation and demand-curve methodology directly affect hydro and PSH revenue from capacity markets, particularly the periodic review process that sets accreditation reference points and the demand-curve adjustments that drive cleared capacity prices.
ai_summary: NYISO's tariff Section 5.14 establishes the ICAP Spot Market Auction mechanics and demand-curve parameters that clear monthly unforced-capacity obligations. The document redlines the periodic review methodology (every four years, next review for 2025/2026 capability year), which assesses the levelized cost of a peaking plant, net energy and ancillary-services revenue offsets, and seasonal differences in capacity availability. Beginning with 2025/2026, demand curves will account for seasonal variations in capacity availability—summer and winter curves now reflect different excess-capacity assumptions. The 2025/2026 NYCA summer curve peaks at $21.69/kW-month; winter at $16.39/kW-month, with locational adders (NYC summer peak $41.30). Hydro and PSH capacity accreditation is measured against these ICAP demand curves translated to unforced-capacity terms; seasonal demand-curve splits will alter how seasonal hydro availability and storage round-trip efficiency factor into capacity showings, potentially reducing winter accreditation if available supply diverges seasonally from the reference peaking-plant assumption.

Resource Scheduling Prior to Day-Ahead phase 2 may alter the timing and constraints on how hydro (and other dispatchable resources) submit day-ahead schedules relative to load forecasting and commitment sequencing, affecting hydro's ability to optimize offer timing and capture scarcity revenue. ai_summary: PJM proposes a process allowing projects with existing Capacity Injection Rights (CIRs) obtained through interconnection studies to change fuel type—for example, from solar to storage—without forfeiting those CIRs, provided the change does not materially impact the transmission system. The proposal aims to accelerate capacity availability and reduce duplicate study work by leveraging previously completed interconnection studies when market conditions or developer preferences shift. PJM notes that other ISOs/RTOs have implemented similar approaches through FERC-approved material modification review processes and says the Planning Committee will evaluate potential Tariff or Manual revisions.

ai_summary: PJM Manual 21B, Revision 06 (effective June 24, 2026), establishes rules for determining generating capability and ELCC accreditation across all resource classes. The document defines two hydropower ELCC classes: Intermittent Hydropower Class (run-of-river generators that cannot appreciably store water) and Hydropower with Non-Pumped Storage Class (facilities that can exert material control over stored water and output, demonstrated by producing at least 110% of daily average power for 4 hours during peak summer afternoons, assessed once per five years). Run-of-river plants are locked into the Intermittent class with no path to reclassification. Testing deadlines and simultaneous-testing coordination rules (June–September summer, December–March winter) create operational scheduling obligations. For owners considering uprates or mothball-to-operational returns, the CAPMOD testing and CIR retention mechanics dictate what incremental MW can be offered and certified.

ai_summary: PJM has drafted minimum voltage and frequency ride-through requirements for Large Computational Loads (LCLs)—data centers and computational facilities with ≥50 MW demand supplied through power electronic conversion equipment at ≥100 kV. The requirements, codified in proposed tariff revisions to Part I, Part III Sections 28.2 and 35.1, and Manual 14B Attachment D, establish voltage and frequency envelopes that LCLs must remain connected through (e.g., continuous operation at 0.90–1.10 p.u. voltage, 58.8–61.2 Hz frequency) with specified ride-through durations at lower voltages and frequencies, and recovery-time requirements. New LCL facilities entering the study process on or after November 1, 2026 must comply as a condition of interconnection; existing facilities with material modifications or those in-study or under construction before November 1, 2026 are "Transition LCL Facilities" with compliance deadline no later than November 1, 2027 or one year after commercial operation, whichever is later. PJM may accelerate compliance to 90 days for any LCL contributing to transient voltage instability, cascading load loss, or voltage collapse. Transmission Owners may establish requirements more stringent than PJM's minimum on a non-discriminatory basis. The document is a draft dated September 1, 2026, and remains under development.
hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage directly. However, the rules establish binding ride-through performance standards for large power-electronic loads that, when interconnected at transmission voltages, will constrain the voltage and frequency operating windows available on the grid. Hydro plants—especially synchronous generators at transmission-connected scales—must maintain stable operation around these newly-mandated load behaviors, and voltage-support and frequency-response services that hydro traditionally provides may face changing demand profiles as LCLs impose their own protective and recovery constraints. Additionally, if a hydro plant is co-located with an LCL ("where the LCL is co-located with a Generation Resource or Energy Storage Resource, at the Point of Interconnection"), the LCL's compliance is measured at the shared POI, meaning hydro's voltage and frequency profile must meet dual standards—its own operating requirements plus the LCL's ride-through envelope—opening a new revenue mechanism (behind-the-meter load support) but also a new operational constraint.

ai_summary: PJM Planning Committee received an informational update on the Storage As Transmission Asset (SATA) combined package, clarifying how SATA will be analyzed in Market Efficiency submissions and studied through the RTEP process. Phase 2 of the SATA work, initiated in August 2025 in the Operating Committee, was moved to Markets and Reliability Committee in June 2026. The proposal treats SATA as transmission-only, not generation; SATA does not participate in PJM markets, carries no capacity value, and operates automatically to mitigate identified RTEP violations. Operations include automatic discharge for designed mitigation, coordinated charging by asset owner to maintain state of charge, revenue-grade metering, and cost recovery through Transmission Enhancement Credits per Schedule 12. Planning design components address charge/discharge sensitivity, sizing and timing, seasonal modeling (summer/winter/light load), no-harm testing, facility lifespan, operational modes, and cost-benefit analysis under FERC Order 1000 market-efficiency criteria. The timeline shows MRC review and first read in September 2026, endorsement by October–November 2026, and FERC submission of conforming language thereafter.

The key precedent is the exclusion from market participation and capacity value, and the cost-of-service recovery mechanism tied to Transmission Enhancement Credits — PSH owners should monitor whether this framework later becomes the basis for competitive transmission-planning bids against conventional wires, and whether pumped storage could participate in such a model or would be barred by existing market-participation rules.

ai_summary: PJM Manual 12 Revision 58 (effective December 1, 2026) restructures the Regulation ancillary service into two separate market products: Regulation-Up (RegUp) and Regulation-Down (RegDn). The revision modifies Sections 3.1, 3.2, 4.3, and 4.4 to accommodate this split, including changes to regulation assignment, qualification testing procedures, and performance-score calculation methodology. All resources providing Regulation must now certify separately per product (RegUp or RegDn), achieving two consecutive test scores of 75 percent or better per product. The Performance Score Calculation Engine (PSCE) evaluates compliance on a rolling 200-interval (30-minute) historical performance basis, with disqualification occurring when performance falls below 40 percent per product. Resources that have not met the 40-percent threshold will be notified by PJM and blocked from offering, but may re-qualify by scheduling and passing a new certification test. Regulation qualification testing may be self-administered (up to three per day per resource) or PJM-administered (one per day per resource), with tests evaluated against the PJM RTO Regulation Market Obligations specified in Section 4.3.1.

ai_summary: PJM Interconnection Process Subcommittee meeting (24 August 2026) on the two interconnection service types defined under FERC Order 2003: Energy Resource Interconnection Service (ERIS) and Network Resource Interconnection Service (NRIS). PJM maps NRIS to its "Capacity Resource" designation and ERIS to its "Energy Resource" designation. Capacity Resources are eligible for the energy market (with must-offer requirement) and the Reliability Pricing Model (RPM) capacity market, receive Capacity Interconnection Rights (CIRs), and feed into resource-adequacy calculations (Reserve Requirement Study and Effective Load Carrying Capability). Energy Resources are eligible for the energy market (without must-offer) and marked "as available," do not receive CIRs, and do not count toward resource adequacy. Both undergo reliability studies (short circuit, stability, affected-systems assessments); the key distinction is that Capacity Resources face a Generator Deliverability Test (aggregated with other generation) while Energy Resources face only an Individual Plant Deliverability (IPD) Test, resulting in potentially lower network-upgrade requirements for Energy Resources. Developers elect the service type at application. No action items or votes are noted in the material.
hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage directly. However, this PJM educational presentation codifies the eligibility gates that determine whether a generating facility — including new hydro or PSH interconnection requests — qualifies as a Capacity Resource for RPM accreditation and resource-adequacy input, or as an Energy Resource without those revenue streams. Most conventional hydropower would be economic only as a Capacity Resource (full deliverability, capacity-market eligibility, must-offer requirement); most run-of-river or variable hydro might seek Energy Resource status to avoid must-offer. The IPD Test carve-out for Energy Resources could reduce network-upgrade costs and study burden, making that election strategically valuable. Seasonal maximum net energy capability testing (mentioned for the IPD Test) is relevant to seasonal hydro availability patterns. The document establishes the framework; a hydro developer weighing interconnection applications would need to understand which election maximizes revenue net of must-offer penalties and grid-upgrade costs.

ai_summary: PJM is transitioning its Interim Deliverability Study methodology from a serial study approach to a cluster-based approach beginning with the 2027/2028 Delivery Year. The proposed change to Manual 14-H Section 4.10.1.3 divides IDS applicants into two subclusters: Subcluster 1 includes projects provisionally operational from prior years, and Subcluster 2 includes all other eligible projects. PJM allocates deliverable capacity first to Subcluster 1, then to Subcluster 2, both using proportional allocation based on each project's MW impact and distribution factor. The methodology is designed to provide operational continuity for provisionally operational resources, reduce project-developer risk of curtailment after prior deliverability determinations, and improve alignment with capacity-market must-offer rules. The application window for 2027/28 IDS closed on June 30, 2026, and PJM must complete the study by October 30, 2026. The Markets and Reliability Committee held a first read and voting on August 19, 2026, with additional approvals expected at PC first read on July 7, 2026, and PC second read and voting on August 4, 2026.

The shift from serial to cluster-based allocation protects projects that have already achieved provisional operation from losing that status in favor of newly submitted projects competing for the same transmission headroom. For run-of-river and variable hydro seeking provisional capacity accreditation, and for pumped-storage plants in queue, this methodology's commitment to operational continuity for provisionally operational resources reduces the risk of being curtailed after IDS approval, which in turn supports their ability to obtain must-offer capacity obligations and plan revenue. initiatives: Fuel Cost Policy Clarifications for Affiliated Fuel Suppliers [awaiting senior committee approval]
ai_summary: PJM's revised Manual 15 Section 2.2 establishes fuel-cost-policy submission and review procedures for market sellers. Market Sellers must submit PJM-approved Fuel Cost Policies consistent with fuel type; regulation-only resources are exempt. The Market Monitoring Unit has an initial 10 business days to review, with an additional 5 business days per revision; PJM then has 20 business days to review, with an additional 5 business days or an agreed date per revision. All approved policies take effect the next operating day following approval or a later date set by PJM. Policies may be immediately expired by PJM if circumstances make them inconsistent with governing documents; market sellers receive a 3-business-day rebuttal period and, if their rebuttal succeeds, receive uplift payment for the period of expiration. The temporary cost-offer methodology serves as a fallback for new resources, transferred resources, or resources whose policies have expired, using index settle prices multiplied by heat input curves. Market sellers must review and document fuel costs in MIRA at least monthly (12 times per year) and within 40 days of the preceding review; fuel-cost calculation methods may be updated no more than once every 12 months unless required by regulatory change. Cost-based offers may not include unauthorized gas-pipeline penalties or gas-balancing charges from ratable take; however, tariff-based gas-storage, park, and loan charges are permitted once incurred. Market sellers using affiliated fuel suppliers must employ transparent and verifiable methodologies based on independent third-party or publicly available market data. Total Fuel Related Cost includes fuel costs, emission allowance costs, maintenance cost, and operating cost. Units receiving Renewable Energy Credits (RECs) and/or Production Tax Credits (PTCs) that submit non-zero cost-based offers must identify how RECs and/or PTCs are accounted for in the Fuel Cost Policy.
hydro_read_through: The document never mentions hydro, hydropower, or run-of-river generation; however, these fuel-cost-policy rules govern cost-based-offer development for all dispatchable generators in PJM, including conventional hydroelectric facilities. Hydro's revenue from energy markets depends entirely on the cost-offer floor set by these policies—the approved Fuel Cost Policy determines the minimum offer price at which a hydro plant can compete. The 12-month update cycle and monthly documentation requirements create compliance burdens for hydro operators; more significantly, the requirement to justify affiliate-fuel-supplier quotes and the prohibition on certain pass-through charges (gas penalties, balancing charges) establish the data-transparency framework PJM uses to police opportunity-cost offers from use-limited resources, which is the mechanism most directly affecting hydro's ability to recover scarcity rents. The REC/PTC carve-out in Section 2.2.2 is especially relevant: hydro plants in regions with clean-energy credits or production incentives must now explicitly declare how those credits reduce their fuel-cost offer, potentially capping the cost-based offer below the true marginal cost of generation. The rebuttal and uplift process (Section 2.2.1.2(e)) offers a safety valve if PJM overreaches in expiring a policy, but hydro operators face the operational risk of zero-offer constraints during policy disputes.

initiatives: Reserve Certainty and Resource Flexibility Incentives [solution alternatives proposed]
ai_summary: The Independent Market Monitor (IMM) presented a counter-proposal to PJM's Reserve and Shortage Task Force (RCSTF) recommendation to the Markets and Reliability Committee on 2026-08-19. PJM proposes to increase Operating Reserve Demand Curve (ORDC) prices to $2,100 per MW maximum (vs. current $850–$1,750) and introduce new reserve products and locational reserve requirements to address net-load uncertainty from variable renewable generation and load-forecast error. The IMM argues that PJM's proposal goes beyond addressing operational needs and intentionally raises shortage-pricing levels to increase generation revenues, and proposes instead to maintain the status-quo energy and reserve market design with day-ahead reserves matching real-time requirements, unchanged ORDC levels, performance-based penalties (rather than higher reserve requirements), and subzone locational reserves instead of constraint-specific ones. The IMM analysis shows transmission constraint penalty factors (TCPFs) have become the second-largest LMP component, accounting for $5.97 billion in January–June 2026 load costs (vs. ORDC shortage pricing at $269 million over the same period). PJM's proposal would also restrict all 10-minute reserves to online-only resources and eliminate the offline 10-minute NSR product, whereas the IMM proposal permits offline reserves. No vote or decision date is stated; the presentation is informational to the MRC.
hydro_read_through: The document does not name hydroelectric or pumped-storage resources; it addresses reserve market and energy-price design affecting all dispatchable generators. However, the competing proposals directly shape how hydro plants are compensated for flexibility and reserve provision. PJM's proposal to raise ORDC shortage-pricing levels and require more online-only reserves would increase revenue opportunity during tight periods but imposes higher production costs on fast-start resources (hydro's typical mode). The IMM counter-proposal to freeze ORDC levels and permit offline reserves reduces the revenue uplift but lowers operating costs. The sharp rise in TCPF-driven LMP components (10% increase in 2026 vs. 2025) indicates transmission scarcity is now the primary shortage signal; a hydro owner needs to understand whether PJM's proposed constraint-specific reserve requirements or the IMM's subzone model better preserves hydro's ability to arbitrage locational scarcity and serve transmission-constrained areas.

initiatives: Reserve Certainty and Resource Flexibility Incentives [solution alternatives proposed]
ai_summary: PJM's Reserve Certainty Senior Task Force (RCSTF) proposes comprehensive reforms to reserve markets approved at first read on August 19, 2026, with MRC vote scheduled for September 24, 2026 and Market Committee vote on November 18, 2026. The PJM package (receiving 66% support and 77% support over status quo) introduces new reserve products including 10-minute and 30-minute Ramp and Uncertainty Reserves (RUR), Day-Ahead Scheduling Reserves, and Energy Gap Reserves, alongside updates to reserve offer rules, non-performance consequences, and cost allocation, and shifts from sub-zonal to nodal reserve procurement. Resources must be online and dispatchable to provide RUR products within specified response times (10 or 30 minutes); soft offer caps are set at $10/MWh for day-ahead markets. ORDC changes include a single-step Synchronized Reserve ORDC at $2,100/MWh and Synchronized Reserve performance factor of 1.2 currently. Energy Gap Reserves would be procured on medium- and high-risk winter days (estimated 3–10 days annually) based on the 90th percentile shortfall in physical supply relative to load forecast. The proposal incorporates reserve nesting where multiple products contribute to meeting a single requirement.
hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydroelectric or pumped-storage resources explicitly; however, the RCSTF proposal directly affects conventional hydroelectric and PSH operators because they are among the primary dispatchable resources that PJM relies on to provide reserve products. The introduction of new ramp and uncertainty products with defined uncertainty percentages (0.4–0.6% load, 1.9–2.7% wind, 3.1–4.0% solar) and soft offer caps at $10/MWh increases the menu of products hydro owners can offer while also constraining the prices they can submit, affecting revenue realization from flexibility services that hydro is uniquely positioned to supply. The shift to nodal procurement and the unnesting of reserve services to recognize energy-endurance needs creates both opportunity—allowing energy-limited resources to signal their true scarcity cost—and risk: hydro owners will face new locational and nesting constraints that change how their reserve capacity translates to revenue, especially in periods when energy availability is constrained.

ai_summary: PJM Manual 18 Revision 63 (effective 09/01/2026) updates the PJM Capacity Market operational rules, including Variable Resource Requirement (VRR) curve parameters, resource performance assessments, and penalty structures. The revisions to AUCAP derate penalties and performance assessment rules directly affect hydro revenue stability if availability falls short of accredited levels. Pumped-storage facilities, if participating as generation resources, face the same framework; no distinct storage participation model is visible in this excerpt, suggesting PSH would follow generation rules rather than a dedicated storage pathway.

ai_summary: PJM Regulation Redesign Phase 2, approved by FERC on June 14, 2024, splits the single-signal bidirectional Regulation product into two separate products—RegUp and RegDn—each with distinct requirements, offers, clearing prices, and settlements, effective December 1, 2026. Key changes include bifurcated performance metrics and clearing-price credits (both capability and mileage components) by product type; separate opportunity-cost calculation for RegUp and RegDn, with a single intra-commitment opportunity cost accounting for both assignments and 'Regulation signal bias' (energy produced while providing regulation); and new MSRS settlement reports including a dedicated 'Regulation Hydro Opportunity Cost Details' report for hydro units. The settlement changes take effect December 1, 2026, with the first billing statement issued January 8, 2027, following sandbox testing in August–September 2026 and education sessions in October–November 2026.
hydro_read_through: Hydro operators in PJM depend on regulation revenue, which is highly sensitive to how opportunity costs are calculated and whether deployment actually compensates them for forgone energy sales. Phase 2's bifurcation of RegUp and RegDn signals means hydro must now offer separately for each direction and will be paid separate clearing prices and opportunity-cost credits for each, potentially improving precision in compensation but requiring operational and bidding-system changes. The explicit treatment of 'Regulation signal bias' in opportunity-cost settlement is significant for hydro because it recognizes that regulation activity produces or consumes energy incidentally—a design nuance that directly affects how much uplift hydro receives when it isn't compensated by the clearing prices alone.

PJM's presentation documents the event sequence, protection operation, voltage and frequency response, and generator behavior during recovery. NERC Project 2026-02 is developing reliability standards for large computational loads (defined as on-site data centers and similar facilities ≥50 MW at ≥100 kV) to establish interconnection requirements, modeling data standards, and minimum voltage and frequency disturbance-performance requirements. Currently, Attachment D prescribes 11:00 AM EPT the next business day for Market Sellers to submit exception requests with supporting documentation when offers fail Markets Gateway validation. This touches hydro and pumped-storage operators directly: when water availability or dispatch constraints create genuine economic scarcity, both must justify offers above $1,000/MWh through documented cost or opportunity-cost cases, and tight submission deadlines during multi-day events can prevent recovery of legitimate incremental costs. The outcome of this charge will determine whether that recovery pathway remains viable during resource-constrained periods.

title: Item 04 1 – Hybrid Resources Market Model Selection – Problem Statement
relevance_reason: MECHANISM: Hybrid resources market-model rules directly affect how pumped-storage and co-located hydro+storage systems can participate in capacity and energy markets; the problem statement identifies that current PJM rules requiring unified classification across capacity, energy, and ancillary-services markets prevent SIS (Surplus Interconnection Service) projects—including battery-added hydro facilities—from obtaining capacity accreditation, which limits the revenue pathway for storage additions at existing hydro POIs and constrains a strategic tool for new capacity deployment.
ai_summary: PJM's existing rule requires Mixed Technology Facilities (MTFs) that participate in the capacity market as a Hybrid Resource to also operate as hybrids in energy and ancillary-services markets, creating operational and settlement complexity. The issue is particularly acute for Surplus Interconnection Service (SIS) projects—e.g., a battery added to an existing solar facility—which cannot obtain their own capacity interconnection rights (CIRs) and must become hybrids to leverage the host resource's CIRs and gain UCAP. PJM staff are flagging this as an impediment to capacity deployment and seeking stakeholder input on whether MTFs should be permitted to maintain one classification for capacity while using separate units in energy and ancillary services, consistent with how non-hybrid resources are treated. This directly affects pumped-storage and hydro owners considering co-location or additions via SIS, who currently face hybrid-operation mandates that may be technically infeasible or economically unviable when storage has separate offtakers or operational constraints.

title: Item 04 2 – Hybrid Resources Market Model Selection – Issue Charge
relevance_reason: Hybrid-resource market participation rules for mixed-technology facilities, especially pumped storage co-located with conventional hydro via Surplus Interconnection Service, directly affect PSH revenue accreditation in capacity and energy markets and the operational flexibility PSH can offer.
ai_summary: PJM staff is opening a work item to decouple how hybrid resources (mixed-technology facilities) are modeled in the capacity market from how they must operate in the energy and ancillary-services markets. Currently, a facility seeking capacity-market accreditation as a Hybrid Resource must also operate as a single hybrid unit in energy and AS markets, even when its components (e.g., pumped storage + conventional hydro) have different offtakers or could operate independently. This constraint is particularly binding for projects using Surplus Interconnection Service (SIS), which lack their own capacity interconnection rights and must be modeled as hybrids to obtain UCAP; once hybrid in RPM, they lose the option to bid energy and AS as separate units. The work will examine whether facilities can receive capacity accreditation as hybrids while electing to bid energy and AS as independent units, and map the downstream settlement, must-offer, and performance-assessment implications. Decision timeline is consensus-based on a single proposal, expected monthly work, priority level medium, starting August 2026. This proposal directly affects PSH owners considering co-location with conventional hydro under SIS and those seeking to optimize capacity accreditation without sacrificing energy-market dispatch flexibility.

stakeholders: Monitoring Analytics, LLC (Monitoring Analytics (Independent Market Monitor for PJM))
ai_summary: PJM proposes a transparent 'Advanced Scheduling' process for committing coal, gas, and other thermal units 1–2 days before the day-ahead market to mitigate winter performance risk—a practice PJM has expanded post-Winter Storm Elliott. The proposal requires units self-identified as 'at risk' (cold-weather, gas-procurement) to submit 'Indicative Offers' before the day-ahead deadline; PJM then evaluates which units to commit economically based on a multi-day minimization tool. Committed units' uplift is capped at the lesser of the Indicative Offer and final offer, and all uplift is allocated as reliability charges. Operating parameters allow committed units to set economic minimum to their advanced-scheduling MW level. The mechanism directly competes with hydro's natural slot as a dispatchable, lower-cost alternative to pre-committed thermal capacity, and the Indicative-Offer requirement (mandatory for self-identified at-risk units) mirrors offer-control rules that constrain use-limited resources. Pumped-storage and conventional hydro operators should monitor how PJM's risk-assessment criteria classify units and how the reliability-charge allocation burden (vs. energy-market-based cost recovery) affects the economics of flexible hydro participation. No comment deadline or vote date is stated in this proposal document.

title: Item 07 1 – PJM Energy Storage Resource Model Enhancements – Market Based Battery Operations – Brattle Group
relevance_reason: MECHANISM: Market power mitigation rules for energy storage directly affect pumped-storage hydro's offer-pricing rights and real-time dispatch economics — the document analyzes how PJM's cost-based mitigation and offer-lock rules suppress opportunity-cost offers and cause inefficient discharge timing, a problem that applies equally to PSH as to batteries under PJM's offer-driven ESR model.
initiatives: PJM Energy Storage Resource Model Enhancements [evaluation in progress]
ai_summary: Brattle Group presents PJM staff analysis of market-power mitigation (MPM) rules applied to battery energy storage, arguing that conventional fuel-based mitigation caps—designed for fossil generators—are poorly fitted to storage resources and cause two problems: (1) capping mitigated offers below inter-hour opportunity cost causes early, inefficient discharge and misallocates stored energy away from peak-scarcity hours, reducing reliability; (2) PJM's t-65-minute offer-price lock prevents sellers from updating offers as conditions change, locking in discharge decisions that become counterproductive when actual prices spike (illustrated by Winter Storm Elliott case study showing 42% of battery SOC misallocated). The document is preparing PJM Markets Implementation for a policy decision on whether to revise MPM and offer-timing rules to allow storage sellers to include opportunity costs in competitive offers and to permit real-time offer updates before dispatch. This affects pumped-storage hydro owners in PJM because PSH operates under the same ESR participation model and would be subject to identical MPM caps and offer locks; relaxing these constraints would restore PSH's ability to manage state-of-charge optimally for scarcity value, while tightening them further would suppress PSH revenue from peak-hour energy and ancillary services.

ai_summary: PJM's 2026/27 Market Efficiency (ME) cycle studies 2031 transmission congestion across its footprint using PROMOD IV simulation. Preliminary 2031 base case was posted July 15, 2026, with stakeholder feedback solicited through September 2026; PJM will finalize the base case and congestion drivers by January–February 2027, open a proposal window February–May 2027, and complete board approval by October–December 2027. The study identifies $1M–$50M+ annual simulated congestion on 40+ constraints across COMED, AEP-served West, MAAC, DOM, and external M2M tie lines, including several COMED–MISO and PJM–MISO interfaces. Per Operating Agreement Schedule 6 section 1.5.7(b), PJM will compare accelerating existing RTEP reliability projects, modifying them to relieve economic congestion, or building new projects solely for congestion relief—a process that can reprioritize transmission investment based on economic benefits. Hydro owners relying on eastbound or interregional export paths—particularly in the Carolinas (DOM), Virginia (COMED-adjacent), and MAAC regions with identified >$50M annual congestion—face the prospect of either relief via accelerated or modified projects (which could lower congestion rents) or delayed relief if no economic case is found, affecting scarcity pricing during high-value periods.

ai_summary: PJM is proposing to establish a defined process allowing projects with completed interconnection studies and Capacity Injection Rights (CIRs) to change fuel type—such as from solar to storage—while retaining those CIRs, provided the change does not materially impact the transmission system. The rationale addresses PJM's capacity shortfalls, the accumulation of "stranded CIRs" at studied sites that are no longer being developed, and inefficiencies from duplicative restudies when market demand shifts. The proposal is framed as interconnection policy design and system planning efficiency, falling within the Planning Committee's scope. Other RTOs/ISOs have implemented similar fuel-change review processes through FERC-approved material modification frameworks; PJM would evaluate potential tariff or manual revisions to establish its own procedure.

However, a fuel-switching rule that preserves interconnection positions and avoids re-study work affects all resources in the queue, including hydro and PSH developers. If PJM adopts a flexible fuel-change process that treats storage (including PSH) changes as non-material under certain conditions, or if it allows existing solar or wind positions to convert to storage without losing queuing priority or requiring full restudy, that would lower the barriers to PSH development at already-studied sites and could shift the strategic calculus for choosing between resource types given the same transmission infrastructure. Conversely, if the rule narrows (e.g., storage-to-non-storage changes are deemed material), it could lock in resource mixes that were planned years earlier and reduce flexibility for existing hydro or PSH projects considering upgrades or re-dispatch strategies.

ai_summary: PJM Manual 21b (Revision 06, effective 06/24/2026) defines ELCC Classes and procedures for determining Accredited UCAP and capacity accreditation. The manual explicitly establishes two hydropower classes: Intermittent Hydropower Class for run-of-river generators that cannot appreciably store water, and Hydropower With Non-Pumped Storage Class for facilities that can capture and store incoming flow with material control. Material control is demonstrated by evaluation of whether the resource can consistently produce power equal to or in excess of 110% of the daily average power baseline for at least 4 hours, assessed once per five years using the ratio of average output during the 4 highest load hours of summer afternoons versus all other hours over a five-year period. An existing Hydropower with Non-Pumped Storage resource that fails this evaluation will be reclassified as Intermittent Hydropower, unless PJM exercises discretion to retain the prior classification due to exceptional circumstances including recreational and public safety factors, unit outages, market prices, or ancillary-market participation. Capacity Storage Resource Classes include pumped-storage resources characterized by 4-, 6-, 8-, and 10-hour durations, defined by the ratio of modeled MWh energy-storage capability to modeled MW power capability. Testing requirements apply to hydro resources: Hydro with Non-Pumped Storage units must complete one (1) contiguous hour capability verification tests for summer and winter periods, with deadlines of September 20th and March 20th respectively. Data submission for hydro resources must include complete time series from June 1, 2012 through most recent May 31 unless previously submitted and unchanged.
hydro_read_through: This manual is the foundational capacity-market accreditation document for PJM hydro owners. The Intermittent Hydropower versus Hydropower With Non-Pumped Storage distinction directly determines ELCC Class placement and thus seasonal capacity revenue: storage-capable plants can claim higher ELCC factors through the controlled-output standard, while run-of-river plants are trapped in the lower-value Intermittent class. The five-year evaluation cycle and PJM's discretion to override a failed demonstration based on market participation or operational factors creates ongoing compliance risk and opportunity — owners of marginal plants must monitor their seasonal output ratios closely and may argue exceptional circumstances to avoid reclassification. Pumped-storage accreditation by duration class (4/6/8/10-hour) makes state-of-charge management and energy-balance assumptions critical to ELCC value; the manual does not here address charging-energy treatment or AS-stacking rules, which remain open in PJM's separate storage-participation framework. Testing obligations (annual summer/winter verification by September 20th and March 20th deadlines) are compliance-critical for all capacity resources and particularly onerous for multi-unit plants subject to simultaneous testing coordination.

initiatives: Enhancements to the Cluster-Based Interim Deliverability Study Methodology [awaiting senior committee approval]
ai_summary: PJM is revising Manual 14-H Section 4.10.1.3 to transition from a serial study approach to a cluster-based Interim Deliverability Study methodology, effective for the 2027/2028 Delivery Year. Under the new approach, IDS requests are grouped into two subclusters: Subcluster 1 (projects already provisionally operational from prior Delivery Years) receives priority allocation of deliverable capacity and energy, with remaining capacity allocated to Subcluster 2 (all other eligible projects). The methodology uses proportional allocation based on project MW impact and distribution factor (DFAX). The Planning Committee will hold first read on August 4, 2026, second read and voting in September 2026, and the MRC will conduct first read and voting on August 19, 2026, with IDS results due October 30, 2026. PJM states the proposal is intended to reduce project developer risk from curtailment or cessation of generation after provisional operation and to ensure operational continuity and Capacity Market alignment.
hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage directly. However, IDS methodology is the mechanism determining whether generation projects—including hydro and PSH facilities—can deliver capacity and energy reliably before permanent network upgrades are complete, and whether they retain provisional capacity rights year-to-year. The cluster-based change prioritizes continuity for already-operational projects in the allocation queue, which would favor a provisionally operational hydro or PSH project in subsequent IDS determinations over new entrants competing for the same flowgate headroom. This affects both revenue certainty (capacity rights carry must-offer obligations in subsequent capacity auctions) and operational flexibility (projects deemed deliverable obtain protection against cessation-of-generation risk).

initiatives: Critical Issue Fast Path (CIFP) - Reliability Backstop Procurement [awaiting implementation & ferc approval]
ai_summary: PJM's Board has approved a two-path Reliability Backstop Procurement (RBP) mechanism to address a megawatt shortfall in the 2028/2029 Base Residual Auction, combining a central procurement administered by PJM and a facilitated bilateral matchmaking process. The RBP will procure long-term capacity-only UCAP commitments for a fixed 15-year term from 2028/2029 DY to 2042/2043 DY, structured as pay-as-bid offers in $/MW-day with a maximum willingness-to-pay cap of $555/MW-day UCAP (Point 1 of the unconstrained 2028/2029 BRA VRR Curve). Eligible supply is defined as "new" resources—those bringing new ICAP, new MFO, or transferred CIRs from deactivated resources, with an online date no later than June 1, 2032—and includes new annual Demand Response and DER. Resources with RBP commitments become PJM capacity resources subject to a mandatory RPM Must-Offer Obligation at $0 (price taker) and are settled as contracts for differences against weighted-average RPM clearing prices. The central procurement window runs September 30 to October 21, 2026, with selection and results October 22 to December 2, 2026. Resources face a 20% shortfall-charge rate (based on RBP commitment price) if delayed or failing to come online, with a 3-year delay threshold triggering commitment rescission. Cost allocation is pro rata by zone/area based on load-growth megawatts, and resources must post collateral equal to 0.2 × (RBP Sell Offer Price × committed UCAP × 365 × 3 years). The framework includes provisions for Transmission Owner exit scenarios and default allocation among LSEs.
hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower, pumped storage, or run-of-river resources. However, the RBP directly affects all capacity resources in PJM, including conventional hydro and PSH facilities, in several material ways: (1) the 15-year fixed commitment structure and $0 must-offer obligation fundamentally change the revenue-stacking and bidding flexibility that hydro owners use to optimize across RPM and energy markets, constraining how seasonal and intra-year dispatch strategies interact with capacity pricing; (2) the "new" resource eligibility rule—requiring online date by June 1, 2032, and excluding resources already holding RPM commitments—determines which existing hydro and PSH plants can participate, creating a cliff for resources without RBP coverage; (3) the settlement as a CfD against weighted-average RPM clearing prices rather than energy-market or hybrid-contract structures shifts risk allocation and may reduce revenue capture for flexible resources whose value depends on being held offline for scarcity events. Hydro and PSH owners operating in PJM need to understand whether their existing plants qualify as "new," what the mandatory $0 offer means for their forward contracting, and how the long-duration commitment interacts with their water-management and transmission constraints.

initiatives: Implementation of Connect and Manage Framework for Large Load Interconnections [solution alternatives proposed]
ai_summary: PJM proposes the Interim Resource Adequacy Service (IRAS), a framework to manage capacity shortages by requiring new Large Loads (≥50 MW at a single site) that do not 'Bring Your Own New Capacity' (BYONC) or have not received Reliability Backstop Procurement credit to reduce load during periods when PJM clears short of its Reliability Requirement. Large Loads must register by March 1, 2027 (existing) and before in-service date (new loads); PJM will maintain a registry and allocate Interim Resource Adequacy Service obligations by zone/area. When triggered, Interim Resource Adequacy Service load reduction will occur before Pre-Emergency Load Management actions. Loads subject to Interim Resource Adequacy Service will receive compensation at the Non-Performance Assessment Interval rate (50% of the existing Performance Assessment Interval rate, approved by FERC on June 26, 2026). BYONC-eligible supply includes new generation, uprates, surplus interconnection, and fuel-switching; Demand Response and Distributed Energy Resources are also eligible. New Large Loads incremental to the 2028/2029 BRA forecast will be excluded from future RPM auctions (starting 2029/2030) unless new supply sufficient to cover them clears an RPM auction. The Board integrated this proposal from stakeholder feedback; tariff language is being prepared for FERC submission.
hydro_read_through: This document does not mention hydro or pumped storage. However, the framework directly affects the competitive environment for all conventional generation: by allowing large new loads to interconnect without self-supplied capacity (subject to mandatory curtailment in shortage), PJM narrows the market-clearing price signal that would otherwise reward existing generation during tight periods. Hydro owners will see the scarcity premium dampened during events when Interim Resource Adequacy Service loads are curtailed instead of being served by costly-to-operate backup units. The framework also changes the dispatch rules—hydro will be dispatched normally in day-ahead and real-time markets, but it will not be exempt from system needs during Interim Resource Adequacy Service events, meaning its revenue during such events is exposed to a new form of involuntary dispatch constraint. Conversely, if Interim Resource Adequacy Service prevents deeper energy-market scarcity, hydro's expected energy prices will be lower than they would be under a regime that allowed all new load to clear at any price.

ai_summary: PJM Manual M14D Revision 71 clarifies voltage and reactive-power control requirements for generators 20 MVA and above, establishing that only automatic voltage control mode (AVR controlling voltage) is acceptable without documented exception. The revision defines volt-var boundaries at ±32.87% of maximum MW output, specifies acceptable reactive-control range per MW output, and requires PJM approval for any deviation from automatic voltage mode. A three-party investigation process is established for reactive-control performance issues. The changes respond to NERC's May 15, 2026 lowering of IBR registration thresholds to 20 MVA (bringing mid-sized inverter-based resources under Category 2 GO registration) and PJM's stated concern about increasing low-voltage risks, exemplified by the 2025 Spain blackout in which insufficient synchronous-generator voltage support contributed to a major outage.
hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage. However, conventional synchronous hydropower plants—especially large run-of-river and reservoir facilities—are among PJM's primary sources of dynamic voltage support and will be directly subject to these tightened automatic-voltage-control requirements and the new D-curve boundaries. Hydro owners operating in PJM must now ensure their AVR equipment is configured to automatic voltage mode unless they obtain explicit documented exemptions from both PJM and the transmission owner; plants already running in constant-MVAR or constant-power-factor mode will require engineering review and possible operational changes. The higher clarity on volt-var boundaries may also change how hydro operators bid reactive-power capability into PJM's voltage-schedule process, affecting both revenue opportunities and compliance risk if their equipment cannot meet the new boundaries.

ai_summary: PJM has implemented a new Expedited Interconnection Track (EIT) process as a parallel track to the standard interconnection queue for generators meeting three criteria: (1) written support from a Primary Siting Authority, (2) commercial operation within 36 months, and (3) at least 250 MW of Accredited UCAP. The EIT process compresses interconnection review into three phases—Application Review (~180 days), Study (~60 days), and Final Agreement Negotiation (~60 days)—operating outside but parallel to the PJM Cycle Adequacy Process to expedite state-sponsored generation projects. PJM filed EIT tariff revisions with FERC on April 9, 2026 (Docket No. ER26-1563) and submitted a Limited Effective Date Answer and Amendment on July 31, 2026. Manual 14H revisions to implement the EIT process were endorsed by the Planning Committee on June 24, 2026, and received first reading at the Markets and Reliability Committee on July 7, 2026, with final endorsement scheduled for July 28, 2026.
hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage. However, the 250 MW UCAP threshold and tight 36-month development timeline make the EIT track potentially accessible to larger run-of-river or peaking hydro plants and pumped-storage projects with state backing seeking to qualify for resource-adequacy accreditation faster than standard-queue timelines allow. The elimination of milestone-extension options (blocking the one-time postponement available in standard GIA processes) imposes stricter compliance discipline on expedited applicants, which would tighten capital and permitting schedules for hydro developers pursuing this path versus the standard process.

ai_summary: PJM GDECS (Governing Document Enhancements Cleanup Series) April 2026 package proposes seventeen tariff revisions to Attachment DD (Reliability Pricing Model), Operating Agreement, and interconnection procedures. Key changes: (1) Capacity Storage Resources and Intermittent Resources must now offer as annual (not seasonal) into RPM Auctions, with the categorical must-offer exception removed per FERC 190 FERC ¶ 61,117 (2025); (2) Commercial aggregation of these resources limited to those granted additional winter Capacity Interconnection Rights; (3) UCAP definition revised to align with effective load-carrying capability (ELCC) analysis per Schedule 9.2; (4) Planned Generation Capacity Resources that clear an RPM Auction become Existing Generation Capacity Resources for subsequent Incremental Auctions in the same Delivery Year; (5) Mixed-Technology Facility definitions clarified for participation as single ELCC Resource or multiple stand-alone resources, with five-year modeling election periods. hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped-storage facilities by name, but the revisions directly govern resource types to which hydro and PSH are subject or compete with. Removal of the must-offer categorical exception for Capacity Storage Resources and Intermittent Resources means PSH and conventional hydro's seasonal flexibility value faces heightened must-offer obligations for annual capacity commitments—affecting their auction bidding strategies and accreditation calculations. The ELCC-aligned UCAP definition will rebase how hydro's seasonal and peak-period capacity is accredited: owners will need to track effective load-carrying capability analysis rather than EFORd-based forced-outage rates, directly changing seasonal accreditation factors and thus capacity-market revenue. The aggregation limits and five-year modeling elections for mixed-technology facilities also matter if hydro co-locations with solar or battery storage are pursued. MOPR and Market Seller Offer Cap rules applying to DER aggregations set a pathway and precedent affecting how small hydro may participate in future Order 2222 aggregation pilots.

ai_summary: The Deactivation Enhancement (DESTF) Phase II Scope Status Report presents PJM's framework for managing generator deactivations. Phase II scope addresses three new areas: (1) procedures to evaluate grid-enhancing technologies, reconductoring, demand-side management, and energy storage as long-term transmission solutions to avoid Reliability Must-Run (RMR) contracts; (2) alternative solutions to RMR contracts including new generation assets, energy storage, demand-side solutions, transmission enhancements, generation-replacement proposals from deactivating generators (CIR transfers), and accelerated interconnection processing, with evaluation frameworks comparing costs and benefits across resource types; and (3) a pro forma RMR arrangement and capacity market rule updates for deactivating generators temporarily retained for reliability. Three proposals were developed for Scope Areas 4/5 (PJM, Coalition, and Independent Market Monitor), none achieving >50% support; for Scope Area 6 (pro forma RMR), PJM's proposal received >50% support and preference over status quo, and is offered for consideration at the June 24, 2026 Markets & Reliability Committee meeting.

However, Phase II addresses how PJM will treat deactivating generators facing reliability retention through RMR contracts and what alternatives to RMR exist—a critical issue for aging or economically stressed hydro plants. The framework's treatment of "new generation assets" and "energy storage" as alternatives to RMR, and PJM's obligation to evaluate competing solutions and their costs, will set precedent for whether retiring hydro can be replaced by storage, demand-side resources, or transmission upgrades, and what retention compensation would look like if a hydro asset is deemed necessary for reliability. ai_summary: PJM's redlined tariff amendment to Attachment DD, Section 5.3, modifies the treatment of Generation Capacity Resources committed through Reliability Must Run Service Agreements or transmission-retention rate schedules. Resources that do not clear the Base Residual Auction but meet specified criteria—including obligation to operate throughout the Delivery Year and FERC acceptance of the rate schedule at least three months prior to planning-parameter posting—are deemed to submit a Sell Offer at $0/MW-Day for their full Accredited UCAP (up to Capacity Interconnection Rights) in the Base Residual Auction. The amendment extends these provisions through the 2028/2029 Delivery Year (unless extended by the Office of Interconnection and accepted by FERC). Additional UCAP accruing after Base Residual Auction posting is deemed to clear at $0/MW-Day in the Third Incremental Auction; any shortfall is sought through the same auction. Capacity revenues from these resources are credited to the Transmission Owner or zones assigned financial responsibility for reliability upgrades associated with the resource's deactivation. This amendment was presented for first read at the June 24, 2026 Markets and Reliability Committee meeting.

However, the tariff change governs the capacity-market participation pathway for Generation Capacity Resources retained by transmission operators to address reliability—a category that includes synchronous conventional hydro and PSH units held for grid support. The revision establishes that such retained resources clear at $0/MW-Day (administratively set, not market-competitive), which locks out revenue through the auction mechanism and channels all capacity revenues to load in zones paying for transmission upgrades rather than to the resource owner. For a hydro or PSH facility retained under a transmission-reliability rate schedule, this means capacity-market revenue flows are predetermined and administratively controlled, not responsive to scarcity or demand-curve clearing. The through-2028/2029 sunset also creates scheduling risk for post-2029 operations if the provision is not extended.

The pro forma specifies that PJM shall not be required to call an emergency to dispatch the RMR resource, that generation owners must offer unavailable resources into markets using "Unavailable" status, that RMR resources are excluded from Reliability Pricing Model Auctions during the term, and that termination by generation owner is permitted only upon Catastrophic Force Majeure or PJM's failure to approve necessary Project Investment. The RMR term ends on the "[Enter the Anticipated In-Service Date of Transmission Upgrades]" or the conclusion of the delivery year in which the resource is administratively included in an RPM auction, whichever is later. The document does not identify the authors or PJM contacts; signature and designation blocks remain template placeholders.
hydro_read_through: While the document does not name hydropower or pumped storage, the RMR agreement applies to any generation resource—including hydro and PSH units—that PJM designates as necessary for transmission reliability. A hydro or PSH owner under RMR faces a choice between accepting the Deactivation Avoidable Cost Credit (a fixed PJM-defined mechanism) or undertaking a cost-of-service rate filing to recover avoided costs; the agreement's restrictions on market offerings (forced "Unavailable" status, exclusion from RPM auctions, obligation to run when dispatched regardless of market price) and its affirmative requirement to invest in "Project Investment" (repairs, replacements, regulatory-compliance work, and maintenance) mean that an RMR-designated hydro plant's revenue and operational flexibility are materially constrained by this tariff structure. The mechanics shown here—particularly the net-revenue crediting rule in Section 5.0, which offsets any energy and ancillary-services sales against RMR compensation—and the 61-day termination notice period establish the financial and operational framework RMR plants must navigate.

ai_summary: PJM presented revised tariff language for Part V (Generation Deactivation) at the 2026-07-28 Markets and Reliability Committee meeting. The Office of the Interconnection shall post preliminary estimates by 150 days prior to each auction's offer period. For combustion turbines and combined-cycle resources, PJM applies the same BLS Composite Index used for the Variable Resource Requirement Curve CONE adjustment; for all other resource types including solar, wind, and storage, a different BLS Producer Price Index component (Final Demand, Goods Less Food & Energy, Private Capital Equipment) is used. The adjusted gross costs are then modified by a factor of 1.022 for nuclear, coal, combustion turbine, and combined-cycle resources or 1.01 for solar, wind, and storage resource types to reflect annual changes in bonus depreciation under federal corporate tax law. ai_summary: PJM is revising Manual 14H to adopt IEEE 2800-2022 interconnection requirements for inverter-based resources (IBRs) in Phase 1, covering definitions, ride-through specifications, and primary frequency response parameters. The revision creates new Section 9.15 and Attachment K, effective June 22, 2027, and applies to IBRs interconnecting with transmission and sub-transmission systems. Key technical parameters include enter-service voltage thresholds (0.9–1.05 p.u.), frequency ranges (58.8–60.12 Hz), and voltage ride-through times ranging from 0.16 to 1800 seconds depending on voltage magnitude; frequency disturbance ride-through requirements exclude fast frequency response. PJM Markets and Reliability Committee is scheduled for first read July 28, 2026, with Planning Committee first read May 8, 2026 and endorsement votes on June 2 and August 19, 2026.
hydro_read_through: The document does not mention conventional hydropower or pumped-storage resources. However, the ride-through and frequency-response standards being adopted apply to the general category of synchronous and grid-forming resources interconnecting at the transmission level, which includes conventional hydro units. Hydro owners in PJM would need to assess whether existing units meet the mandated voltage and frequency ride-through envelope (particularly the 0.16–0.32 second ride-through times at very low voltages) and the primary frequency response droops and deadbands; units falling short could face retrofit costs or operational restrictions. The June 22, 2027 effective date would establish new technical requirements for any plant modifications or uprates proposed by that deadline.

ai_summary: PJM Manual 18 Revision 63 (effective September 1, 2026) updates the PJM Capacity Market operational procedures across multiple areas. Key changes include: periodic-review updates to the Variable Resource Requirement curve parameters and cost-of-new-entry (CONE) methodology for delivery years 2025/2026 through 2028/2029; new penalty frameworks for capacity-resource derates caused by reductions in accredited AUCAP (Accredited Unforced Capacity) factors; billing and credit-requirement changes for bilateral transactions; revisions to accommodate forecast-load adjustments through RPM and Fixed Resource Requirement processes; and updates to generation-resource classification (existing vs. planned), must-offer-exception administration, and aggregate-resource rules including seasonal capacity performance and DER-aggregation compliance. The manual addresses resource-performance assessments, settlement-charge calculations, load obligations, and locational reliability charges. The redline document reflects conforming changes and clarifications to existing tariff filings (ER26-455-000, ER25-783-000, ER25-2002, ER24-2447-003, ER26-980) that are in compliance phases with FERC.

However, Manual 18 establishes the accreditation, capacity-pricing, and settlement rules that apply to all dispatchable and use-limited resources in PJM's capacity market. Conventional hydro and pumped-storage facilities are subject to the ELCC-based accreditation mechanics, VRR-curve-driven clearing prices, seasonal capacity performance rules, and non-performance penalties documented here—changes to AUCAP derating, forced-outage treatment, and aggregate-resource rules materially affect hydro's accredited capacity and capacity revenue. The shift in VRR-curve parameters and CONE methodology for 2026/2027 forward also directly resets the demand curve that determines hydro's capacity clearing price, making the specific curve equations and reference-resource ELCC divisors (sections 3.3–3.4) critical revenue drivers.

ai_summary: PJM Manual 21B Revision 06 (effective June 24, 2026) specifies the rules and procedures for determining generating capability and ELCC accreditation across all resource classes in the PJM capacity market. The manual defines two hydro-specific ELCC classes: Intermittent Hydropower Class (run-of-river resources that cannot appreciably store water) and Hydropower With Non-Pumped Storage (resources that can capture and store incoming streamflow and exert material control over output—demonstrated by producing at least 110% of daily average power baseline for 4 hours during the four highest load hours of summer afternoons over a five-year rolling period). Existing Hydropower With Non-Pumped Storage resources failing this evaluation may be reclassified as Intermittent Hydropower, though PJM may retain the prior classification for exceptional circumstances including "recreational and public safety factors, unit outages, locational market energy prices, ancillary market participation, and other exceptional operational factors or market factors." Testing requirements differ by class: Hydro with Non-Pumped Storage units must conduct one-hour contiguous capability verification tests (summer June 1–September 1, deadline September 20; winter December 1–March 1, deadline March 20), while Limited Duration Resources' test duration must equal their applicable ELCC Class characteristic duration. The manual also defines Hybrid Resource Classes (including combinations of storage with variable or unlimited resources) and Component DER frameworks for distributed energy resources, all subject to ELCC-based accreditation.
hydro_read_through: Hydro owners' capacity-market accreditation and seasonal revenue now turn critically on ELCC class assignment. The material-control test for conventional (non-pumped) storage hydro—requiring 110% of daily average output for 4 hours in the four highest summer load hours over five rolling years—creates a measurable but stringent threshold; failure triggers reclassification to intermittent status and a steep loss of accredited MW. PJM's discretion to retain prior classification for "exceptional circumstances" including ancillary-market participation and market-driven operational constraints opens a compliance and advocacy pathway, but the burden is on the owner to document and request relief. Testing deadlines (September 20 summer, March 20 winter) and single-hour duration for conventional hydro are tighter than multi-hour Limited Duration Resources, reflecting the traditional assumption that hydro can ramp quickly; owners must plan annual test coordination with PJM Dispatch. Hybrid resource rules now formally accommodate co-located storage and variable resources at a single point of interconnection, expanding options for hydro owners seeking to blend storage or renewable capacity into a single market-accredited asset—a significant strategic opening if ELCC accreditation for hybrids is favorable.

ai_summary: PJM Resource Adequacy Planning presented the 2029/30 BRA Installed Reserve Margin (IRM), Forecast Pool Requirement (FPR), and Effective Load Carrying Capability (ELCC) results to the Markets and Reliability Committee on July 28, 2026. Storage resources saw ELCC rating changes: 4-hr Storage declined from 59% to 57%, 6-hr Storage from 68% to 67%, 8-hr Storage from 71% to 69%, and 10-hr Storage from 78% to 77%, driven by higher winter risk share. Winter risk now dominates the seasonal adequacy picture—the LOLH winter share jumped from 60.5% to 77.4%—which systematically depresses accreditation for resources with weaker winter performance and benefits those that contribute in winter. Run-of-river (Hydro Intermittent) holds steady at 35%, but the compression in storage ratings and the widening winter-risk share signal a market tightening around seasonal scarcity where dispatchable hydro and pumped storage (if present) could gain strategic value, while variable hydro faces ongoing accreditation pressure in peak-risk hours.

ai_summary: PJM's Storage As Transmission Asset (SATA) Combined Package, developed over Phase 1 (2020–Planning Committee) and Phase 2 (August 2025–Operating Committee), prescribes design and operational rules for storage resources deployed to solve RTEP transmission violations. SATA assets operate automatically to discharge for intended violations and charge afterward (coordinated with PJM), use revenue-grade metering and telemetry matching energy-storage standards, operate at voltages studied in RTEP, and are excluded from the interconnection queue and PJM markets with no capacity value. Cost recovery occurs through Schedule 12 Transmission Enhancement Credits (TEC) in a separate sub-account. The combined Planning and Operations package moved to Markets and Reliability Committee in June 2026; MRC first read occurred in July 2026, with endorsement and FERC submission (conforming language changes) targeted for October–November 2026.

title: Item 01a – Ron Mcnamara Phd Presentation

ai_summary: Ron McNamara (First Principles Economics) presents a conceptual framework for PJM's capacity adequacy problem to the PRTMDW, arguing the root issue is inadequate investment, not market design per se. He emphasizes that restructured markets eliminated the guaranteed cost-recovery and stable counterparty that regulation provided, forcing capacity investment to compete as economic/commercial ventures bearing price, policy, and rule-change risks — a fundamentally different risk profile than pre-restructuring. McNamara recommends PJM adopt an agreed end-state vision (5–20 year horizon) against which all capacity proposals should be evaluated, with preferences for decentralized solutions and accelerated permitting/build timelines. The presentation does not propose specific rule changes but frames the investment-scarcity nexus as central to hydro's strategic positioning: in a market now "managing scarcity," the value of reliable, dispatchable generation (hydro's signature) rises, but only if the market and regulatory framework create stable revenue streams and counterparties for that capacity.

title: Item 01b – Revisiting Root Causes And Their Implications In Pjms Powering Reliability Through Market Design – Pa Oca Presentation

title: Item 04b – Bifurcated Capacity Market Under PJM Path A Option 2 – Michael Kurtz Presentation
